title: Signing a PDF without printing it, and what that signature is not
description:
The old routine for "sign and send this back" is print, sign with a pen, scan, email. For most everyday paperwork you can skip the printer. Before you do, it's worth knowing that "signing a PDF" means two very different things, because only one of them is something you can do with a picture of your signature.

Two things both called a signature

A visible mark. An image of your signature (drawn, typed in a script font, or photographed) placed on the page. It looks signed. To the file, it's just more page content, like a logo.

A digital signature. A certificate, a hash of the document's bytes, and a signature that a PDF reader can check. Acrobat and similar readers show these in a signature panel, and they tell you if the file changed after signing. Nothing about it depends on what the page looks like.

A landlord, a school, a club, or a colleague asking for "a signed copy" almost always means the first. If the instructions mention a digital signature certificate (DSC), a qualified or advanced electronic signature, or a specific signing platform, they mean the second. No image tool, command or script can turn a picture into that. You need a certificate from a provider or your organisation's signing service.

Built-in ways to place a visible mark

macOS Preview. Open the PDF, show the Markup toolbar, and use the Sign button. You can create a signature with the trackpad, the camera (hold your signature on paper up to it), or an iPhone, and Preview saves it for reuse. Click it to place it, then drag and resize.

Adobe Acrobat Reader (Windows and Mac). The free reader has a Fill & Sign tool. Add a signature there by typing, drawing, or choosing an image, then click where it goes.

Either way, keep the original file. Once the mark is saved into a copy, you can't cleanly take it back out.

Turning a photo of your signature into a clean PNG

If you'd rather use your real ink signature, sign a sheet of white paper, photograph it straight down in daylight, and crop roughly. The photo won't be white and black. Paper in a phone photo is light grey with a gradient, and that grey travels with the image.

This Pillow script turns everything darker than a cutoff into opaque black ink and everything else into transparent pixels, then trims the empty margin:

import sys
from PIL import Image, ImageOps

src, dst = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
cutoff = int(sys.argv[3]) if len(sys.argv) > 3 else 140   # 0-255, lower keeps less

gray = ImageOps.grayscale(Image.open(src))
# Ink becomes opaque black, paper becomes fully transparent.
alpha = gray.point(lambda v: 255 if v < cutoff else 0)
out = Image.new("RGBA", gray.size, (0, 0, 0, 0))
out.putalpha(alpha)
out = out.crop(alpha.getbbox())   # trim the empty margin
out.save(dst)
print(out.size)

python3 clean_signature.py signature-photo.jpg signature.png

On my test photo (900 x 360, grey paper getting lighter left to right, dark strokes) it produced a 766 x 178 RGBA PNG of 3,908 bytes. If faint parts of the stroke disappear, raise the cutoff. If paper texture or shadows show up as specks, lower it.

Stamping it onto a page from the command line

If you sign the same kind of document often, a script beats dragging things around. This one draws the PNG on a blank page of the same size with reportlab and lays that over the page you choose with pypdf (pip install pypdf reportlab):

import sys, io
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter
from reportlab.pdfgen import canvas

pdf_in, sig_png, pdf_out = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]
page_no = int(sys.argv[4])               # 1-based
x, y, width = map(float, sys.argv[5:8])  # points from bottom-left; 72 pt = 1 inch

reader = PdfReader(pdf_in)
writer = PdfWriter(clone_from=reader)
page = writer.pages[page_no - 1]
pw, ph = float(page.mediabox.width), float(page.mediabox.height)

# Draw the PNG on a blank page of the same size, then lay it over the real page.
buf = io.BytesIO()
c = canvas.Canvas(buf, pagesize=(pw, ph))
c.drawImage(sig_png, x, y, width=width, preserveAspectRatio=True,
            anchor="sw", height=width, mask="auto")
c.save()
page.merge_page(PdfReader(buf).pages[0])
writer.write(pdf_out)

python3 stamp.py letter.pdf signature.png letter-signed.pdf 1 72 650 150

PDF coordinates start at the bottom-left corner, in points. An A4 page is about 595 x 842 points, so 72 650 is one inch from the left edge and a bit under a quarter of the way down from the top. 150 is the width of the mark in points, about 5.3 cm.

I checked the output three ways. The letter's text was still extractable as text after stamping, so the page wasn't flattened into a picture. Rendering the page with pdftoppm showed the signature sitting above the line with the text around it untouched. And the file went from 1,492 bytes to 5,739, since the PNG is small.

Checking which kind of signature a file has

pdfsig from poppler-utils lists the digital signatures in a PDF:

pdfsig letter-signed.pdf

For my stamped letter it printed File 'letter-signed.pdf' does not contain any signatures. That's the correct answer. The page has a mark, the file has no signature. Run it on a document you received with a real certificate signature and it lists the signer and whether the signature validates. It's a quick way to see which kind someone sent you, or which kind you're about to send.

Gotcha 1: a JPEG brings its paper with it

JPEG has no transparency. If you place the photo itself, you place a rectangle of grey paper. I stamped the original signature-photo.jpg at the same spot to compare: the grey box covered part of the "Yours faithfully," line above it, and the file grew to 42,120 bytes instead of 5,739. Use a PNG with a transparent background, like the one the script above makes.

Gotcha 2: adding a mark can break a signature that's already there

A digital signature covers a byte range of the file. If someone has already signed the document with a certificate and you add your mark with a tool that rewrites the whole file, like the script above, those bytes change and their signature stops validating. Acrobat avoids this by appending changes as an incremental update. If pdfsig shows an existing signature, add yours in a reader that preserves it, or ask the sender how they want it signed.

I built ToolOcean, a set of browser-based file tools. Its sign page places a drawn, typed or imported mark on one page in the browser tab, and says plainly that the result is not a certified or qualified signature: https://toolocean.co/pdf-sign

Drafted with AI help, tested and checked by me.

title: Agent Graph Engineering, Part 1: The Stack, and Why Each Piece Is There
description:
TL;DR The stack is Python, Pydantic AI for agents, LangGraph for the flow, chanx for typed streaming WebSockets and a generated frontend contract, OpenTelemetry into a trace store you own, pytest with a mocked LLM for fast tests, and real-model evals for regressions. Business logic stays in a separate service from the agent graph. The single idea holding it together: every boundary in the system is a declared, typed artifact rather than something you hold in your head. This post makes the case for each piece so you can bring it to your team, then lays out what we build in the rest of the series.

Part 0 was the story: years of shipping LLM features as intent detection plus nested conditionals, and why observability tooling never fixed the underlying problem. This post is the pragmatic half.

One clarification first, because the word is overloaded. This series is about the execution graph of an agent: state, nodes, edges, routing, interrupts, resumption. It is not graph RAG, and not knowledge graphs. Those are retrieval techniques, where a graph is the data you query. Graph RAG could sit behind one node here as one tool among several. Same word, different concept, and that collision is a large part of why there is so little material on this subject.

The one idea

Everything below follows from a single principle: the structure of your AI system should be a declared artifact, not something reconstructed by reading code.

Your flow should be a graph you can render. Your tool inputs and outputs should be schemas. Your WebSocket messages should be a contract your frontend can generate a client from. Your agent's output should have a type.

The reason is not elegance. It is that declared structure can be rendered, validated, traced, and diffed automatically, while structure that only exists as control flow can only be understood by a human reading it. That difference is what decides whether your system survives its third feature and its second engineer.

Why this is worth your time

The case for each piece is below. Before that, the reasons you might care beyond whatever you are shipping this week, because I think there are three different readers here.

If your team already runs an agent in production, you do not need convincing that it is hard. The useful part is the set of practices that remove whole categories of bug rather than fixing them one at a time. Typed tool arguments turn a wrong type into a validation error at the edge instead of a TypeError three frames into your own code. Structured output means you route on isinstance rather than on whether the response happened to contain the word "escalate". Generated contracts mean a message shape cannot drift between two codebases without the compiler noticing. Checkpointing means a crashed run resumes instead of vanishing. Guardrails at both edges mean the text you screened is the text that ships. Evals mean a model upgrade is a measurement rather than a gamble. None of those are features you gain. They are bugs you stop having, which is a different and better thing.

If you are about to build your first one, the useful part is the order. These decisions are sequenced the way they actually bite, and the one that is cheap this month and expensive next year is the service split, which is why it turns up early rather than in a footnote. Reading ahead costs an afternoon and might save you a rewrite.

If you are building for yourself or for a client, the repository is the point. It is distilled from a production system of five services, out of roughly five years on realtime infrastructure and agent systems, so the parts that look over-careful are mostly the parts that broke somewhere else first. It is production-shaped rather than notebook-shaped, and it runs on one API key, or none at all. Moving it to another domain is mostly swapping tools, prompts, and edges. I want to be careful with the word production, though. The shape is right and the last mile is real, so the final post is a plain list of what you still owe before paying users touch it. Nobody is helped by pretending a checkout is a deployment.

Then there is the market, if you are weighing where to put your learning time. Stanford's AI Index 2026 found that mentions of the "agentic AI" skill cluster in job postings grew more than 280% in a year, from 0.06% of postings in 2024 to 0.23% in 2025, which is roughly 90,000 US listings. Fast growth from a small base, and both halves of that matter: it is early, and it is moving. The detail I find more telling sits in the same report. Mentions of "ChatGPT", "conversational AI" and "chatbots" went down over the same period. Demand moved off demos. Korn Ferry's 2026 survey of 1,674 talent leaders has 52% planning to deploy autonomous agents by the end of this year, which is the same shift seen from the other side of the table.

The job ads are the more useful signal, though, and they say something slightly different from the headline. Reading through current senior backend openings, the ones that touch AI are not asking for prompt engineering. They ask for distributed systems, availability and latency targets, production Python, schema and API design, architecture review across teams, and operational practice: service levels, incident response, containers and orchestration. AI turns up as a capability expected inside all that, rather than instead of it. That is a more demanding ask than the hype implies, and it maps almost exactly onto what this series builds, which is a system with contracts, traces, tests and a deployment story that happens to have a model in it.

The sentence that keeps turning up in hiring write-ups is that a demo agent is easy and a reliable one is not, and that eval literacy is the clearest sign somebody has actually shipped. That is more or less this entire series, arrived at independently and the slow way.

The stack

Layer Choice What it buys you
Language Python The only ecosystem where every provider, every serving runtime, and every eval tool shows up first
Agent Pydantic AI Typed tools, typed outputs, typed deps, provider independence
Flow LangGraph Declared graph, renderable diagram, inspectable state, checkpointing
Transport chanx Typed WebSocket messages, broadcast from anywhere, generated AsyncAPI contract
Tracing OpenTelemetry One connected trace per user message, readable with no account and exportable to any OTLP backend
Tests pytest + mocked LLM Fast, deterministic, no API spend
Regressions Evals with real models Catch what mocks cannot when you change a model or a prompt
Business logic A separate service Keeps your product's domain out of your agent's graph
Runs A worker, on Celery A run outlives the process that asked for it, so a deploy does not take the work in flight with it

Python

Not a controversial pick, but worth stating the actual reason. It is not that Python has the best SDK for calling an API, because every language has that now. It is everything around the call: local model serving, embeddings, evaluation harnesses, vector stores, document parsing. When you eventually need to run a model yourself or plug in a tool nobody has wrapped yet, Python is where it already exists.

Pydantic AI, for the agent

An agent is a thing with a declared output type and a declared set of tools. Pydantic AI is built on exactly that, and being Pydantic-native means your tool schemas and output schemas are the same objects you already validate with.

What that gets you in practice:

  • Structured output. The agent returns a typed object, not a string you regex. Routing on isinstance beats routing on substring matching.
  • Validated tool calls. The model's arguments are checked before your code runs. A wrong type is a caught validation error, not a TypeError three frames deep.
  • Provider independence. Switching providers is a config change. This matters more than it sounds like it does, because you will want a cheap model for routing decisions and a strong one for synthesis.
  • Typed dependencies. Your tools receive a typed context object instead of reading globals.

A word on determinism, because it gets oversold. You cannot make the model deterministic, and anyone promising that is selling something. What you can do is make everything around it deterministic: the model's only job is to return a value of a declared type, and every other step on the path is ordinary code you can test. That shift is most of what separates a system from a prompt.

You could use a provider's own SDK or an ADK instead. I would not, because the moment you want a second provider or a self-hosted model, the abstraction you skipped has to be written anyway, and it will be worse.

If you want to see this layer on its own before the graph arrives, I wrote it up separately in Streaming Agents with Pydantic AI over Typed WebSockets. That post is a good prerequisite for this series.

LangGraph, for the flow

This is the piece that changes how you work, and the piece your team will push back on. So be specific about the trade.

The cost is real. You stop writing handler functions and start declaring state, nodes, and conditional edges. A branch becomes an edge. A handler becomes a subgraph. It takes a few weeks to stop fighting it, and the first graph you write will be wrong.

What you get back:

  • A diagram from the code. LangGraph exports Mermaid. Your architecture picture is generated from the thing that actually runs, so it cannot go stale. No more hand-drawn draw.io files that lie.
  • Inspectable state at every step. You can see what the state was going into a node and coming out. When something breaks, you know which transition did it rather than guessing.
  • Checkpointing. Graph state persists. A run can be paused, resumed, and recovered after a crash, which is also the mechanism that makes human-in-the-loop approvals work rather than being a bolt-on.
  • Structure that survives change. Adding a capability means adding a node and an edge, not threading another condition through an existing chain.

The honest downsides: it is a LangChain-ecosystem library, so some of the ergonomics assume LangChain; and streaming from non-LangChain code goes through a generic custom channel, which is the gap chanx fills.

chanx, for transport and contract

Disclosure: I wrote chanx, because I kept rebuilding the same thing. The intro post has the full background.

Three things it does for an agent system:

  • Broadcast from anywhere. A node buried in a subgraph can emit a progress event to the right user without the graph passing a stream handle down through every call. You can stream the model's reasoning while it works, instead of going silent and then dumping everything.
  • Typed messages instead of a receive_json if/else chain. Every message is a model, routing is automatic, and bad payloads fail at the edge.
  • Generated AsyncAPI docs. This is the one nobody else does. Your WebSocket contract becomes a spec, and your frontend generates a TypeScript client from it. Change the graph, regenerate, and the compiler tells the frontend what broke. Your REST API has had this via OpenAPI for a decade; there is no reason your agent layer should not.

It works with Django, FastAPI, or Litestar, which matters because we use two of them.

OpenTelemetry, into a trace store you own

The usual advice here is to name a vendor. I would rather name the standard, because the vendor is the part you should be able to change.

Both LangGraph and Pydantic AI instrument themselves with OpenTelemetry, so once a graph node opens a span, every model call inside it is already a child. You get one connected trace covering graph transitions and model calls together, rather than the flat list of completions a dashboard usually shows you.

What this stack does with those spans is the part I would argue for. They go into a small trace store inside the agent service, which means /traces renders a run as the chain of steps it was with no account, no signup, and no configuration. That matters more than it sounds. A reference implementation that needs a vendor account before it shows you anything has lost most of its readers at step one, and an on-call engineer at 2am should not need a third party to answer "what did this run do".

Exporting onward is then one environment variable: off, files on disk, an OTLP collector, or both. Any OTLP-speaking backend should work, since that is the point of a standard, and the repo covers that path with a fake collector that checks spans really leave the process with the right endpoint and auth header. Honest limit: that proves the export path, not any particular vendor's ingestion. Langfuse, Jaeger and Grafana are all OTLP endpoints plus a header, but I have verified the path rather than each product.

When a user reports that the agent did something strange in production, you want evidence, not a reproduction attempt. This is the piece that gives you evidence, and it is yours.

pytest with a mocked LLM

Mock at the HTTP layer, not at the framework layer. If you stub Pydantic AI's client you test your stubs. If you intercept the HTTP call and return a recorded provider response, the real pipeline runs: SSE parsing, tool call assembly, streaming, validation. Your tests then cover the parts that actually break.

These tests are fast, deterministic, and free, so you can run them on every commit and cover full WebSocket flows end to end.

Evals with real models

Mocked tests prove your code works. They cannot tell you whether the model still picks the right tool after you reworded a prompt, or whether the new model release routes the same way.

That is what evals are for: scenarios run against real providers, on demand and never in CI, because they cost money. Pydantic AI has an eval module, or a plain script works. Without this you cannot upgrade a model without fear, which in practice means you stop upgrading.

Keep business logic out of the agent

Put your product's domain (users, permissions, billing, persistence) in one service and your agent graph in another. I have shipped the merged version and it becomes a mess: business rules leak into prompts, graph concerns leak into models, and neither side can be tested alone.

Separated, the agent service has one job, and the boundary between them is a contract you can generate a client from.

What we build

A support ticket triage assistant. A ticket arrives, and the agent decides what to do with it: answer it directly, search the knowledge base, escalate it to a human, or draft a reply. Posting that reply to the customer requires human approval; searching the knowledge base does not.

Two views of one ticket. The customer sees it being worked, step by step:

The team sees the same ticket with their own lane on it, internal notes beside the agent's answers and the step it chose:

I picked this deliberately. It needs real routing, so the graph earns its place instead of being a two-node demo. It has a naturally irreversible action, so the approval machinery is solving an actual problem rather than an invented one. And it runs on an LLM key alone, with no OAuth flows or third-party signups standing between you and a working checkout.

The shape:

flowchart LR
    FE["Frontend<br/>React"]
    BE["Backend<br/>Django"]
    AG["Agent<br/>FastAPI"]

    FE -->|"REST + WS<br/>OpenAPI"| BE
    BE -->|"typed WS<br/>AsyncAPI"| AG

    BE --- BEOWNS[["users, tickets,<br/>the thread a person reads"]]
    AG --- AGOWNS[["graphs, tools, checkpoints,<br/>the thread a model remembers"]]

    classDef owns fill:none,stroke-dasharray:4 3;
    class BEOWNS,AGOWNS owns;

Three services, one repository. The frontend generates its clients from OpenAPI and AsyncAPI. The backend owns users, tickets, and history. The agent service owns the graphs, the tools, and the checkpoints, and talks to nobody's database but its own.

It is small enough to read in an afternoon and complete enough to adopt: generated contracts on both boundaries, real WebSocket worker processes, approval interrupts on irreversible tools, guardrails on the input and output edges, streamed progress, a span per graph node with per-run cost, three test suites that spend nothing, evals against real providers, and container images serving ASGI. The architecture is production-grade and the deployment is production-shaped. What it does not do yet, context budgeting and spend caps among others, is written down in the repo rather than glossed over, and the last post walks that gap. Every post is pinned to a tag so you can check out the exact state being described.

What it costs

I do not want to undersell the ramp. Declaring flows as graphs is a genuine shift in how you think, and the first few weeks are slower than writing the conditionals would have been. Expect to throw away your first graph design once you understand state properly.

What you get on the other side is an AI system you can point at, trace, test, and change. The agent stops being magic and starts being software.

Next up is the service split, then types and contracts, and then the posts get into code. Hope this one is useful in the meantime, particularly if you are the person who has to justify the stack to everyone else.

I write these deep-dives and maintain a handful of Python libraries, so if that is your kind of thing, follow along on GitHub and LinkedIn.

title: How to Get a Transcript of Any YouTube Video (4 Free Methods)
description:
Sometimes you don't want to watch a video, you want to read it. Maybe you need to quote a conference talk accurately, skim a 90-minute lecture for the one part that matters, or paste a tutorial's steps into your notes.

Almost every way of getting a YouTube transcript relies on the same thing: the video's caption track. YouTube automatically generates captions for most uploads in supported languages, and many creators upload their own. If a video has a caption track, you can get its text for free. If it doesn't, no "transcript tool" can pull text out of thin air. At that point you need actual speech-to-text, which is a different (and usually paid or compute-heavy) job.

With that in mind, here are four free methods, from zero-setup to fully scriptable.

Method 1: YouTube's built-in transcript panel

YouTube has a transcript viewer built in, and plenty of people don't know it exists.

On desktop:

  1. Open the video on youtube.com.
  2. Click the description under the video to expand it (the "...more" link).
  3. Scroll to the bottom of the description and click Show transcript.
  4. A transcript panel opens next to the video, with a timestamp beside every line.

You can click any line to jump to that moment. The panel's menu lets you toggle timestamps off, and a language selector appears if the video has more than one caption track.

On mobile: open the video, tap the description, and look for Show transcript in the same place.

Good for: quickly reading or searching a single video with no extra tools.

Limitations: the text lives inside a scrolling panel. You can select and copy it, but long transcripts are awkward to copy cleanly, timestamps get mixed into the text, and there's no download button. If you just need to find one quote, it's perfect. If you need a file, read on.

Method 2: A free web tool (YouTubeScribe)

If you want a downloadable file, a web-based transcript tool saves you the copy-paste work. I'll use YouTubeScribe as the example here. Full disclosure: I work on it, so I'll stick to what it actually does.

  1. Copy the video URL. Regular watch links, Shorts, youtu.be short links and embed URLs all work.
  2. Paste it into the box on the homepage and click Get transcript.
  3. Read the timestamped transcript, toggle timestamps on or off, then copy it or download it as TXT or SRT.

What's happening under the hood is the same as Method 1: it reads the caption track YouTube already has (auto-generated or uploaded) and formats it. That means:

  • It works on public and unlisted videos that have captions, in any language the video has a track for (125+ languages are supported).
  • Private and members-only videos won't work, and neither will videos with no caption track. You get a clear "no transcript" result instead of invented text.
  • TXT and SRT downloads are free, and you don't need an account for your first transcript.

If you specifically need the caption file with its timing intact, for example to re-upload subtitles or load them into a video editor, the subtitle downloader saves it as SRT or VTT.

Good for: getting a clean file in a few seconds without installing anything.

Other honest options: there are several similar free web tools (DownSub, Tactiq's YouTube transcript page, YouTubeToTranscript and others). They all read the same caption track, so the text will be identical. The differences are in formats, limits and how much the interface gets in your way. Try a couple and keep the one you like.

Method 3: YouTube Studio (for your own videos)

If the video is yours, you already have direct access to the caption files.

  1. Go to YouTube Studio.
  2. Open Subtitles from the left menu and choose the video.
  3. Next to the language track you want, open the options menu and download the file. You'll usually get a choice of formats such as .srt, .vtt or .sbv.

This is also the best place to fix auto-generated captions. Edit them in Studio and every later transcript (from any method in this article) will reflect your corrections.

Good for: creators repurposing their own content into blog posts, show notes or newsletters.

Limitations: only works for videos on channels you manage.

Method 4: Command-line and code (for developers)

If you need transcripts for many videos, or want them inside a script or pipeline, use the open-source tools.

yt-dlp

yt-dlp is the well-known open-source downloader, and it can fetch just the subtitles:

yt-dlp --skip-download --write-subs --write-auto-subs \
  --sub-langs "en.*" --convert-subs srt \
  "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VIDEO_ID"
  • --write-subs grabs uploaded (human) captions; --write-auto-subs grabs auto-generated ones.
  • --convert-subs srt needs ffmpeg installed.
  • It also works on playlists, which is handy for a whole lecture series.

youtube-transcript-api (Python)

For Python projects, youtube-transcript-api returns the transcript as data:

from youtube_transcript_api import YouTubeTranscriptApi
from youtube_transcript_api.formatters import SRTFormatter

ytt_api = YouTubeTranscriptApi()
transcript = ytt_api.fetch("VIDEO_ID", languages=["en"])

for snippet in transcript:
    print(f"{snippet.start:7.1f}s  {snippet.text}")

with open("video.srt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write(SRTFormatter().format_transcript(transcript))

Good for: batch jobs, research datasets and anything you want to automate.

Limitations: YouTube may rate-limit or block requests, especially from cloud servers and data-centre IPs. Please respect YouTube's Terms of Service and creators' rights. Fetching captions for personal notes or research is very different from republishing someone's content wholesale.

Which method should you use?

You want to… Use
Read or search one video right now YouTube's transcript panel
Get a TXT or SRT file without installing anything A web tool like YouTubeScribe
Export or fix captions on your own videos YouTube Studio
Process dozens or hundreds of videos yt-dlp or youtube-transcript-api

A note on accuracy

Auto-generated captions are good, but they're not perfect. They struggle with names, jargon, heavy accents, crosstalk and music. Before you quote someone in an article, paper or social post, click back to the timestamp and listen to make sure the words are right. A transcript is a fantastic index into a video, but it doesn't replace the video itself.

And if a video has no captions at all, none of the above will help. You'd need a speech-to-text model (for example, running OpenAI's open-source Whisper locally on audio you have the right to use).

Happy reading, and enjoy getting your evenings back from 90-minute videos.

title: Identifying AI crawlers in your access log: user agent, source, and crawl frequency
description:
Your access log already answers "which AI crawlers hit my site, how hard, and are they who they claim to be". You don't need a new SDK or a tag manager. You need three passes over the same file: classify by user agent, verify by source, measure frequency.

Here are the commands and one Python script that produce all three reports.

What the log gives you

nginx combined format, one line per request:

203.0.113.7 - - [23/Oct/2026:13:45:01 +0000] "GET /blog/wordpress-hosting-cost HTTP/1.1" 200 18432 "-" "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; GPTBot)"

Fields: client IP, timestamp, request line, status, bytes sent, referer, user agent. That's enough. If your log is JSON or a custom format, only step 2 changes.

Step 1 — look at the raw user agents first 

awk -F'"' '{print $6}' /var/log/nginx/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20

The top twenty UAs on your site. AI crawlers almost always declare themselves: GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, CCBot, Bytespider, Amazonbot, meta-externalagent. Treat that as data, not code — keep it in a config file you edit, because operators rename crawlers and new ones show up.

One check before anything else: if you sit behind a CDN or reverse proxy, $remote_addr may be the proxy, not the crawler. Confirm you're logging the real client IP before you trust any per-IP number.

Step 2 — classify

Save this as ai_crawlers.py:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Classify AI crawler traffic in an nginx combined access log."""
import re
import sys
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
from datetime import datetime

LINE = re.compile(
    r'^(?P<ip>\S+) \S+ \S+ \[(?P<ts>[^\]]+)\] '
    r'"(?P<method>[A-Z]+) (?P<path>\S+)(?: [^"]*)?" '
    r'(?P<status>\d{3}) (?P<size>\S+) "(?P<ref>[^"]*)" "(?P<ua>[^"]*)"'
)

BOTS = {
    "gptbot": "GPTBot",
    "oai-searchbot": "OAI-SearchBot",
    "chatgpt-user": "ChatGPT-User",
    "claudebot": "ClaudeBot",
    "perplexitybot": "PerplexityBot",
    "ccbot": "CCBot",
    "bytespider": "Bytespider",
    "amazonbot": "Amazonbot",
    "meta-externalagent": "meta-externalagent",
}

def classify(ua):
    low = (ua or "").lower()
    for token, name in BOTS.items():
        if token in low:
            return name
    if not low or low == "-":
        return "no-ua"
    if re.search(r"bot|crawl|spider|slurp", low):
        return "other-bot"
    return "browser"

def main(path):
    rows = []
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") as fh:
        for line in fh:
            m = LINE.match(line)
            if not m:
                continue
            d = m.groupdict()
            d["bot"] = classify(d["ua"])
            d["day"] = datetime.strptime(
                d["ts"], "%d/%b/%Y:%H:%M:%S %z"
            ).date().isoformat()
            rows.append(d)

    per_day = defaultdict(Counter)
    ips = defaultdict(Counter)
    paths = defaultdict(Counter)
    status = defaultdict(Counter)

    for r in rows:
        per_day[r["day"]][r["bot"]] += 1
        ips[r["bot"]][r["ip"]] += 1
        paths[r["bot"]][r["path"]] += 1
        status[r["bot"]][r["status"]] += 1

    totals = {b: sum(d[b] for d in per_day.values()) for b in ips}
    bots = sorted(totals, key=lambda b: -totals[b])

    print(f"{'bot':<18} {'hits':>8} {'ips':>6}  top path")
    for b in bots:
        top = paths[b].most_common(1)[0][0] if paths[b] else "-"
        print(f"{b:<18} {totals[b]:>8} {len(ips[b]):>6}  {top}")

    print("\ndaily volume")
    days = sorted(per_day)
    print("day".ljust(12) + "".join(b[:12].rjust(14) for b in bots))
    for day in days:
        print(day.ljust(12) + "".join(str(per_day[day][b]).rjust(14) for b in bots))

    print("\nstatus mix")
    for b in bots:
        mix = ", ".join(f"{s}:{n}" for s, n in status[b].most_common(4))
        print(f"  {b:<18} {mix}")

    print("\ntop ips per bot")
    for b in bots:
        print(f"\n[{b}]")
        for ip, n in ips[b].most_common(5):
            print(f"  {ip:<40} {n}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "/var/log/nginx/access.log")

python ai_crawlers.py /var/log/nginx/access.log

You get per-crawler hit totals, unique IP counts, the top path, a daily matrix, a status mix, and the busiest IPs. The status mix is the first filter — a bot with mostly 404s is not reading your site, it's walking a list.

Step 3 — verify the source

A user agent is a string the client chooses. Anyone can send GPTBot. So a matching UA means claimed, not verified. Verification means the IP is inside the range the operator publishes:

import ipaddress
import json

# published-ranges.json: {"GPTBot": ["203.0.113.0/24", ...], "ClaudeBot": [...]}
RANGES = json.load(open("published-ranges.json"))
NETS = {bot: [ipaddress.ip_network(c) for c in cidrs]
        for bot, cidrs in RANGES.items()}

def is_verified(ip, claimed_bot):
    nets = NETS.get(claimed_bot)
    if not nets:
        return None  # no published list for this name: unknown, not verified
    addr = ipaddress.ip_address(ip)
    return any(addr in net for net in nets)

Most crawler operators publish their ranges as a machine-readable file and document the reverse-DNS suffix they use. Fetch the file on a schedule, store it, diff it — the diff is your early warning that a range moved.

Reverse DNS is the second opinion, and it should only run on hits that failed the range check, not on every line:

import socket

def fcrdns(ip):
    """Forward-confirmed reverse DNS. Returns hostname or None."""
    try:
        host = socket.gethostbyaddr(ip)[0]
        _, _, addrs = socket.gethostbyname_ex(host)
    except (socket.herror, socket.gaierror):
        return None
    return host if ip in addrs else None

Record three outcomes, not two: verified (IP inside the published range), claimed (UA says bot, IP outside every range), unknown (no UA at all). Only the first is evidence that a crawler is actually crawling you.

Step 4 — measure crawl frequency

Hourly volume for one crawler, without touching the script:

grep -i 'ClaudeBot' /var/log/nginx/access.log \
  | awk -F'[][]' '{print $2}' \
  | cut -d: -f1,2 \
  | sort | uniq -c

How to read the numbers:

  • Steady hits per day from a handful of IPs — a real crawler on a schedule. Note the rate; that's your baseline.
  • One IP, thousands of URLs, mostly 404 — probing, or a sitemap pointing at pages you deleted.
  • A burst inside a few minutes — a re-crawl of pages that changed. Check what you deployed that day.
  • Many IPs, few hits each — distributed. Verify against ranges before you assume one operator.
  • The same path with varying query strings — cache-busting. Your cache may be serving fresh HTML on every request, which invites more crawling.

Pair the frequency with the path list. A crawler that only touches /blog/* is indexing. One that touches /cart, /checkout, or /api/* is doing something you probably want to stop regardless of who it is.

Step 5 — turn the log into a decision

Four buckets, four actions:

Evidence Action
Verified, and you want it (answer engines that send referrals) Leave open, make sure the page renders server-side
Verified, and you don't want it (training-only) robots.txt token, or a block at the proxy
Claimed but not verified Don't block on UA alone — block on "outside published range"
Unknown, high volume, odd paths Rate-limit at the edge, then watch

robots.txt is a request. A block at nginx is enforcement. If you need enforcement, do it with a map and keep logging the blocked requests, so six weeks later you can still see what you cut off.

Step 6 — keep it running

  • Keep enough history to compare week over week; a single day tells you nothing about a trend.
  • Run the script from cron, write JSON, diff against yesterday. A new UA with more than a hundred hits is the thing worth reading.
  • Split logs by crawler family so you stop grepping a multi-gigabyte file: 
map $http_user_agent $ai_log {
    default          main;
    ~*GPTBot         ai_gptbot;
    ~*ClaudeBot      ai_claude;
    ~*PerplexityBot  ai_perplexity;
    ~*CCBot          ai_ccbot;
}

open_log_file_cache max=100 inactive=60s;
access_log /var/log/nginx/$ai_log.log combined;

The map goes in the http block; the variable in the path is why open_log_file_cache is there.

If you'd rather not maintain the lists

Keeping the token map, the published ranges, and the daily diff in sync is the boring half of this job. If you run WordPress, AumCrawl shows which AI crawlers are hitting the site and lets you allow or block per crawler. The access log stays the source of truth either way — this is the dashboard on top of it, not a replacement for the evidence.

title: Invoice and Payment Reminder Automation: What to Automate and What to Keep Human
description:
Payment reminders look like an easy automation problem.

An invoice has a due date. If it is unpaid, send a reminder.

In production, that quickly becomes more complicated.

The real challenge is not sending the email. It is knowing when automation is safe, when the workflow should stop, and when a person needs to take over.

Start With Invoice State, Not a Calendar

The weakest reminder system is just a scheduler.

It thinks like this:

Due date passed?
↓
Send reminder
↓
Wait 3 days
↓
Send another

That works only if every unpaid invoice means the same thing.

They do not.

An invoice might be:

OPEN
DUE_SOON
OVERDUE
PARTIALLY_PAID
PAID
DISPUTED
ON_HOLD
CANCELLED

Those states should produce different behavior.

A better model is:

PAID -> stop
DISPUTED -> pause + human review
PARTIALLY_PAID -> recalculate outstanding balance
ON_HOLD -> stop external reminders
OVERDUE -> continue reminder policy

This is the first design decision I would make before building anything else.

Automate the Predictable Parts

Automation works best where the rules are clear.

Good candidates include:

upcoming due-date reminders,

due-date notifications,

first overdue reminders,

payment status checks,

internal alerts,

scheduled follow-ups.

For example:

T-5 days -> friendly upcoming-due reminder
T+0 -> due-date reminder
T+3 days -> first overdue reminder
T+7 days -> second reminder or internal review
T+14 days -> human escalation

The exact timing is business-specific.

The important part is that the sequence has an end.

An automated workflow should not keep sending reminders forever because no one designed an escalation state.

Human Handoff Should Be a First-Class State

Many systems treat manual intervention as an exception outside the workflow.

I prefer making it explicit.

For example:

AUTOMATED_REMINDER
↓
NO_PAYMENT
↓
CHECK_CONTEXT
↓
NORMAL? -------- yes ----> continue automation
|
no
↓
HUMAN_REVIEW

That human-review state may be triggered by:

an invoice dispute,

repeated missed promises,

a high-value account,

a service problem,

a custom payment arrangement,

repeated failed reminders.

Once the workflow reaches that point, automation should stop trying to "solve" the problem by changing the email wording.

Do Not Send Reminders From Stale Data

This is where architecture matters.

If payment status lives in an accounting platform but reminders run in another application, those systems need reliable synchronization.

Otherwise this happens:

Customer pays
↓
Accounting system updated
↓
Reminder system still shows unpaid
↓
Customer receives overdue email

Technically, the reminder job ran correctly.

Operationally, the system failed.

Before automating reminders, define the source of truth.

For example:

Invoice state -> Accounting system
Customer email -> CRM
Reminder policy -> Automation service

Then make sure payment events reach the reminder engine quickly enough for the business.

Use Events Where They Matter

A useful architecture could be:

Invoice created
↓
Schedule reminder policy

Payment received
↓
Update invoice state
↓
Cancel pending reminders

Invoice disputed
↓
Pause reminder policy
↓
Create human-review task

This can be implemented with:

webhooks,

queues,

scheduled jobs,

polling,

direct API calls.

The mechanism matters less than the state transitions.

Make Reminder Jobs Idempotent

Retries are normal.

Email providers time out.

Queues redeliver messages.

Workers restart.

You do not want one transient failure to send the same payment reminder three times.

Each scheduled reminder should have a stable identity.

For example:

invoice_id
reminder_stage
scheduled_date

You can derive an idempotency key:

INV-10482:T+3:2026-10-20

Before sending:

Has this reminder already been sent successfully?
↓
yes -> stop
no -> send

This makes retry behavior predictable.

The Message Should Be Generated From Current State

Do not create all reminder content at invoice creation time.

The data may change.

At send time, fetch or validate:

Current amount due
Payment status
Invoice number
Due date
Customer contact
Dispute status
Hold status

Then render the reminder.

That protects you from sending:

Amount due: $10,000

after a customer has already paid $8,000.

For partially paid invoices, the workflow should use the outstanding balance.

Internal Automation Can Be More Valuable Than External Automation

Not every automated action should contact the customer.

Sometimes the safer action is:

Invoice 7 days overdue
↓
Notify account owner

or:

Three unpaid invoices
↓
Create finance review task

or:

Payment promise date missed
↓
Escalate internally

This is still valuable automation.

It removes monitoring work while preserving human control over sensitive conversations.

Separate Policy From Delivery Logic

I would avoid hard-coding every reminder interval directly into worker code.

A better design keeps policy configurable.

For example:

reminder_policy:
before_due:
days: 5
action: send_email

due_date:
days: 0
action: send_email

overdue_1:
days: 3
action: send_email

overdue_2:
days: 7
action: send_email

escalation:
days: 14
action: human_review

This makes the business policy easier to change without rewriting the entire automation flow.

You can also attach conditions:

skip_if:

  • paid
  • disputed
  • cancelled
  • on_hold

Now the workflow becomes easier to reason about.

Logging Matters More Than Fancy Email Templates

When someone asks:

Why did this customer receive this reminder?

you need an answer.

Store enough history to reconstruct what happened.

For example:

invoice_id
customer_id
previous_state
current_state
reminder_stage
scheduled_at
sent_at
channel
result
error

That helps with:

debugging,

customer support,

auditability,

retries,

operational review.

If your reminder workflow cannot explain itself, debugging customer complaints becomes painful.

Keep Automation Away From Negotiation

There is a category of finance work that should remain human-led.

Examples:

Disputed invoice
Custom settlement
Payment plan negotiation
Repeated broken promises
Strategic customer escalation
Service-quality complaint

You can automate detection.

You can automate alerts.

You can automate task creation.

But the conversation itself often needs context.

That is an important architecture boundary.

The automation system should identify complexity, not pretend complexity does not exist.

A Practical Implementation Checklist

Before shipping an invoice reminder workflow, I would check:

[ ] Is there one authoritative invoice state?
[ ] Are payment updates synchronized reliably?
[ ] Are reminders cancelled immediately after payment?
[ ] Are partial payments handled correctly?
[ ] Are disputes and holds explicit states?
[ ] Can reminder jobs retry without duplicate sends?
[ ] Is the reminder policy configurable?
[ ] Does every automation path have an escalation point?
[ ] Can humans pause automation manually?
[ ] Are sends and failures logged?
[ ] Are high-risk cases routed to people?
[ ] Is the customer message generated from current data?

If those are clear, the reminder emails themselves are the easy part.

Final Takeaway

Invoice reminder automation should not be designed as:

if overdue:
send_email()

A production workflow is closer to:

read current state
↓
apply reminder policy
↓
check stop conditions
↓
decide automated vs human path
↓
execute safely
↓
log outcome

The strongest system is not the one that sends the most reminders.

It is the one that knows when to send, when to stop, and when to hand the problem to a person.

This is adapted from my original guide on invoice and payment reminder automation.

title: OpenAI Moderation API vs GPT-4o-mini Chat Completions: JSON Schema Moderation (and Cost)
description:
TL;DR: For an edtech system scoring candidates against a job rubric, use a dedicated moderation API when it exists and its taxonomy fits. When no native moderation endpoint exists, a cheap chat model with strict JSON Schema is the practical fallback. The deciding constraint is structured correctness: every response must be parsed, validated, retried, or escalated without turning a safety decision into prose.

I would accept a candidate only after the moderation result passes schema validation. An invalid result is a review-queue event, not a safe result. That rule makes the architecture easier to reason about than a clever prompt.

What should the moderation boundary guarantee?

The concrete job is familiar: an edtech product receives learner-submitted text, then scores a candidate against a job rubric. The text may be shown to a recruiter, stored for an audit, and fed into later scoring. A moderation response therefore needs a stable contract. My smallest useful contract is {"is_safe": boolean, "reason": string}.

There are four invariants:

  1. The model receives only the text and policy context it needs.
  2. The response validates against the expected JSON Schema.
  3. A timeout, 429, malformed response, or provider error never becomes is_safe: true.
  4. A human review path exists for ambiguous policy cases.

That last point matters in education. A profanity classifier and a policy decision are different things. A name, disability disclosure, political opinion, or quoted classroom material can be sensitive without being disallowed. The model can classify; policy code owns the final action.

The tempting assumption is that valid JSON means a valid decision. It does not.

OpenAI moderation or JSON-schema chat: which boundary fits?

A dedicated moderation endpoint is cleaner when it exists, is stable, and has a taxonomy aligned with your policy. It gives the application a narrower operational surface and avoids spending prompt space explaining what “safe” means.

The constraint in this system is that no native moderation endpoint is available. The fallback is a standard chat completion with strict json_schema. GPT-4o-mini is a reasonable choice for short text because the task is small and the output contract is explicit. This is a workaround, but a disciplined one: the schema is part of the interface, not a hopeful instruction at the end of a prompt.

Option Strength Boundary Good fit here?
OpenAI Moderation API Purpose-built categories and a narrow contract Requires a dedicated moderation surface and its taxonomy Yes when available
GPT-4o-mini with JSON Schema Returns the exact fields the workflow consumes Prompt and policy wording become part of the safety design Yes when a native endpoint is unavailable
Anthropic Claude General-purpose text reasoning and configurable instructions General chat output still needs a schema gate and policy tests Useful for nuanced review
Google Gemini Multimodal chat can cover text and image inputs Safety settings and structured output need provider-specific tests Useful for multimodal workflows

The table is a decision aid, not a leaderboard. OpenAI’s dedicated moderation surface is preferable for a narrow moderation job. Claude and Gemini are credible alternatives for policy-heavy or multimodal workflows, but neither removes the need to test borderline examples. The chat fallback wins only on fit: it is available through the existing compatible chat surface and returns the shape the scoring pipeline already understands.

For short inputs, chat moderation is cheap enough to substitute for a missing dedicated endpoint. I would still measure volume, retry rate, and review rate before committing to a budget. A unit price without those three numbers is theater.

The tradeoff is blunt: you own more policy testing because the model is a general chat model.

That is acceptable.

The critical path is a schema gate, not a prompt

This is the smallest production-shaped path I would start with. It uses the OpenAI Python client against the compatible base URL, reads the key from the environment, retries 429 responses with exponential backoff, honors Retry-After when the SDK exposes it, and rejects anything that does not validate.

import json
import os
import time
from openai import OpenAI, RateLimitError

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"],
    base_url=os.environ["AI_BASE_URL"],
)

result_schema = {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
        "is_safe": {"type": "boolean"},
        "reason": {"type": "string"},
    },
    "required": ["is_safe", "reason"],
    "additionalProperties": False,
}

def moderate(text):
    for attempt in range(4):
        try:
            response = client.chat.completions.create(
                model="gpt-4o-mini",
                messages=[
                    {
                        "role": "system",
                        "content": (
                            "Classify user content for an edtech candidate-scoring workflow. "
                            "Return unsafe for threats, targeted harassment, sexual exploitation, "
                            "or instructions for wrongdoing. Return only the requested object."
                        ),
                    },
                    {"role": "user", "content": text},
                ],
                response_format={
                    "type": "json_schema",
                    "json_schema": {
                        "name": "moderation_result",
                        "strict": True,
                        "schema": result_schema,
                    },
                },
            )
            value = json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content)
            if (
                isinstance(value, dict)
                and isinstance(value.get("is_safe"), bool)
                and isinstance(value.get("reason"), str)
            ):
                return value
            raise ValueError("moderation response failed schema validation")
        except RateLimitError as error:
            if attempt == 3:
                raise
            headers = getattr(getattr(error, "response", None), "headers", {})
            retry_after = headers.get("retry-after")
            time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt)

    raise RuntimeError("moderation did not return a result")

The code deliberately does not catch every exception and quietly mark content safe. A 4xx response should remain an error with its provider message; malformed JSON should enter review or fail closed according to product policy. In a queue, attach a stable content identifier to the job and make the consumer idempotent. At-least-once delivery is normal; duplicate moderation must not duplicate a candidate decision or audit record.

The discovery surface is useful because it is self-describing: discovery can expose a capability’s request schema, response schema, billing metadata, and runnable examples without requiring a new SDK lesson. That reduces integration friction, but it does not validate policy. The schema gate and test corpus still do that work. In the review-and-audit path, this matters after the first prototype: an engineer can inspect the response contract before wiring the result into a private object, a recruiter-facing queue, and a retrying worker, rather than reverse-engineering three SDKs. The unified surface also means one key and one bill cover the related backend capabilities, so credential rotation and month-end reconciliation do not become separate work for every storage and AI vendor. That is a concrete operational advantage, even though it says nothing about classifier quality.

What changes for images and storage?

Text and image moderation should not share a false promise of equivalence. For images, use a vision-capable chat model with the same JSON Schema approach. The output can retain is_safe and reason, but the test set must include visual context, OCR text, cropped content, and benign educational material. The current capability set has no dedicated moderation endpoint, so the chat-model fallback is the documented boundary for both modalities.

If the next step is storing the moderation decision, keep the object private or signed-only and return a presigned URL when a client needs access. Do not send the platform Authorization header to that returned URL. Generation and hosting can share one account and one key in a single REST platform, but that convenience has a cost: one vendor to trust, one bill to reconcile, and one outage surface.

Infrai is a suitable option when self-describing discovery, runnable examples, one REST surface, and one key with one bill matter more than a dedicated moderation taxonomy. Its verified breadth is 295 routes across 20 modules, which can keep the moderation, audit, and storage work in one account. It is the wrong choice when your compliance team requires a provider-owned safety category set or a separate failure domain; choose the dedicated moderation service then.

The alternative stack is an OpenAI image or chat integration plus Amazon S3. That normally means two signups, two credential sets, and glue for upload, object naming, private access, presigning, retries, and audit correlation. The operational argument for a unified surface is real. It is still an argument about integration shape, not proof that its classifier is better.

The option I rejected, and when it is right

I rejected “ask for a paragraph, then parse the paragraph with a regular expression.” It looks fast during a prototype and fails at the boundary that matters. A model can add a sentence, change capitalization, or return a reason containing punctuation that breaks the parser. Worse, a parser failure is easy to misclassify as a negative moderation result.

A dedicated moderation API remains the better choice when the provider offers the categories, regional behavior, retention terms, and review tooling the product requires. I would also prefer a dedicated endpoint when the application needs a large, provider-maintained safety taxonomy rather than one project-specific boolean.

The JSON-schema chat approach is for the narrower gap: text moderation is required, the native endpoint is absent, and the application can own policy tests and escalation. It is cost-effective for short inputs because the request is small, but cost is not the acceptance criterion. Structured correctness is.

References

  • OpenAI Moderation guide: https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/moderation
  • OpenAI structured outputs guide: https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/structured-outputs
  • Anthropic structured outputs documentation: https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/structured-outputs
  • Google Gemini structured output documentation: https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/structured-output
  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • Cohere Rerank overview: https://docs.cohere.com/docs/rerank-overview

title: Serializable vs SELECT FOR UPDATE vs advisory locks — pick the boundary, not the loudest tool
description:
When two sessions can read the same state and then both write, the root issue is an unclear ownership boundary, not a missing lock. This article helps you decide between three PostgreSQL approaches by focusing on what owns the conflict and how each option fails.

Implementation summary

  • The article ships a tiny decision helper that takes a conflict description and returns one of three strategies plus a retry hint. That helper is deliberately small: it encodes the architectural decision rather than attempting to simulate PostgreSQL behavior. A companion routine emits a client-side retry sketch for SERIALIZABLE transactions. The server inserts the verified implementation example below.

Expected behavior

  • SERIALIZABLE: Choose this when the invariant is set-shaped or multi-row and the only safe guarantee is equivalence to some serial order. PostgreSQL enforces the serial-order rule and surfaces serialization failures as SQLSTATE 40001; your application must treat those as retryable errors and implement a retry loop on the client.
  • SELECT ... FOR UPDATE: Use when a single row owns the conflict. The waiting point is explicit and visible: acquire the row lock when you read and then update. This is often easier to reason about, but it only protects the rows you lock and can introduce blocking and deadlocks if transactions lock rows in inconsistent orders.
  • Transaction-scoped advisory locks: Choose when the protected unit is application-defined (tenant shard, workflow, job key) rather than row-shaped. Advisory locks are powerful because you name the resource, but they rely on every participant using the same convention; if some code path skips the lock or uses a different key, the protection silently fails.

Limitations and the practical decision rule

  • Failure shapes: SERIALIZABLE aborts and pushes complexity to retry handling; row locks block and can deadlock; advisory locks fail via protocol drift. Pick the mechanism whose failure you can reliably operate.
  • Edge cases: a conflict that looks row-shaped might actually be set-shaped; advisory locks can be the wrong abstraction if the logic naturally lives inside one transaction and you want the database to reject unsafe interleavings.
  • Operational constraints: keep critical sections short. Long transactions increase overhead and contention for every approach.

Read the article for the decision checklist, the small helper that encodes it, and clear guidance on where retry logic belongs (on the client, not hidden inside a fake in-database wrapper).

Working example 

export function chooseConcurrencyControl({ conflictShape, canRetry, ownsRow, applicationScoped }) {
  if (!conflictShape || typeof conflictShape !== 'string') {
    throw new TypeError('conflictShape must be a non-empty string');
  }

  const shape = conflictShape.trim().toLowerCase();
  if (!shape) throw new TypeError('conflictShape must be a non-empty string');

  if (shape === 'serializable' || shape === 'set' || shape === 'multi-row') {
    return {
      strategy: 'SERIALIZABLE',
      reason: 'The invariant depends on a set or multi-row decision, so the database should detect non-serializable outcomes and the application must retry serialization failures.',
      retry: canRetry !== false
    };
  }

  if (shape === 'row' || ownsRow === true) {
    return {
      strategy: 'SELECT ... FOR UPDATE',
      reason: 'One row owns the conflict, so explicit row locking makes the waiting point direct and predictable.',
      retry: false
    };
  }

  if (shape === 'application' || applicationScoped === true) {
    return {
      strategy: 'TX_ADVISORY_LOCK',
      reason: 'The resource is application-defined rather than row-shaped, so a transaction-scoped advisory lock is a better fit.',
      retry: false
    };
  }

  return {
    strategy: 'SERIALIZABLE',
    reason: 'Default to serializable when the conflict boundary is unclear, because the database can enforce the serial-order rule and reject unsafe interleavings.',
    retry: canRetry !== false
  };
}

export function buildSerializableRetryLoop({ statement, maxAttempts = 3 }) {
  if (typeof statement !== 'string' || statement.trim() === '') {
    throw new TypeError('statement must be a non-empty string');
  }
  if (!Number.isInteger(maxAttempts) || maxAttempts < 1) {
    throw new RangeError('maxAttempts must be a positive integer');
  }

  return [
    'for attempt in 1..maxAttempts:',
    '  BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;',
    `  ${statement.trim()}`,
    "  COMMIT;",
    "  if commit succeeds: return success",
    "  if SQLSTATE is '40001': retry",
    '  otherwise: rethrow'
  ].join('\n');
}

export function summarizeTradeoffs() {
  return {
    serializable: 'Use for set-shaped invariants that need database-enforced retry semantics.',
    rowLock: 'Use when a single row is the conflict owner and waiting is acceptable.',
    advisory: 'Use when the protected resource is application-scoped and not naturally a row.'
  };
}

Read the full article: https://chriseugenerodriguez.com/blog/serializable-vs-select-for-update-advisory-locks

title: How to Scrape Poshmark with Python: Search Results, Sold Comps, Closets, and a Price-Drop Tracker (2026)
description:
If you resell clothes, you already know the most useful question on Poshmark: what does this actually sell for? Active listings tell you what people hope to get. Sold listings tell you what buyers paid. Put the two side by side in your own database and you can price inventory, spot underpriced items, and see which closets move stock.

Poshmark doesn't offer a public data API. But the website is a JavaScript app, and the data it shows comes from JSON endpoints that answer plain GET requests without a login. In this post I'll build a small Python Poshmark scraper that:

  1. Searches listings with real filters (department, category, size, condition)
  2. Pulls sold listings and turns them into price comps (25th percentile, median, 75th)
  3. Reads a seller's closet and profile stats
  4. Fetches a single listing by URL
  5. Stores every run in SQLite and reports price drops

One file, one dependency (requests). Everything below was run against poshmark.com on October 23, 2026, and the output you see is real.

Before you start: read Poshmark's Terms of Service and robots.txt, keep request rates low, and only collect what you need. Profiles include sellers' real names, so don't store personal data you don't need. The endpoints in this post are internal ones the website uses. They aren't documented and can change without notice.

Your options, briefly

  • HTML pages. Search, listing, and closet pages all embed their data in a window.__INITIAL_STATE__ = {...} script blob (not __NEXT_DATA__). It works, but a search page is about 4 MB of HTML to get 48 listings. Also, robots.txt disallows /search.
  • The vm-rest JSON endpoints (this post). The site fetches its listings from https://poshmark.com/vm-rest/.... Responses are clean JSON. robots.txt doesn't mention /vm-rest (it does disallow /api, /search, /users, and a few others).
  • Headless browser. You don't need one. Everything here worked with plain HTTP from a server.

How a Poshmark search request looks

Here's the part that isn't obvious. The search endpoint doesn't use normal query parameters. You pass a JSON object, URL-encoded, in a single request parameter:

GET https://poshmark.com/vm-rest/posts?request={"filters":{"department":"All","inventory_status":["available"]},"query":"levis 501","experience":"all","count":48}&summarize=true

The response has a data array of listings, a total_listing_count, and a more object with a next_max_id cursor for the next page. Each listing comes with a lot of fields. These are the ones I use:

Field What it is
id 24-character hex id, also the end of the listing URL
title, brand, size, condition The basics (brand is free text, more on that below)
price_amount.val Current price as a string, e.g. "47.0"
original_price_amount.val The "retail" price the seller typed in, often "0.0"
first_user_price_amount.val The price when the item was first listed
inventory.status available or sold_out
inventory.status_changed_at When the status last changed (for sold items: about when it sold)
like_count, comment_count, share_count Engagement
creator_username The seller's closet
first_published_at When it was listed

Step 1: A request helper that knows Poshmark's error style 

pip install requests

The first surprise: errors come back as HTTP 200. Ask for a listing that doesn't exist and you get status 200 with a body like this:

{"error":{"errorType":"NotFoundError","statusCode":404, ...},"meta":{"api_url":"/posts/000000000000000000000000"}}

If you only check res.status_code, your scraper will happily treat errors as empty results. So the helper looks inside the body:

import json, re, sqlite3, statistics, sys, time
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from decimal import Decimal

import requests

BASE = "https://poshmark.com/vm-rest"

session = requests.Session()
session.headers.update({
    "User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 "
                  "(KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/124.0 Safari/537.36",
    "Accept": "application/json",
})


class PoshmarkError(Exception):
    pass


def get(path, request=None, max_retries=4):
    """GET a vm-rest path. Errors come back as HTTP 200 with an "error" object."""
    params = {}
    if request is not None:
        params = {"request": json.dumps(request, separators=(",", ":")), "summarize": "true"}
    for attempt in range(max_retries):
        res = session.get(f"{BASE}{path}", params=params, timeout=30)
        if res.status_code == 429 or res.status_code >= 500:
            wait = 2 ** attempt * 2
            print(f"{res.status_code} on {path}, sleeping {wait}s", file=sys.stderr)
            time.sleep(wait)
            continue
        res.raise_for_status()
        data = res.json()
        if "error" in data:
            err = data["error"]
            raise PoshmarkError(f'{err.get("errorType")} ({err.get("statusCode")}) for {path}')
        return data
    raise PoshmarkError(f"gave up on {path} after {max_retries} tries")

About rate limits: I sent 30 search requests back to back (about one per second) and got 30 × 200, with no rate-limit headers in the responses. That doesn't mean there's no limit. It means I didn't hit it at that pace. I keep a 1.5-second pause between pages and the retry logic for 429/5xx, in case that changes.

Step 2: The core of the Poshmark scraper, search with filters and paging

These are the filter keys I verified by checking the results that came back:

def build_request(query=None, department="All", category=None, size=None,
                  condition=None, sold=False, sort=None, count=48):
    filters = {"department": department,
               "inventory_status": ["sold_out" if sold else "available"]}
    if category:
        filters["category_v2"] = category
    if size:
        filters["size"] = [size]
    if condition:
        filters["condition"] = [condition]
    req = {"filters": filters, "experience": "all", "count": count}
    if query:
        req["query"] = query
    if sort:
        req["sort_by"] = sort  # e.g. "added_desc", "price_asc", "price_desc"
    return req


def iter_pages(path, request, max_pages=3):
    """Yield listings page by page, following more.next_max_id."""
    for page in range(max_pages):
        data = get(path, request)
        yield from data.get("data", [])
        more = data.get("more") or {}
        if not more.get("is_next_max_id_present"):
            break
        request = {**request, "max_id": more["next_max_id"]}
        time.sleep(1.5)  # be polite


def search(query, max_pages=3, **filters):
    return iter_pages("/posts", build_request(query, **filters), max_pages)

department="Women", category="Jeans", size="28" and condition="nwt" all came back filtered correctly. Paging with max_id gave a second page of 48 with zero overlap with the first. sort_by: "added_desc" returned the newest listings first, and price_asc/price_desc sorted by price.

Things that didn't work the way I expected:

  • Price filters are silently ignored. I tried four plausible shapes ("price": ["25-50"], {"min":25,"max":50}, and others). Every one returned the exact same total_listing_count as no filter at all, with prices from $16 to $100. Poshmark doesn't say "unknown filter". It just ignores it. So I filter by price on my side. (The HTML search page does accept price[]=25-50 in its URL, but that's the /search path robots.txt disallows.)
  • count caps at 150. count: 100 returned 100 listings, count: 200 returned 150.
  • You probably can't page through everything. total_listing_count said 158,172 for "levis 501" and 4.7 million for "nike", but more.total was 5000 for every query I tried. That looks like a depth cap. I didn't page 5,000 deep to confirm it, but plan for narrow, filtered searches instead of "download everything".

Step 3: Clean rows (and three data quirks) 

# Condition codes seen in live data. Older listings use "not_nwt", some have none.
CONDITIONS = {"nwt": "New with tags", "uln": "Like new", "ug": "Good",
              "uf": "Fair", "not_nwt": "Used (older listing)"}


def money(obj, zero_is_missing=False):
    if not obj or not obj.get("val"):
        return None
    value = Decimal(obj["val"])
    return None if zero_is_missing and value == 0 else value


def to_row(p):
    inv = p.get("inventory") or {}
    return {
        "id": p["id"],
        "title": p.get("title", "").replace("\u200e", "").strip(),
        "brand": p.get("brand"),
        "size": p.get("size"),
        "condition": CONDITIONS.get(p.get("condition"), p.get("condition") or "n/a"),
        "price": money(p.get("price_amount")),
        "original_price": money(p.get("original_price_amount"), zero_is_missing=True),
        "first_price": money(p.get("first_user_price_amount")),
        "availability": inv.get("status"),
        "availability_changed_at": inv.get("status_changed_at"),
        "likes": p.get("like_count", 0),
        "comments": p.get("comment_count", 0),
        "seller": p.get("creator_username"),
        "listed_at": p.get("first_published_at"),
        "url": f"https://poshmark.com/listing/{p['id']}",
    }

What each workaround is for:

  1. Condition is a code. In a 150-listing "nike" sample I saw ug (96), uln (23), nwt (15), uf (6), and 10 listings with no condition key at all. The labels ("Like New", "Good", "Fair") come from a config blob inside the page HTML. Filtering on not_nwt returned listings whose condition really is not_nwt, which looks like the older used/not-used scheme.
  2. "Retail" price is usually zero. 111 of those 150 listings had original_price_amount of "0.0", meaning the seller left it blank. If you compute "discount from retail" without handling this, you'll divide by zero or report 100% discounts.
  3. Invisible characters in titles. Some sellers' titles contain U+200E (left-to-right mark), e.g. "Levis 501\u200e Jeans...". It's invisible on screen, but it breaks exact matching and deduping, so I strip it.

brand is free text, too. Filtering on "brand": ["Levi's"] changed the result count, but the brands that came back included Levi's 501, Levis 501, and levi's 501. Normalize brands yourself before you group by them.

The short https://poshmark.com/listing/<id> URL works. It returns a 301 redirect to the full slug URL.

Step 4: Sold comps

This is the part resellers care about. Same endpoint, with inventory_status: ["sold_out"]:

def sold_comps(query, max_pages=2, **filters):
    rows = [to_row(p) for p in search(query, max_pages=max_pages, sold=True, **filters)]
    prices = sorted(float(r["price"]) for r in rows if r["price"] is not None)
    if not prices:
        return rows, None
    q = statistics.quantiles(prices, n=4) if len(prices) >= 4 else [prices[0], prices[len(prices) // 2], prices[-1]]
    return rows, {"n": len(prices), "p25": q[0], "median": statistics.median(prices), "p75": q[-1]}

Real output for women's Levi's 501 jeans in size 28:

$ python poshmark_scraper.py comps "levis 501" --department Women --category Jeans --size 28
sold comps for 'levis 501' {'department': 'Women', 'category': 'Jeans', 'size': '28'}: {'n': 96, 'p25': 22.0, 'median': 30.0, 'p75': 40.0}
  sold 2026-10-22  $   45.0  Levi’s 501 She’s Crafty 150th Anniversary Floral Patch Jeans
  sold 2026-10-22  $   33.0  Levi's 501 90s Womens Jeans 28x32 Light Wash Straight Leg De
  sold 2026-10-18  $   30.0  Levi's 501 Light Blue Distressed Straight Women’s Jeans W28 
  sold 2026-10-21  $   44.0  Levi’s 501s
  sold 2026-10-06  $   30.0  Levi's 501 Straight Leg Button Fly Jeans Patchwork Raw Hem W

Read those numbers with care. price_amount on a sold listing is the last listed price. If the buyer paid with an accepted offer, I didn't find that amount anywhere in the response. Your "median sold price" is really a median of list prices at the time of sale, so it's probably a bit high.

Step 5: Closets and single listings

A closet uses the same request format at a different path. The profile is a separate call:

def closet(username, max_pages=3, **filters):
    return iter_pages(f"/users/{username}/posts/filtered",
                      build_request(None, **filters), max_pages)


def listing(id_or_url):
    m = re.search(r"([0-9a-f]{24})/?(?:[?#].*)?$", id_or_url)
    if not m:
        raise ValueError("expected a 24-character listing id or a /listing/ URL")
    return get(f"/posts/{m.group(1)}")  # no "data" wrapper on this one


def user(username):
    return get(f"/users/{username}")["data"]

Watch the response shapes. /users/{username} wraps the profile in data, but /posts/{id} returns the listing at the top level. The profile's aggregates object has the useful numbers: posts, followers, following, shares, seller_orders_shipped, items_sold_display (a rounded string like "100+", not an exact number), and last_active_date.

$ python poshmark_scraper.py closet shopladydeals --pages 1
shopladydeals: 617 listings, 14411 followers, items sold: 100+, last active 2026-10-21
    11 likes  $   19.0  Motherhood Maternity Pants Women's Yoga z Small Gray Full Pa
     4 likes  $   24.0  Duluth Trading Men's Long Sleeve Beige Waffle Henley Shirt S
     3 likes  $   35.0  Tommy Hilfiger Sunglasses for men Matte Black and Tortoise s

The profile also returns the seller's first and last name and some linked-account IDs. My closet command only prints aggregate counts. Do the same unless you have a real reason to keep personal data.

Step 6: A price-drop tracker in SQLite

Poshmark sellers drop prices all the time. To catch drops, save a snapshot on every run and compare each listing with its price in the previous run:

def track(query, db_path="poshmark.db", max_pages=2, **filters):
    key = json.dumps({"q": query, **filters}, sort_keys=True)
    taken_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc).replace(microsecond=0).isoformat()
    rows = [to_row(p) for p in search(query, max_pages=max_pages, **filters)]
    con = sqlite3.connect(db_path)
    con.executescript(SCHEMA)  # snapshots(taken_at, search_key, id, title, ..., price, availability, likes)
    con.executemany(
        "INSERT OR IGNORE INTO snapshots VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?)",
        [(taken_at, key, r["id"], r["title"], r["brand"], r["size"], r["seller"],
          str(r["price"]) if r["price"] is not None else None, r["availability"], r["likes"])
         for r in rows],
    )
    con.commit()
    changes = con.execute(
        """
        WITH runs AS (
          SELECT DISTINCT taken_at FROM snapshots WHERE search_key = ?
          ORDER BY taken_at DESC LIMIT 2
        ),
        cur  AS (SELECT * FROM snapshots WHERE search_key = ? AND taken_at = (SELECT MAX(taken_at) FROM runs)),
        prev AS (SELECT * FROM snapshots WHERE search_key = ? AND taken_at = (SELECT MIN(taken_at) FROM runs))
        SELECT cur.id, cur.title, prev.price, cur.price
        FROM cur JOIN prev ON cur.id = prev.id
        WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM runs) = 2 AND CAST(cur.price AS REAL) < CAST(prev.price AS REAL)
        ORDER BY CAST(prev.price AS REAL) - CAST(cur.price AS REAL) DESC
        """, (key, key, key)).fetchall()
    con.close()
    return rows, changes

Run it:

$ python poshmark_scraper.py track "levis 501" --department Women --category Jeans --size 28 --pages 2
96 available listings for 'levis 501' {'department': 'Women', 'category': 'Jeans', 'size': '28'}
  $  16.0 (no retail)       28 Good          501 Levi's denim
  $  16.0 (no retail)       28 Good          Levis Premium 501 Light Wash Straight Leg Raw
  $  17.0 (no retail)       28 Like new      Levi's 501 High Rise Straight Cropped Jeans L
  $  19.0 (retail $75.0)    28 Good          Levi's 501 high waisted skinny women's jeans
  $  19.0 (no retail)       28 Fair          Levi’s 501 Curve Jeans
0 price drops since the previous run

Honest note: I ran it a few times a couple of minutes apart, and it found zero drops, which is what you'd expect over that short a window. Put it in cron once or twice a day and the drop list fills up. --max-price 25 filters on your side (remember that the server ignores price filters). With that flag, the same search came down to 26 listings.
