Two design choices worth knowing about:

  • Only listings that appear in both runs are compared. Search results move around, so a listing that drops off page 2 isn't "removed". It's just out of view. Narrow filters with fewer total results make the tracker more reliable.
  • Prices are stored as text so Decimal values round-trip exactly. Cast them in SQL when comparing.

The full script, with a small CLI (track, comps, closet, listing), is about 240 lines.

The walls you'll hit

  • Undocumented endpoints. vm-rest is the website's internal API. The JSON-in-a-query-parameter format, filter names, and response shapes can change at any time. Log loudly when a field you expect is missing.
  • Silent filter failures. An unknown or wrong filter is ignored, not rejected. After every change, check that total_listing_count actually moved.
  • HTTP 200 errors. Check for the error key every time.
  • Search depth. more.total says 5000 even when there are millions of matches. Split big searches by category, size, or condition.
  • Sold prices aren't transaction prices. Accepted offers and bundle discounts aren't visible in what I pulled.
  • Free-text brands and missing fields. Normalize brands, and expect condition or retail price to be missing.
  • Scale. 30 requests at about one per second went through fine from a single server IP. Polling thousands of searches is a different story, and I didn't test it.

When DIY stops being worth it

For a few saved searches checked once or twice a day, the script above is plenty. It gets tedious when you need server-side price filters, many closets, or data the search endpoint doesn't give you, like seller reviews or Posh Parties. Then you're maintaining a reverse-engineered client.

That's the point where I'd use a hosted API. I use ScrapeAtlas* for this. Its GET /v1/poshmark/search takes query, department, category, size, condition, availability (available, sold, or all), sort, minPrice/maxPrice (so price filtering happens on the server), plus cursor and limit:

import os
import requests

def api_sold(query, cursor=None):
    params = {"query": query, "department": "Women", "category": "Jeans",
              "size": "28", "availability": "sold", "maxPrice": "60"}
    if cursor:
        params["cursor"] = cursor
    res = requests.get(
        "https://api.scrapeatlas.com/v1/poshmark/search",
        params=params,
        headers={"x-api-key": os.environ["SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY"]},
        timeout=60,
    )
    res.raise_for_status()
    data = res.json()
    # data["status"] is "success" or "partial"; data["coverage"]["warnings"] explains gaps
    return data.get("listings", []), data.get("nextCursor")

The listings keep Poshmark's field names (price_amount, original_price_amount, inventory, like_count, ...), so most of to_row() keeps working. There are also /v1/poshmark/listing, /closet, /profile, /love-notes (the five-star reviews on a closet's About page), and /parties with /party-listings.

Wrapping up

  • Skip the HTML. Poshmark's site loads its data from vm-rest JSON endpoints that answer plain GET requests.
  • Send a JSON request parameter, and check that every filter actually changes the result count. Price filters don't.
  • Look for error in 200 responses.
  • Clean up the data: condition codes, "0.0" retail prices, free-text brands, and invisible characters in titles.
  • Sold comps are list prices, not exact transaction prices. They're still the best pricing signal you can get for free.

Found a filter key I missed, or a field that moved? Tell me in the comments and I'll fold it into the script.

*I build it.

title: ByBet Casino: A Closer Look at Its Mobile Gaming Experience
description:
A casino page may look sharp on a phone, yet smooth use needs more than bright tiles. Small screens make menu size, load time, and cash status harder to judge than desktop pages. For Filipino adults aged 21+, these details matter when game sites handle both money and private data.

The ByBet Casino website says its games and account pages work on phones and tablets. It lists slots, live tables, promotions, and banking, though its speed claims lack public test results. This review studies mobile user experience through public pages, without claiming access to private test data.

Mobile Friendly Claims Need More Than A Label

The homepage calls its mobile pages easy to use and quick to load on many phones. It also claims that smaller screens retain key features, including game menus and banking tools. Those are site claims, not proof of quick loads on each phone or mobile network.

A good phone review asks whether tabs stay clear when screens turn narrow or tall. Text should stay easy to read without zoom, while tabs should respond to light taps. A layout that fits one phone may still fail on another screen or browser version.

The site's Login and Register links lead to bybet.com, not to an account page here. That change shows the guide and account service play distinct roles for people who use phones. A safe handoff needs a clear web address, so users know which site now gets their data.

Touch Menus Reveal Problems That Desktop Screens Hide

ByBet's homepage groups slot games, live casino games, and specialty games under separate page sections. On small screens, large tap zones and clear labels help users tell these groups apart. A bright game tile is not enough if nearby controls are too small to select.

A good test would check scrolling, back links, and page shifts without making any paid bets. Tests should cover screen turns and text size changes, which can push tabs out of view. No published test proves those checks pass, so claims about the design still need real proof.

Live Casino Video Adds Pressure To Weak Connections

The site lists live blackjack, baccarat, and roulette alongside its main groups of slot games. Unlike still images, live video needs a steady stream to keep a dealer in clear view. A clear picture does not prove a bet was accepted, since video and wager logs differ.

When data drops, the screen may lag while a game server keeps its own round log. The player may see a late frame, though the account could show a settled round already. A late screen is not proof of a changed result, which needs a full log check.

For coders, network tests should track failed loads, long pauses, and switches from WiFi to data. A good report must state the phone and network used, not claim fast speeds for all. The site does not publish such test logs, so its speed claims remain unproved in this review.

Payment Screens Need Clear Status And Error Messages

The homepage names GCash, Maya, and bank transfers as ways to move funds in the Philippines. A phone cashier should show whether a payment is pending, done, or declined after each request. A wallet charge alone does not prove the game balance changed, as two systems hold separate logs.

A good error screen needs a clear status and reference code, without showing private account data. Small screens should keep cancel and retry taps far apart, to cut the risk of mistakes. No live cashier test was done here, so the site's cash claims lack direct checks.

Phone Browsers Carry Privacy And Session Risks

The site's privacy page says it may gather device type, browser details, IP address, and cookies. It also lists account, cash, and game activity data, which could put private details at risk. A privacy policy states intended rules, but cannot prove all safeguards work in real life.

On a shared phone, saved logins and browser history may leave account clues in sight for others. Moving from the guide to the account site can also change the web address shown. The full domain matters more than a logo, mainly before users type a password or code.

The homepage has an age notice for adults over 21, plus links to safer play guidance. Those links explain age rules and support, but do not prove live checks of a person's age. An age popup does not replace ID checks, and mobile ease must not weaken those steps.

Developers Can Test The Journey Without Guessing Results

A fair test starts with a small screen, slow data, and clear notes on each page change. It checks tap size, text wrap, and load states, rather than treating bright icons as proof. Test results should name the phone and date, since sites and phone software can change.

Another test tracks the jump from guide page to login page, and notes each web address. It should flag strange redirects and missing error text, but should never store real account secrets. An open guide page cannot prove private account behavior, which would need a separate test.

JavaScript Example: Checking Mobile Layout With Playwright

// Illustrative test only; no results are claimed.
// Setup: npm install playwright
// Then: npx playwright install chromium
// Save as mobile-layout.mjs
// Run: node mobile-layout.mjs

import { chromium } from "playwright";

const browser = await chromium.launch();

try {
  for (const width of [360, 390, 430]) {
    const context = await browser.newContext({
      viewport: { width, height: 800 },
      isMobile: true,
      hasTouch: true
    });

    try {
      const page = await context.newPage();

      await page.goto("https://bybetcasino.net/", {
        waitUntil: "domcontentloaded"
      });

      const result = await page.evaluate(() => ({
        viewportWidth: document.documentElement.clientWidth,
        contentWidth: document.documentElement.scrollWidth
      }));

      const overflow = Math.max(
        0,
        result.contentWidth - result.viewportWidth
      );

      console.log({
        screenWidth: width,
        horizontalOverflowPx: overflow,
        needsLayoutReview: overflow > 0
      });
    } finally {
      await context.close();
    }
  }
} finally {
  await browser.close();
}

Illustrative, read-only test using Playwright and Chromium. It checks page-wide horizontal overflow at three mobile viewport widths without logging into accounts or placing bets. Results have not been collected, and passing this check alone does not establish full mobile accessibility.

Public Claims And Verified Experience Must Stay Separate

The site presents mobile access as a core feature, but posts no public phone test report. That leaves load speed and live table stability as open questions, not as proven strengths. A developer review must separate site claims from test results, or it becomes sales copy.

For readers, game menus, account pages, and payment screens need distinct checks on each phone. Fast menus do not prove instant cashouts, and smooth reels do not verify a game provider's license. Good mobile design means clear states and honest limits, not a promise of wins or safety.

The ByBet Casino mobile gaming section describes access through phones, tablets, and the site's main features. Its public claims cover game menus and banking access, but lack independent phone speed tests. The main point remains: phone access is advertised, yet public tests do not prove claimed speeds.

title: A wrong "closed" never comes back: measuring a job-posting liveness checker on real pages
description:
career-ops is an open-source job-search pipeline: Node.js scripts driven by AI coding CLIs, with about 76k stars on GitHub. Before it adds a posting to your pipeline, scan --verify checks that the posting is still open. Where the job board has a public API, it asks the API. Otherwise it loads the page in a headless browser and reads it.

A "closed" or "blocked" verdict goes into your scan history for good, and that posting is skipped on every later scan. So the two ways to be wrong cost very different amounts. A wrong "open" costs one more check later. A wrong "closed" makes a live job disappear from your search without a trace.

Between 3 and 20 October 2026 I had 16 pull requests merged into career-ops, most of them in this liveness checker. This is what I found, how I measured it, and what the fixes look like.

How I found the bugs

The board was busy: 135 open PRs and 208 open issues on 11 October. The project's CONTRIBUTING lets bug fixes go in without an issue, so instead of competing for claimed issues I read modules nobody was working on. I started with the ATS keyword and CV skill checks, which are close to my NLP background, then moved to the liveness checker.

For the checker, I ran it on real postings and read every disagreement. The sources were public job-postings datasets (LinkedIn, USAJOBS) and live boards without an API. Several fixes also came out of the project's own conversations: a merge note from the maintainer, a follow-up the review bot offered, and three follow-ups from my reviews of other contributors' PRs.

A blocked tracker took the whole page down

Many people run a DNS filter that blocks ads and trackers: Pi-hole, AdGuard DNS, Control D, a hosts-file blocklist. Such a filter answers 0.0.0.0 for a tracker it blocks.

The browser check has a security guard that refuses requests to private network addresses, and 0.0.0.0 is on its list. Refusing the tracker is right. But the guard also marked the whole page "blocked", which scan --verify records permanently.

I found it while reviewing another contributor's PR that touches how the guard handles DNS answers. To measure it, I took 35 postings on 19 boards with no API, all live the day before, and checked each one with main's code and with the fix, behind two real filtering resolvers and with no filter as a control:

  • On main, 12 postings behind AdGuard DNS and 20 behind Control D read "blocked".
  • With the fix, none did. Behind Control D, 11 of those 20 read active with a visible Apply button.
  • With no filter, both versions agreed on 32 of 35. The 3 differences were flaky page loads, in both directions.

The fix (#5015) leaves the guard's decision alone. The request is still refused, with the same error. The guard only tags the refusal when the only private addresses in the answer are the filter's:

  if (blocked.length > 0) {
    const denied = new Error(`Access denied: Egress guard blocked private target IP ${blocked[0].ip}`);
    if (blocked.every(({ hit }) => SINKHOLE_ADDRESSES.has(hit))) denied.livenessCode = 'dns_sinkhole';
    throw denied;
  }

A tagged refusal of a tracker, a script or an image no longer decides the page's verdict. Any other private address still counts, even next to 0.0.0.0. I rejected the simpler option, ignoring every private answer for subresources, because it would drop the guard's signal on a host that really resolves into a private network.

The follow-up, #5075, covers the posting's own host. When that host had no usable address, the guard reported "blocked". But no address is often about the run, not the posting: a DNS outage during the scan, or the user's own filter blocking the job board. Now it reads uncertain, and the posting is kept for another check. With the posting's own host failing DNS, 19 of 19 postings from 19 boards were dropped permanently on main, and 19 of 19 were kept with the fix.

The PR states the trade-off: a domain that is really gone now reads uncertain too, because one failed lookup can't tell a dead domain from an outage. A kept dead posting costs one more check later. A pinned live one never comes back.

One failed load failed the rest of the run

This one turned up while I was measuring another fix: a posting whose host no longer resolved broke the checks after it in the same run. I reproduced it on the code from before my DNS change, to rule that out, and traced it to the browser library the next day.

The checker runs every browser check in one tab. When a page fails to load (its host has no address, its certificate has expired, its connection is reset), the browser shows its error page a moment after the checker has moved on, and that interrupts the next page load. The interrupted page then finishes loading late and interrupts the one after it, often to the end of the run. Those checks fail as load errors, so scan --verify keeps the postings without having checked them, and the closed ones among them go into the user's pipeline. The root is a known Playwright issue (microsoft/playwright#35944, closed upstream without a fix).

Through the real CLI, on one list of 45 URLs with 6 failing loads spread among 39 postings that were live the day before:

  • On main, 39 of 39 postings read as load errors, from the first URL to the last.
  • With the fix, none did: 30 active, 1 expired (HTTP 404), 6 "no Apply control", 1 Cloudflare challenge and 1 timeout.

Over 36 failed loads, the browser's error page landed 1 to 69 ms after the failure was reported, median 4 ms. So the fix (#5299) waits for the browser's own signal instead of a fixed delay, for at most 2 s:

async function navigateSettled(page, navigate) {
  try {
    return await navigate();
  } catch (err) {
    const canWait = typeof page.waitForEvent === 'function' && typeof page.mainFrame === 'function';
    if (canWait && err?.name !== 'TimeoutError') {
      await page
        .waitForEvent('framenavigated', {
          predicate: (frame) => frame === page.mainFrame() && frame.url().startsWith('chrome-error:'),
          timeout: FAILED_NAVIGATION_COMMIT_MS,
        })
        .catch(() => {});
    }
    throw err;
  }
}

A timeout is left alone: a timed-out load shows no error page, and the next load cancels it, so waiting would only add 2 s. I rejected parking the tab on a blank page after a failure, which another part of the code does after a search, because that load is interrupted the same way. The review bot pointed out that the old page changing its own address could end the wait too early. I couldn't make that happen in real Chromium in 26 tries, but fixed it anyway, with a test the first version fails.

CI installs no browser, so the tests use a stand-in page that plays out the browser's order of events. The same sequences also run on real Chromium where it can launch.

A ground truth showed a case the issue had missed

I filed #4832 for live postings on seven non-English boards that read as having no Apply button. getManfred, a Spanish tech-job board, was one. Its Apply button says "¡Apúntame!" ("sign me up"), which the checker didn't know, so every live posting read "no Apply control".

getManfred's own feed marks every offer open or closed, so the A/B could measure against the board instead of against my reading of pages. The first run showed a case the issue had missed: one closed posting read open on both versions. Closed postings written in English often have an FAQ button such as "Can I apply if I live outside Spain?", and the English Apply pattern took it for an Apply button.

The page does say the offer is closed, but that sentence renders near the bottom, after the checker's first look on some pages. Above the title, from the start, a closed posting says when it closed ("Oferta cerrada el 27/07/2023"). Closing patterns are read before the Apply button, so an FAQ button can't outvote the date. The fix (#5350) is two patterns:

  /\boferta cerrada el \d{1,2}\/\d{1,2}\/\d{4}/i,  // a closing pattern, read before the Apply button
  /\bapuntame\b/i,                                // an Apply label, accent-free like the others

I left out the verb "aplicar": 73 of the 111 getManfred pages I measured have an FAQ button that uses it, closed ones included. On 136 real page loads:

  • Live: all 28 open offers read active with the fix. On main, 25 read "no Apply control", and the other 3 read active only through their FAQ button.
  • Closed: all 83 read closed with the fix. On main, 17 read active, all of them written in English and read through the FAQ button.

The board already knew the answer

No Fluff Jobs, a Polish tech-job board, was the last of my board families from #4832, and the checker read it backwards. A live posting puts its Apply button ("Aplikuj") inside a page header, which the checker skips as page chrome, so every live posting read "no Apply control". A closed posting moves to a search page with a promo link that also says "Aplikuj", so most closed postings read as open.

I'd planned label patterns. Then I found that the board's per-posting API says directly whether a posting is open. So the fix (#5428) is an API rung, as several other boards already have. The API answers "published" (open), "expired" (closed) or "does not exist". A status the rung doesn't know reads uncertain, never closed, and an answer it can't read falls back to the browser.

Through the real CLI on 102 postings (40 live from the board's search API, 59 closed from Wayback Machine archives, 1 gone and 2 made up):

  • On main, all 40 live postings read "no Apply control", and 42 of the 59 closed ones read active.
  • With the fix, 40 of 40 read active and 59 of 59 read closed, without opening a browser: 26 s against 348 s.

The review bot raised two valid points on it. I measured that they change no verdict on today's API answers and shipped them as a follow-up, #5533.

VDAB, the job board of Flanders' public employment service, looks like the second case. A closed vacancy there keeps its page and its Apply button, and only a banner says it's closed. Reading the page while it renders, main read 13 of 84 loads of closed vacancies as open. My open PR, #5703, asks VDAB's per-vacancy API, which the page itself uses. One choice in it is deliberate: a "pending" vacancy reads uncertain, not closed, because one pending vacancy had never been published at all, and a closed verdict is recorded for good.

How each fix was tested

Every PR adds tests that fail on main and pass with the fix. I checked each one with mutation variants: deliberately broken versions of the fix that the tests must catch. On #4810, 13 of 13 were caught; on #4833, 12 of 12. I also ran the full suite on each branch against main. Over three weeks it grew from about 11,600 to about 16,800 tests.

Among the things the maintainer's merge notes thanked were the edge-case tests: in the keyword check, the ones that keep "IT", "HR" and "AWS" from matching ordinary words; in the checker, the one for a button that is hidden or sits in the navigation.

The rest of the work

  • Four fixes to the ATS keyword-coverage and CV skill-gap checks. The keyword check, for one, looked for a single English heading, so reports in the translated modes stopped with an error. Here is the same report under each mode's heading on main, from #4725: 
  en  ## Keywords extracted         exit 0  coverage 80%
  de  ## Extrahierte Keywords       exit 1  No "## Keywords extracted" block found (or it is empty).
  es  ## Palabras clave extraídas   exit 1  same
  ko  ## 추출한 키워드              exit 1  same
  zh  ## ATS 关键词提取             exit 1  same

On the branch, all five exit 0 at 80%.

  • One fix to the Gupy provider, whose API had moved to another host. It closed #4831, which I filed.
  • Reviews of five other contributors' liveness and scan PRs, all merged. Four authors applied my findings or suggested tests before merge, and a fifth took my suggestion into a new version.
  • #4832 is closed: every board in it has a merged fix. We split it by approach instead of racing. The contributor who wrote the providers for its Chinese boards moved them to per-posting APIs, another contributor took CareerViet, and I did the Dutch boards, getManfred and No Fluff Jobs.

Three more PRs are open: #5535 (HiringRoom's "Postularse" label, approved), #5691 (Tech in Asia's Apply link in the page header) and #5703 (VDAB's API). Since 9 October I've been on the project's contributors team. Thanks to the maintainer for quick merges and for merge notes that say exactly what they valued.

What I learned

  • Mistakes aren't symmetric when a pipeline makes permanent decisions. A false "open" costs one more check later. A false "closed" can't be undone. Most of my liveness fixes move an unsure case from permanent to retry-next-time.
  • Find a ground truth before trusting an A/B. getManfred's feed and VDAB's API measured the fixes, not my reading of pages. getManfred's feed also showed a case the issue had missed.
  • Look for the board's own API before patching the page reader. No Fluff Jobs looked like a label-and-pattern job. Its API answered both sides directly, needed no browser, and left the rules every board shares untouched.
  • Measure before changing a rule every board shares. The header skip looked like a bug on every board, but 821 real pages from 268 sites showed it hid only one board's Apply button. So #5691 (open) reads one narrow case, a link to the posting's own page, instead of every button in every header.
  • Separate the change from the page. Live pages differ from one load to the next, so two runs can disagree for reasons that have nothing to do with the code. Running both versions on the same loaded page at the same moment settles it: on #5691's control pages, all 5 verdict differences came with identical button lists.
  • Some bugs live between two systems. The failed-load chain came from the browser and its automation library disagreeing about when a failed load is over. Waiting for the browser's own signal stops the chain, at a cost of a few milliseconds per failed load.
  • Reviews count as contributions. Reviewing another contributor's DNS change led straight to the bug #5015 fixes.

All 16 merged PRs: https://github.com/career-ops-hq/career-ops/pulls?q=is%3Apr+is%3Amerged+author%3Aroydonsequeira

title: Your Agent Boots. Phoenix Still Doesn’t Know It Exists.
description:
A MatrixOS agent can start, emit a beacon, and do useful work—while Phoenix’s swarm workspace still has no idea it exists. That is not a mysterious boot failure. It is usually a missing contract between two projects.

The agent source defines what the process does. Phoenix’s per-agent metadata file tells the workspace how to find, configure, constrain, and present that agent. Leave out either half and you get the software equivalent of an operator arriving at the gate with a working radio and no badge. The radio is excellent. The gate remains unimpressed.

This walkthrough follows the real layout: an agent package in MatrixOS, a JSON manifest in Phoenix, and optional configuration editors and custom panels. We’ll also look at how Phoenix treats signing and certificate requirements, so nobody puts a private key in a JSON file and calls it “automation.”

Two projects, two jobs

Keep the responsibilities separate:

MatrixOS repository
└── agents/python_core/shift_scribe/
    ├── __init__.py
    └── shift_scribe.py              # runtime behavior

Phoenix repository
├── agents_meta/shift_scribe.json    # workspace contract and defaults
└── matrix_gui/
    ├── swarm_workspace/cls_lib/agent/config_editors/
    │   └── shift_scribe.py          # optional configuration dialog
    └── core/panel/custom_panels/shift_scribe/
        └── status_panel.py          # optional custom controls

The metadata file belongs to the agent type, not to each swarm instance. Phoenix reads the JSON files in agents_meta to populate the agent palette. When you add an agent to a workspace, its defaults become the starting configuration for that node; the workspace then saves the operator’s edits.

1. Start with the MatrixOS source skeleton

Create a package whose folder and Python module share the agent’s snake_case name. The environment path setup must run before imports from the MatrixOS tree. Guard each environment value: os.getenv() can return None, and sys.path.insert(0, None) is not a fun way to begin a mission.

Here is a small scaffold based on the supplied template. It includes the mixin import that the original snippet needs, and uses consistent spaces:

import os
import sys

for env_name in ("SITE_ROOT", "AGENT_PATH"):
    env_path = os.getenv(env_name)
    if env_path and env_path not in sys.path:
        sys.path.insert(0, env_path)

from core.python_core.boot_agent import BootAgent
from core.python_core.mixin.reflex_alert import ReflexAlertMixin
from core.python_core.utils.swarm_sleep import interruptible_sleep
from core.python_core.class_lib.packet_delivery.utility.encryption.utility import (
    identity,
)
IdentityObject = identity.IdentityObject


class Agent(BootAgent, ReflexAlertMixin):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.AGENT_VERSION = "1.0.0"

        # BootAgent loads the directive in super().
        cfg = self.tree_node.get("config", {})
        self.report_role = cfg.get(
            "report_to_role", "hive.forensics.data_feed"
        )
        self.alert_role = cfg.get("alert_to_role", "hive.rpc")
        self.interval = int(cfg.get("interval", 30))

        # Monitor the worker thread.
        self._emit_beacon = self.check_for_thread_poke(
            "worker", timeout=60, emit_to_file_interval=10
        )

    def worker_pre(self):
        self.log("Shift Scribe on station.")

    def post_boot(self):
        self.log("Shift Scribe booted. Ready.")

    def worker(
        self,
        config: dict = None,
        identity: IdentityObject = None,
    ): 
        cfg = config or self.tree_node.get("config", {})
        self._emit_beacon()
        self.log("Worker cycle complete.")
        interval = int(cfg.get("interval", self.interval))
        interruptible_sleep(self, interval)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    agent = Agent()
    agent.boot()

The bootstrap and imports are the load-bearing part of the source contract. Keep lifecycle methods and the worker(config, identity) signature in the shape expected by the MatrixOS runtime. BootAgent provides the loaded tree_node; read this agent’s settings from its config, then supply sensible fallbacks. Use interruptible_sleep for a recurring worker so the runtime can stop it cleanly. Emit a beacon for the actual worker thread you want monitored.

The sample you supplied also imports threading, datetime, and OrderedDict. Add those only when the implementation uses them. Python will not award extra professionalism points for unused imports. If a class inherits from ReflexAlertMixin, import it; otherwise the class definition will fail before the first log line gets its moment in the sun.

The example worker is intentionally boring in the productive way: it reads configuration, reports liveness, does one cycle, and sleeps. Replace the log line with the agent’s job. Add dedicated threads only when the work needs them, and give each monitored thread its own beacon.

2. Add the Phoenix meta-file

Create agents_meta/shift_scribe.json. The filename stem and the name should match exactly; Phoenix uses that name to find the manifest and the runtime package. Here is a starter manifest:

{
  "name": "shift_scribe",
  "universal_id": "shift-scribe",
  "constraints": [
    {
      "packet_signing": {
        "in": true,
        "out": true
      }
    }
  ],
  "config": {
    "ui": {
      "agent_tree": {
        "emoji": "🧭"
      }
    },
    "interval": 30,
    "report_to_role": "hive.forensics.data_feed",
    "alert_to_role": "hive.rpc"
  }
}

The top-level fields have distinct jobs:

  • name is the stable agent-type name used by Phoenix’s palette and module lookup. Keep it aligned with the MatrixOS folder and module.
  • universal_id is useful metadata, but a workspace node gets its own runtime identity when it is added. Don’t hard-code one live swarm instance ID into a reusable agent type.
  • constraints declares requirements the workspace must resolve. Phoenix checks that a constraint has a registered editor or auto-generation handler; an unknown name is not a wish Phoenix can grant.
  • config holds defaults and Phoenix UI hints. The workspace copies these into a new node, and the agent reads the operational values from its directive.

The little compass under config.ui.agent_tree.emoji is the return icon: it labels the agent in the palette/tree. Pick an emoji that survives your terminal font and looks different from the other thirty-seven shields.

3. Let constraints provision security material

Phoenix’s constraints are more than badges. They tell the workspace and deployment path what resources an agent needs. For example, the real matrix_https metadata declares packet signing in both directions, a connection certificate, and HTTPS transport:

"constraints": [
  { "packet_signing": { "in": true, "out": true } },
  { "connection_cert": {} },
  { "https": {} }
]

If the agent needs to phone home to Phoenix, give it a signing key pair. In this metadata, packet_signing in and out are both enabled: the agent needs its private signing key for outbound packets and the appropriate public key to verify inbound traffic. Phoenix’s registered packet_signing auto-generation handler creates the key material during deployment and injects only the fields required by the directive. The connection-certificate handler can likewise generate certificate bundles. For connection certificates, the transport matters: the current injection map uses them for HTTPS and WSS connections.

That is the point of declaring the requirement in the type metadata: Phoenix can ask for or generate the matching resource and block deployment when a required item is unresolved. It does not mean you should paste a private key or certificate into the public meta-file. Keep secrets in Phoenix’s protected vault/provisioning path, and let the deployment flow inject only what the agent needs.

Use a constraint name the Phoenix version actually registers. If you invent a new one, you must also implement and register the editor or auto-generation handler. Otherwise the workspace can reject the agent before deployment—with the digital equivalent of “your paperwork is in a language we do not speak.”

4. Defaults, configuration editors, and panels

Put ordinary operational defaults under config: polling intervals, paths, role names, safe-mode flags, or feature toggles. The MatrixOS agent should still validate values and apply defensive fallbacks; a default is not input validation wearing a nicer jacket.

Phoenix has a useful fallback for configuration. When an operator double-clicks an agent node, it looks for a module named after the agent under config_editors and a class named in CamelCase. For shift_scribe, that means:

matrix_gui/swarm_workspace/cls_lib/agent/config_editors/shift_scribe.py
class ShiftScribe(...)

If no specialized editor exists, Phoenix uses its generic editor for simple fields. A custom editor is worthwhile when the config needs typed controls, validation, grouped sections, or role pickers. Its save action should update the node’s config and mark the workspace dirty.

A custom operations panel is a separate, optional module. Add its path to config.ui.panel, for example:

"ui": {
  "agent_tree": { "emoji": "🧭" },
  "panel": ["shift_scribe.status_panel"]
}

Then create matrix_gui/core/panel/custom_panels/shift_scribe/status_panel.py. Phoenix resolves that dotted path beneath custom_panels, imports the module, and looks for a class named StatusPanel. Custom panels implement the Phoenix panel interface and can contribute buttons or views for agent-specific operations. If you declare a panel path, ship the matching module and class; otherwise Phoenix will politely log that the panel is missing and continue without it.

5. Service roles are the command contract

A service-manager entry advertises service roles and handlers that can be routed to the agent. It is not the custom panel itself. A simplified entry might look like:

"service-manager": [
  {
    "role": ["shift_scribe.status@cmd_status"],
    "scope": ["parent", "any"]
  }
]

The agent must implement the matching handler, and any custom panel button that calls it must send a compatible service request. Think of the role string as the radio frequency: listing it in Phoenix does not install a radio in the agent. Keep the declared role, handler name, payload shape, and panel request aligned.

The existing matrix_https manifest shows this pattern with perimeter toggle and status roles. Its config.ui.panel points to matrix_https.matrix_https; that path leads to a real custom panel, while service-manager lists the services it can request. One is the cockpit; the other is the set of commands it can call. They work together, but they are not interchangeable.

6. Put the two halves together and verify

Before adding the new type to a real swarm, check the small integration contract:

  1. In MatrixOS, confirm the folder, init.py, module name, Agent class, imports, and lifecycle methods follow the existing agents under agents/python_core.
  2. In Phoenix, confirm agents_meta/shift_scribe.json parses and its filename, name, and MatrixOS package agree.
  3. Add the type in the Swarm Workspace palette. Confirm the icon appears, drag it into a test workspace, and inspect the constraints Phoenix loaded.
  4. Open its configuration. Check defaults, save an edit, and reopen it. If you declared a custom editor or panel, verify its module and CamelCase class load.
  5. Resolve the required constraints and deploy to a test environment. Verify the directive contains the intended config and provisioned fields, then confirm the worker logs, beacons, and service handlers behave as expected.

If the agent is missing from the palette, begin with the JSON path and filename. If it appears but cannot be added, inspect the constraint registry. If the worker boots but behaves as though every setting is None, compare the editor’s saved config keys with the names read by the agent. If the panel button appears to salute and then do nothing, compare its service request with the role and handler that the agent actually registered.

That is the whole handoff: MatrixOS owns behavior; Phoenix metadata describes how to assemble and operate the type; optional Phoenix modules provide richer editing and controls. The meta-file is not decorative paperwork. It is the map that gets the agent from “Python class exists” to “operator can add it, configure it, provision it, and use it.”

Victory Always.

🌐 Links & Resources:

  • MatrixOS source: https://github.com/matrixswarm/matrixos
  • Phoenix source: https://github.com/matrixswarm/phoenix
  • Try MatrixSwarm: https://matrixswarm.com
  • Join the Community / Discord: https://discord.gg/2USbWVBVV
  • YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCMjiY4_-W2KP5fHXO0eC2ug

title: A Small Model Asks Better: Fine-Tuning Query Clarification for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.28686v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Query clarification is essential for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems that face ambiguous user queries. We consider multi-turn grounded conversational scenarios where a user query is either ill-formed or ambiguous in the context of the prior dialog or, more interestingly, it may be well-formed but when posed against retrieved documents there are multiple relevant interpretations. The task is to recognize both such cases and then generate an appropriate clarification request to the user. We present ClariEdge, a new dataset of approximately 3,900 examples that include such ambiguous queries along with negative examples that do not require clarification. We also show that a lightweight fine-tuned LoRA achieves 96.6% classification accuracy and outperforms prompted baselines of many larger models on both classification and quality of clarification generation. Our study shows that hard negatives are an essential ingredient to separate out queries that are truly ambiguous from queries that may look ambiguous but are not (i.e., can be resolved from the context). The same LoRA achieves high performance in both pre-retrieval and post-retrieval scenarios; thus, it can be used in two places in a RAG pipeline as a check before answer generation. The ClariEdge dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ibm-research/ClariEdge.

title: Scaling in Games: Continued Pre-Training For Embodied Agents In Diverse Virtual Worlds
description:
arXiv:2610.28698v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scaling data, diversity and model capacity has improved embodied learning in physical environments, where diverse experiences remain grounded in shared physical laws. Whether these gains extend to virtual worlds with different visual styles, dynamics, controls, and objectives remains unclear. We investigate this question through a controlled study of continued pre-training (CPT) across three axes: data volume, diversity, and model size. Our 120 training configurations span four model sizes from 0.8B to 27B, six data budgets from 50 to 1,600 hours, and five mixtures ranging from Minecraft-only data to diverse multi-world corpora. We assess performance and generalization using three-level validation losses and gameplay benchmarks from in-corpus worlds to unseen worlds. Our results show: (1) more data improves in-corpus performance, diversity improves transfer to related worlds with limited gains in distant worlds, and model size improves data efficiency but generalizes worse to distant worlds under single-world training; (2) we observe an early interface phase with broad cross-world benefits and a later world phase with gains narrowed to in-corpus and related worlds, and fit an empirical scaling law relating validation loss to data volume, diversity and model size; and (3) our models are competitive with Minecraft specialists and frontier models in 3D worlds, and perform best in real-time settings. However, the limits of imitation and persistent gaps in distant worlds suggest that building generalist embodied agents requires richer training stages beyond continued pre-training.

title: SpecEvo: Speculative Evolution with Large Language Models for Cost-Efficient Scientific Discovery
description:
arXiv:2610.28706v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-driven evolutionary search is a promising paradigm for scientific discovery, but existing methods remain costly and slow, often applying expensive reasoning uniformly while underusing evidence from failed, redundant, and saturated trials. We introduce Speculative Evolution (SpecEvo), a multi-LLM framework that coordinates lightweight and frontier models through continual consolidation of search evidence. Lightweight models power both parallel Speculators, which generate and refine candidate programs, and an Advisor, which distills accumulated successes, failures, and saturated directions into persistent guidance for subsequent exploration. At sparse checkpoints, a frontier-model Navigator inspects the evolving population and intervenes through synthesis, surgical refinement, or reframing according to search stagnation. This speculate-then-consolidate workflow delegates routine exploration and evidence consolidation to inexpensive models while reserving frontier reasoning for strategic interventions whose benefits extend across many subsequent low-cost evaluations. Across 176 tasks spanning four scientific and algorithmic discovery domains, SpecEvo matches or outperforms frontier-model baselines while reducing API cost by up to 80%, achieves up to 1.5x greater evaluation efficiency than cost-efficient baselines on equation discovery, and improves over the strongest CO-Bench baseline by 3.8%. These results support trajectory-conditioned model coordination as an effective approach to cost-efficient scientific discovery.

title: Forging More Tasks into Better Harnesses: Agentic Harness Evolution via Successive Scale Racing
description:
arXiv:2610.28815v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agentic harness evolution optimizes an agent's instructions, tools, and control flow by using its task execution experiences as evolving evidence. While more evolution tasks should intuitively improve performance, our preliminary study reveals a paradoxical failure mode: the performance of existing methods degrades as the task pool expands. Our further analysis demonstrates that this degradation stems from suboptimal evidence selection during optimization, as different evidence combinations lead to substantially different evolution outcomes. To address this issue, we propose Successive Scale Racing (SSR), a framework that adaptively searches for optimal evidence combinations in each evolution round. SSR constructs diverse evidence combinations based on the corresponding task quality and coverage, and efficiently races the resulting candidate harnesses under a small compute budget. Empirically, across three distinct benchmarks, SSR achieves state-of-the-art results in all six configurations. Notably, as the task pool grows from 40 to 200, SSR steadily improves the pass rate from 64.3% to 68.3%, while the baselines' performances all drop. Furthermore, its racing mechanism identifies near-optimal candidates while reducing validation executions by 60%.

title: Decision language models as affordable and rapid alternatives to LLM judges of clinical generative AI
description:
arXiv:2610.28826v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Automated judges of clinical artificial intelligence (AI) outputs are necessary, but large language model (LLM) judges are costly and slow at scale. We compared Jev, a decision language model that returns structured judgments, with frontier and open-weight LLM judges in four use cases. On 118 pediatric answers, Jev's agreement with physicians' ordinal quality ratings (Gwet's AC2 0.50; expected score 0.53) matched or exceeded that of seven of 12 LLM judges, including frontier models, Claude Opus 5.5 (0.49) and GPT-6 (0.38). On physician-graded binary HealthBench criteria, Jev matched or exceeded four of six LLM judges. On MedHELM's open-ended tasks, Jev's agreement with a three-LLM jury approached or exceeded the jurors' internal agreement. On HealthBench Professional, Jev matched the benchmark's reference judge, GPT-5.4, on 91% of criteria (other judges, 91-93%). Frontier judges cost 73-294 times more than Jev and took 7-57 times longer. Jev may enable efficient clinical AI evaluation at scale.

title: Sketch2Sim: an end-to-end modular framework for hand-drawn circuit analysis
description:
arXiv:2610.28836v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This study proposes a sketch-to-simulation system to solve handwritten circuit diagrams. The system converts raw images into a Simulation Program with Integrated Circuit Emphasis (SPICE)-compatible netlist and automatically calculates the circuit's nodal voltages and currents. Another objective is to propose a holistic framework that benefits students and educators by enhancing the teaching and learning experience of electric circuits and expediting engineering design reviews. This article presents a multistage pipeline that converts raw photographs of handwritten electric circuits into executable SPICE-like netlists, providing a solution. A dataset of 1,000 hand-drawn Resistor-Inductor-Capacitor (RLC) circuits was curated and annotated for components, text regions, and character recognition. The proposed system decomposes a circuit diagram into three stages: (i) dual You Only Look Once (YOLO)-based detectors for components and text regions, (ii) a Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (CRNN) with Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) and Optical Character Recognition (OCR)-based domain-aware symbol value extraction, and (iii) image processing with thresholding, skeletonization, and Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) to automatically identify nodes and map them with corresponding components. The proposed system produces the netlist and solves the circuit. The qualitative and quantitative ablation studies on modular stages, as well as end-to-end tests, demonstrate robust performance across various handwriting styles, lighting conditions, and clutter.This study serves as an interactive learning aid and practical tool for professionals, providing a comprehensive user interface (UI), enabling rapid digitization of circuit sketches for study, design, prototyping, or troubleshooting.

title: Speedrunning Relational Foundation Model Pretraining
description:
arXiv:2610.28855v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Progress on foundation model pretraining is gated by who can afford a trial, and relational pretraining is no exception. Recipes are developed inside individual labs, reported under private protocols, and do not accumulate. Speedrun leaderboards remove that barrier by decentralizing the search rather than the training run. The problem is fixed, the stack is open, entries are ranked by wall-clock time to a quality target, and one GPU is enough to hold the record. We introduce modded-nanoRT, the first such leaderboard for Relational Transformers. Which database to hold out decides whether the benchmark can resolve improvements at all, so we fix it by calibration, ranking six candidates by how sharply a 45-minute learning curve separates improvement from seed noise. We open the leaderboard with typed trilinear attention, a relational operator that conditions attention scores and values on the foreign key traversed, together with Muon and SIGReg. The recipe reaches the target in 305.63 seconds on one NVIDIA H200, 8.11x faster than the reference implementation, and wins 13 of 15 pairs outside the development database. We will release the benchmark, its frozen artifacts, and the record runs. Our code is available at https://github.com/kunumi/nanoRT.

title: Fig: Automated Multiagent Behavior Elicitor
description:
arXiv:2610.28891v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many social evaluations for multiagent systems study behaviors as they emerge from environments instead of systematically intervening in the environment to elicit such behaviors. We introduce Fig (Finding Interactions in Games), an agentic system that performs targeted elicitation interventions on game environments. It takes a natural language behavior description, decomposes it into sub-behaviors, generates new social games or selects existing ones, and executes single or combined interventions to the games' engine, opponents, instructions, and context. To evaluate model behavior, it combines built-in mechanical checks and synthetic rubric judgments. We validate the interventions, generated games, and evaluation mechanisms via human review. Models attempt the target behavior in 45.2% of episodes on average for valid scenarios generated by Fig for six test behaviors -- cooperation, exploitation, deception, covert coordination, betrayal, and sabotage. For game-behavior pairs with available controls, Fig's interventions increase attempt rates by 10.9% on average compared to matched control games. Fig shows that multiagent environments can serve as programmable test beds for intentional, controllable, and reproducible behavior evaluation. Code is available at https://github.com/fleet-ai/fig.

title: Hidden Messages Between Diffusion Language Model Agents: Causal Evidence for Latent Communication
description:
arXiv:2610.28905v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion language models form answers through a sequence of revisable continuous states, but multi-agent systems usually discard those states and make agents communicate only after decoding text. We ask whether one independent diffusion trajectory can pass a compact hidden message into another and, crucially, whether the receiver uses what that message means. In Hidden Messages, a sender compresses its denoising state into four signed dense vectors; the receiver consumes them while retaining its own context, canvas, and trajectory. Removing a message tests whether the channel matters; replacing it with a message from another example tests whether its content matters. Across controlled tasks, derangement removes a +63.6-point advantage on Tiny-A2D and a +100.0-point advantage on Dream-7B, while targeted substitutions steer the receiver toward the substituted fact. On QASC with the two supporting facts split across agents, matched communication reaches 80.8%, but a wrong-example message lowers accuracy to 46.8%, a content effect of +34.0 points. The surprising result is temporal: one late transfer reaches 87.8%, exceeding four recurrent exchanges by +7.0 points. These experiments provide causal evidence for continuous hidden communication between diffusion-LM agents and show that when information is transferred can matter more than how many times agents exchange it.

title: DiffResearch: Accelerating Deep Research with Diffusion Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.28909v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep research systems iteratively plan, gather evidence, synthesize, and revise, making end-to-end latency a key bottleneck for interactive use. Almost all production systems are built on autoregressive (AR) language models and inherit left-to-right decoding in planning and long-form writing. We present DiffResearch, an open multi-agent deep research framework that places a diffusion language model (dLLM) at the core of every stage, and measure how a diffusion backbone changes latency and report quality. Holding the agentic scaffold, retrieval code, prompts, and evaluation fixed, we swap the backbone between an open diffusion model and a comparable AR model. Across 100 Deep Research Bench tasks, the diffusion backbone is roughly 6 times faster end-to-end, driven by order-of-magnitude reductions in planning and writing. We further introduce dFast, a decomposition mode that reads intermediate denoising states and extracts subqueries before generation finishes, providing a 1.99 times median speedup for decomposition in isolation with no loss of report quality. On the benchmark's RACE rubric, dFast obtains the best overall score among the three configurations. Finally, in a public system-level leaderboard snapshot, an instance built on a stronger diffusion model ranks above several commercial systems. We release DiffResearch under an Apache-2.0 license.

title: Simply Logical -- The First Three Decades
description:
arXiv:2610.28912v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper charts the evolution of the Prolog textbook Simply Logical -- Intelligent Reasoning by Example from print with runnable programmes on a 3.5-inch diskette published in 1994, via various intermediate online versions, to the fully interactive online edition available today. Our aim is to investigate -- from both the writer's and the reader's perspectives -- the potential impact of technology on educational materials. The three authors of this paper present three distinct and complementary points of view, which come together to shape an interactive online book that offers an immersive learning experience. Peter describes the philosophy behind the original book and experiences teaching from it. Jan demonstrates how contemporary web programming has enabled a fully interactive realisation of the book's philosophy. Kacper reports how different technologies can be adopted to build a versatile authoring toolkit that underpins the interactive online edition of the book. Collating these distinct yet coherent perspectives allows us to reflect on future opportunities for interactive Prolog teaching materials arising from the continuous development of web technologies. The insights we offer should be of interest to teachers of Prolog as well as those wanting to find out about the latest educational technologies.

title: D-Skill: Distilling Teacher Knowledge through Agent Skills
description:
arXiv:2610.28914v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Frontier language-model agents excel at complex tasks, but high inference costs make transferring their capabilities to smaller models essential. Traditional knowledge distillation achieves this through parameter updates, requiring access to the student's weights and additional training compute while encoding the transferred knowledge implicitly in the parameters. We introduce D-Skill, a framework that treats the teacher as a black box and distills its behavioral advantage into an interpretable natural-language skill by analyzing paired rollouts and identifying behavioral divergences and agreements. The resulting lessons are consolidated offline, with any compatible skill-update backend, into a skill document that is provided to the student at inference time. D-Skill constructs the skill entirely offline from fixed trajectories, without labels, further environment interaction, or weight updates after rollout collection. Across SpreadsheetBench-Verified, ALFWorld, and chess puzzles spanning multiple teacher-student pairs, D-Skill closes 75%-95% of the teacher-student gap without touching model weights. After a single offline pass over the paired traces, D-Skill outperforms one-epoch SFT baselines and remains competitive with multi-epoch SFT. Under the same model family, the resulting student also incurs 5.7x-8.3x lower inference cost per task than the teacher. Our results demonstrate that natural-language skill distillation offers a performant, interpretable, and efficient alternative to weight-based capability transfer.

title: Back Up Before You Regret: Measuring Backup Awareness and Automating Backup in Coding Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.28934v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Coding agents now complete tasks autonomously, modifying real-world state such as artifacts, software environments, and configurations along the way. Yet they show limited backup awareness: recognizing that an action will modify state that may later be needed, and preserving it beforehand. To evaluate backup awareness, we introduce RegretBench, a benchmark of 205 executable tasks grounded in regret moments reported on platforms such as X.com, GitHub, and Stack Overflow, where users explicitly regretted not preserving state they later needed. Across six frontier models, agents complete 86.1% of tasks on average yet back up before these moments in only 15.2%, showing that task completion ability does not imply backup awareness. Because it is hard to predict which changes will be regretted, we propose BackUpper, a harness plug-in backup layer that checks every tool call and preserves affected state before modification. It combines rule-based strategies for common operations with a lightweight subagent for complex cases, and its rule table can expand with subagent decisions over time. On RegretBench, BackUpper covers every regret moment action and restores states with 92.2% average similarity to the original. Achieving this costs only $0.014 per task, with 7x fewer tokens than the main-agent self-backup baseline. When users have preferences on what to back up, BackUpper can also narrow its scope accordingly, matching human annotations on whether an action is worth preserving with an 84.5% F1 score. These results suggest that agents can keep actions reversible at low cost while respecting users' preferences.

title: Self-Improving Agents with World Model Predictive Paths
description:
arXiv:2610.28945v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly expected to interact with environments and improve their decisions during deployment. However, how anticipating future outcomes and drawing on accumulated interaction experience can jointly support decision-making remains underexplored. We propose a test-time framework, inspired by Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control, that combines multi-branch predictive analysis with experience-based adaptation. At each step, the agent proposes multiple candidate actions and imagines their outcomes with a world model, so that alternatives can be compared without being executed in the environment. Since language environments provide neither explicit dynamics nor costs, the predicted outcomes are evaluated for task progress and risk, and MPPI-style weights over the resulting costs guide the final decision. A dual-branch experience memory enables self-improvement: the planner branch refines candidate generation and action selection, while the world model branch improves next-observation prediction. Experiments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld across three backbones demonstrate the strong overall performance of our method and the effectiveness of experience-guided predictive control. Our code will be made publicly available.

title: Behavior Beyond Text: Evaluating Refusal Transfer Failure in LLM Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.28982v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While large language models are increasingly deployed as tool-calling agents, their safety evaluations still focus primarily on their ability to refuse harmful requests in text. We investigate whether the refusal behavior in text transfers to tool use. We construct a benchmark of 2,304 prompts across four domains, consisting of matched triplets that present the same harmful or benign request in text-only, standard tool-enabled, and adversarially framed tool-enabled settings. We then assess tool-call safety using 20 predefined forbidden actions. Testing five models of varying sizes and families, we find that requests refused in text frequently result in unsafe tool calls. Under standard tool-enabled prompting, this divergence occurs for 10-52 percent of harmful requests refused in chat. To mechanistically investigate this gap, we identify a refusal-associated direction in the residual stream of each of the five models. We find that in tool-enabled contexts, the activations along this direction decrease in four of five models. Furthermore, lower activation predicts unsafe tool calls across all five models (AUC 0.76-0.86). However, restoring the signal to the respective text-only value through activation patching only prevents a subset of unsafe calls, primarily by suppressing tool use rather than by producing safer calls. Steering along the refusal direction nearly eliminates unsafe calls only at strengths that also suppress benign tool use or degrade the output quality. Our findings indicate that the identified refusal direction contributes to whether a model acts, but only partially explains the refusal divergence. Therefore, evaluating the safety of tool-calling agents requires directly examining their actions along with their textual responses.

title: PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agents via Machine-Checked Integrity Theorems and Scalable Community Trust
description:
arXiv:2610.28987v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Persistent memory is a largely undefended surface for injection and poisoning, and the same risk limits memory sharing among agents. We present PerMIT, a memory architecture with provable integrity guarantees under an explicit trust assumption: only user-typed inputs and values confirmed at a gate are trusted. PerMIT mediates the release and use of untrusted environment-derived values through a finite memory interface, while preserving agent-driven multi-turn planning and tool choice. Over this finite interface, we prove two integrity theorems that are also machine-checked in Lean 4, which together ensure that environment-derived memory reaches a sensitive action only if confirmed at the gate and influences the agent's behavior only through what the gate displays. Every attack in our threat model thereby reduces to a single auditable decision, which a human, an LLM verifier, or both can make in practice. On Trojan Hippo, PerMIT records zero observed attack success with self-verification and lightweight verifiers. Because each confirmation is a logged verdict on exact content, endorsements accumulate across users, and sufficiently endorsed items become community-confirmed with no further verification required. Under explicit assumptions, we prove and corroborate in simulation a co-scaling property: as the community grows, the risks of promoting poison and of wrongly evicting benign knowledge fall, while per-user verification effort does not rise. On $\tau^2$-bench, communities of up to 90 autonomous agents use PerMIT to build shared knowledge bases with no direct memory injection promoted, and the resulting knowledge significantly improves new agents on held-out tasks, suggesting a path toward agents that safely self-improve at test time.

title: AgentPolicyForge: From Executable Environments to Policy Benchmarks and Adaptive Guards
description:
arXiv:2610.28989v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Customized agent deployments define policies over tools, resources, and execution conditions. Providing these policies in the task agent's prompt does not reliably prevent violations. Training a guard requires examples of tool calls that comply with or violate those policies. We introduce AgentPolicyForge, a framework that uses executable environments to construct policy benchmarks and iteratively train policy guards. With this framework, we construct PolicyGym, a dataset across ten policy families using 698 scenarios for training data generation and 254 separate held-out scenarios for human-reviewed test sets. Tool calls are executed and their outcomes recorded to help determine whether they comply with the policy. Every violating case uses a permitted tool, requiring checks of arguments, resources, and context rather than tool identity alone. The case construction process supports iterative guard training: an attacker generates requests using retrieved strategies, and the guard is fine-tuned on balanced, environment-verified examples. Training improves policy enforcement even with a fixed archive. Updating the archive further reduces in-domain attack success compared with keeping it fixed. We compare policy-aware task agent self-regulation with a trained policy guard. On PolicyGym, the final guard-based configuration achieves a 40-44% relative reduction in attack success rate and fewer benign rejections than policy prompting alone.

title: An Evidence-Driven Multi-Agent Compound AI System for Head and Neck Proton Radiotherapy Planning
description:
arXiv:2610.29010v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Radiation treatment planning requires balancing competing objectives to satisfy clinical criteria while accommodating physicians' preferences. This study aims to develop an evidence-driven, multi-agent compound AI system that integrates DRL-based automated treatment planning with LLM-based conversational plan refinement for proton PBS therapy. A policy network trained using PPO first generates multiple plans without human intervention, from which one is selected as the target plan and the others serve as references for subsequent refinements. For challenging cases requiring further adjustments, an LLM-based multi-agent system enables plan refinement through natural language interactions. The system comprises a planning agent that recommends evidence-supported adjustments, a chatbot providing a unified conversational interface, and an evaluation agent that retrieves clinical metrics and identifies constraint violations. To enhance domain-specific reasoning, the planning agent based on Qwen3-14B is designed to justify its recommendations using evidence from previously generated plans and post-trained on task-specific data using SFT and GRPO. The framework was trained and evaluated using 21 patients with H&N cancers, with 5 PPO-generated plans per patient. Of these, 50 plans were selected for instruction-guided refinement. Compared with the base LLM, the post-trained Qwen3-14B demonstrated improved instruction-following, information retrieval and domain-specific reasoning capabilities. The resulting adjustments more effectively improved user-prioritized objectives while limiting deterioration in competing objectives, yielding more clinically appropriate trade-offs in patient-specific plan refinement. The proposed compound AI system provides a user-friendly planning platform, offering a promising approach to personalized proton PBS treatment planning.

title: GenXR-Bench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Interactive XR Development
description:
arXiv:2610.29014v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Coding agents are rapidly advancing from single-file generation to long-horizon repository-scale engineering, yet the evaluation of their capabilities to author interactive extended reality (XR) applications remains an open challenge. Unlike traditional software, XR applications operate within dynamic 3D physical environments where runtime robustness depends jointly on continuous user motion, spatial input, and environmental sensing. We introduce GenXR-Bench, the first benchmark for the end-to-end evaluation of coding agents in XR software development. GenXR-Bench contains 112 expert-authored tasks spanning 24 feature implementations, 21 bug repairs, and 67 application generation tasks. Held-out tests combine scripted and adaptive interactions with programmatic and visual assertions to evaluate core functionality and runtime behavior. GenXR-Bench's testing suite achieves 96.5% accuracy against blinded expert judgments of 124 candidate applications executed on consumer XR hardware. Evaluating 10 models on GenXR-Bench, we find that the strongest configuration achieves only 50.9% overall Pass@1. Failure analysis identifies recurring misunderstandings in asynchronous sensor lifecycles, physical grounding, and embodied interaction semantics. GenXR-Bench establishes a reproducible testbed for evaluating coding agents in the interactive and physically situated conditions of spatial computing.

title: Inheritance as an Admission Test for LLM Prompt Merge Operators
description:
arXiv:2610.29023v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are often improved by iterating until a fixed verifier is done. Once that verifier saturates, the loop has nothing left to climb. We instead score agents against the current population, and a frozen panel records whether anyone got better. The panel mean can rise inside the seeds by elimination alone. We therefore count a run as training only when its final mean beats the best generation-zero member. A merge is admitted only when the child moves toward the donor, past the child the same operator produces at zero dose, and the lower confidence bound on that movement reaches half the requested dose. That is the admission test. A detectable shortfall rejects the operator, and the test is otherwise undetermined. We keep realised fitness \phi as the selector and reference performance \theta as the unused ruler. Every measurement uses gemini-3.1-flash-lite on one negotiation task, and no fixed-oracle arm was run. In the open loop, tactic append grafts short donor rules and is admitted. Free rewrite moves only a third of the requested dose and is rejected. Template append pastes raw donor replies into the child. Its movement clears the bound on the first probe but not on the re-probe, and it is left undetermined. A held-out re-probe on the five situations the merge never saw confirms that both appends move, and it does not rescue free rewrite. Neither append rises with the dose. Constrained rewrite is admitted in the open loop and was not run in the closed loop, which changes only the operator. The population, the scores and the task stay fixed. No free-rewrite run beats the best generation-zero member. Every tactic-append run and every template-append run does. Sampled loop children keep that split. Free rewrite moves no further toward the donor, and both appends still clear the bound, by less than in the open loop.

title: GRAIL: From Saliency to Semantics in Time-Series Explanation
description:
arXiv:2610.29036v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Explaining a time-series model requires both locating the evidence and extracting meaningful knowledge from it. Yet a single timestep is not a semantic unit: the meaningful patterns live across many samples, not in any one of them. Per-timestep saliency is therefore noisy, high-dimensional, and unstable. Existing methods address this by introducing fixed-size windows and treating them as independent players in a cooperative game. Evaluating a coalition of such players requires defining a ``baseline'' region, which prior work tackles with fixed counterfactuals (e.g., a flat line, noise, or a spectral surrogate). This choice frequently dominates the resulting explanation, obscuring the model's true decisions.
  To address these issues, we propose GRAIL, a region-based time-series explanation framework that uses domain-specific intervals, such as the P-wave and the QRS complex of an electrocardiogram (ECG) beat, as players. We describe each region with human-readable features and generate counterfactual baselines with an on-manifold conditional generator. Such a choice of players also admits non-temporal features: static covariates enter as singleton players attributed with the temporal regions on one scale, so a patient's tabular evidence (e.g., age, sex) is weighed directly against the signal. We attribute the predictions to the features via Owen values with common-random-number variance reduction. Experimental results on both synthetic and real data show that the proposed framework produces faithful and robust explanations, evaluated under matched on- and off-manifold operators, offering meaningful knowledge to domain experts.

title: AutoFraming: Synthesizing Dynamic Frames of C Code with LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.29046v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown considerable promise in synthesizing formal specifications from source code. However, existing approaches primarily focus on functional contracts and loop invariants, while largely neglecting frame conditions, which specify the memory locations that may or may not be modified during execution and constitute an essential part of formal specifications. To address this limitation, we propose an LLM-based approach for synthesizing ACSL frame specifications alongside functional contracts from C code. Our approach analyzes code property graphs (CPGs) to extract frame-relevant information from the input code and leverages this information to guide the LLM in generating accurate frame conditions. The resulting specifications capture both region-separation constraints and data dependencies that govern variable modifications. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. On a benchmark of 84 ACSL-compliant functions from non-trivial real-world systems, our method successfully synthesizes error-free frame specifications for 92.9% of the functions, representing a 179% relative improvement over state-of-the-art techniques. On a second benchmark consisting of 51 functions, the success rate increases from 80.4% to 96.1%. Furthermore, when integrated as an auxiliary component into existing LLM-based ACSL-synthesis frameworks, our approach improves frame-specification generation performance by up to 61.9%.

title: Does Every Instance Count Equally? Order Effects in LLM Multi-Instance Processing
description:
arXiv:2610.29057v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Users increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) to analyse collections of independent inputs, such as product reviews or social media posts, and return a single aggregated answer. This setting requires multi-instance processing (MIP), where a model combines information from multiple instances into one prediction. We study a task in which the model must infer a binary label for each instance, and identify the most frequent label among the full instance set. The correct answer should be invariant to instance order. By evaluating fifteen LLMs across five datasets and seven instance order patterns, with each instance set held fixed across patterns, we find substantial order sensitivity. Accuracy can differ by about 90 percentage points between the best and worst order patterns, with models generally more accurate when majority-label instances appear at the start than when they appear in the middle or at the end. For subsets of models, available reasoning traces and gradient-based attribution reveal uneven emphasis across positions. Traces disproportionately mention early instances, while attribution scores are generally higher near the beginning and end than in the middle. These results show that instance order can systematically bias aggregated predictions, highlighting the need to evaluate MIP across different input arrangements.

title: Context-Augmented, Session-Calibrated Blood Pressure Tracking from Photoplethysmography
description:
arXiv:2610.29091v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Objective.To distinguish the contributions of acquisition context and photoplethysmography (PPG) to session-calibrated blood pressure (BP) tracking.Approach. The original comparison used three repeats of five-fold participant-level cross-validation in 653 AuroraBP participants, excluding calibration-labelled prediction targets. Matched analyses separated context and PPG and removed elapsed-time terms. Later exploratory follow-ups retained PPG, accelerometer signals and three initial cuff readings. Separate studies evaluated pulse-rate fusion and an intraoperative VitalDB model. Main results.The original wearable-state model achieved participant-level mean absolute errors (MAEs) of 7.697/6.139 mmHg for systolic/diastolic BP (SBP/DBP). Added context reduced MAE by 0.436/0.126 mmHg (97.5% intervals 0.305-0.573/0.053-0.200). In the matched factorial without the external PPG prior, PPG improved on calibration, time and protocol-provided posture/activity by 0.214/0.135 mmHg; removing time left the DBP interval including zero. Standard PPG descriptors contributed, but additional nonlinear/attractor benefit was not established. In a separate follow-up series, a sensor-history ensemble achieved 7.299/5.445 mmHg versus its static-rich reference's 7.363/5.470, small gains of 0.064/0.025 mmHg. Larger DBP errors did not improve uniformly. Quality-weighted fusion reduced pulse-rate MAE from 3.985 to 3.690 beats per minute. VitalDB MAEs remained 15.375/8.833 mmHg despite small PPG gains. Significance. The contribution is a calibrated evaluation framework with explicit controls, reproducible feature-cache-to-results analyses and retained negative findings. The sensor-history gain is exploratory after repeated dataset reuse. Independently estimated wearable states, complete raw-signal reproduction of the supplied richer features, external transfer and clinical adequacy remain unestablished.

title: Same Answer, Different Reasons: Trace-Level Divergence in Multilingual Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.29092v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multilingual large language models are increasingly deployed in settings where visible reasoning traces support verification, education, and safety auditing, yet standard evaluations typically measure only final-answer agreement or holistic response similarity. As a result, they establish outcome consistency without determining whether users across languages receive comparable supporting evidence. We introduce a trace-level divergence framework that compares visible reasoning traces as structured sequences, decomposing agreement into structural similarity, order consistency, and holistic similarity, with pair-specific calibration to enable comparison across languages. Across three reasoning benchmarks, seven languages, and six frontier LLMs, the natural baseline---embedding each whole response and comparing the two by cosine---systematically overstates agreement: $52.1\%$--$67.3\%$ of examples in the top quartile of holistic similarity are not in the top quartile of structural similarity. This dissociation is stable across sentence encoders and step segmentations, and blind bilingual annotation studies in two English-anchored language pairs show that human judgments align with structural similarity rather than with the holistic baseline. A same-language control shows that the level of divergence is language-specific: two English traces for paraphrases of the same question agree more closely than an English trace and its counterparts in other languages.
