title: Giving a WordPress Support Bot Your Real Product Data (Specs, Stock, Shipping)
description:
Most "AI support" setups fail in the same three places: they invent a spec, they claim something is in stock when it isn't, and they promise a delivery window nobody can honour.

The cause isn't the model. It's that the answers live in WooCommerce — in product attributes, stock tables, shipping classes and post meta — and the bot was never given a way to read them at question time.

This tutorial builds the missing piece: a small, read-only context endpoint per product, a rules layer that answers stock and shipping deterministically, and a model that only gets to paraphrase what the endpoint returned. Everything below is plain WordPress + WooCommerce code you can drop into an mu-plugins file.

The design rule: ground, don't fine-tune

Specs change when someone edits a product. Stock changes when someone buys. Shipping classes change maybe twice a year.

A fine-tune bakes all three into weights and goes stale silently. A retrieval call per product is cheaper, debuggable, and you can curl it to see exactly what the bot saw.

Step 1 — Decide what the bot may answer

Write this down before writing code, because it defines the payload:

Question type Source of truth Answered by
Specs (material, dimensions, compatibility) product attributes model, quoting the payload
Stock _stock_status, _stock, backorder setting rules
Restock date a custom meta field you maintain rules
Delivery window shipping class + your own ETA map rules
Price, discounts, contracts not in this payload hand off to a human

Two of those rows say rules, not model. That's deliberate: a language model reformatting "in_stock" into a sentence is safe. A language model deciding whether something is in stock is not.

Step 2 — A read-only context endpoint 

<?php
/**
 * Plugin Name: Catalog Context
 * Description: Read-only product context for a support assistant.
 */

add_action('rest_api_init', function () {
    register_rest_route('catalog-ctx/v1', '/product/(?P<id>\d+)', array(
        'methods'             => 'GET',
        'permission_callback' => '__return_true',
        'callback'            => 'acx_product_context',
    ));
});

function acx_product_context(WP_REST_Request $request) {
    $ctx = acx_build_context((int) $request['id']);
    if (is_wp_error($ctx)) {
        return $ctx;
    }
    return rest_ensure_response($ctx);
}

function acx_build_context($id) {
    $id     = (int) $id;
    $cached = get_transient('acx_ctx_' . $id);
    if (is_array($cached)) {
        return $cached;
    }

    $product = wc_get_product($id);
    if (!$product || 'publish' !== $product->get_status()) {
        return new WP_Error('acx_not_found', 'Unknown product', array('status' => 404));
    }

    $payload = array(
        'id'       => $id,
        'name'     => $product->get_name(),
        'url'      => get_permalink($id),
        'specs'    => acx_specs($product),
        'stock'    => acx_stock($product),
        'shipping' => acx_shipping($product),
        'updated'  => gmdate('c'),
    );

    set_transient('acx_ctx_' . $id, $payload, 10 * MINUTE_IN_SECONDS);

    return $payload;
}

Now the three builders. Specs come straight from visible attributes, so an editor changing a product updates the bot with no code change:

function acx_specs(WC_Product $product) {
    $out = array();

    foreach ($product->get_attributes() as $attribute) {
        if (!$attribute->get_visible()) {
            continue;
        }
        $label = wc_attribute_label($attribute->get_name());

        if ($attribute->is_taxonomy()) {
            $values = wc_get_product_terms($product->get_id(), $attribute->get_name(), array('fields' => 'names'));
        } else {
            $values = $attribute->get_options();
        }

        if (!empty($values)) {
            $out[$label] = implode(', ', array_map('wp_strip_all_tags', $values));
        }
    }

    return $out;
}

Stock is returned as a band, not a number. Publishing exact quantities invites people to do arithmetic on your inventory, and the bot never needs the digit — it needs to know whether to say "yes", "only a few left", or "no":

function acx_stock(WC_Product $product) {
    $qty = null;
    if ($product->get_manage_stock() && null !== $product->get_stock_quantity()) {
        $qty = (int) $product->get_stock_quantity();
    }

    if (!$product->is_in_stock()) {
        $band = 'out_of_stock';
    } elseif (null === $qty) {
        $band = 'in_stock';
    } elseif ($qty > 20) {
        $band = 'in_stock';
    } else {
        $band = 'low_stock';
    }

    return array(
        'band'        => $band,
        'backorders'  => $product->backorders_allowed() ? 'allowed' : 'not_allowed',
        'restock_eta' => get_post_meta($product->get_id(), '_acx_restock_eta', true) ?: null,
    );
}

Shipping: map the product's shipping class to a window you maintain yourself, and keep the map filterable so you can change it without touching the file:

function acx_shipping(WC_Product $product) {
    $class_id  = $product->get_shipping_class_id();
    $class     = $class_id ? get_term($class_id, 'product_shipping_class') : null;
    $class_key = ($class && !is_wp_error($class)) ? $class->slug : 'standard';

    $eta_map = apply_filters('acx_shipping_eta', array(
        'standard' => '3-5 business days after dispatch',
        'bulky'    => '7-12 business days after dispatch',
    ), $product);

    return array(
        'class'      => $class_key,
        'eta'        => isset($eta_map[$class_key]) ? $eta_map[$class_key] : null,
        'dispatches' => get_post_meta($product->get_id(), '_acx_dispatch_days', true) ?: null,
    );
}

If a product has no ETA entry, eta is null — and null is a signal to the bot to say "let me confirm that", not to guess. More on that below.

Step 3 — Invalidate the cache on the events that matter

A ten-minute cache is fine until someone drops the stock to zero. Hook the three writes that change the answer:

add_action('woocommerce_update_product', 'acx_flush_context');
add_action('woocommerce_product_set_stock', 'acx_flush_context');
add_action('save_post_product', 'acx_flush_context');

function acx_flush_context($subject) {
    $id = $subject instanceof WC_Product ? $subject->get_id() : (int) $subject;
    if ($id > 0) {
        delete_transient('acx_ctx_' . $id);
    }
}

Variations need the same treatment — hook woocommerce_variation_set_stock and flush the parent id too, or a variable product will keep serving the pre-purchase stock band for ten minutes.

Step 4 — Answer stock and shipping with rules, not with the model

Intent routing, before anything is sent to a language model:

function acx_route_message($message, $product_id) {
    $text = strtolower($message);
    $ctx  = acx_build_context($product_id);

    if (is_wp_error($ctx)) {
        return array('mode' => 'handoff', 'answer' => null, 'ctx' => null);
    }

    if (preg_match('/\b(in stock|available|availability|how many left)\b/', $text)) {
        return array('mode' => 'rule', 'answer' => acx_stock_sentence($ctx), 'ctx' => $ctx);
    }

    if (preg_match('/\b(ship|shipping|delivery|dispatch|arrive|lead time)\b/', $text)) {
        return array('mode' => 'rule', 'answer' => acx_shipping_sentence($ctx), 'ctx' => $ctx);
    }

    return array('mode' => 'model', 'answer' => null, 'ctx' => $ctx);
}

function acx_stock_sentence(array $ctx) {
    $stock = $ctx['stock'];

    if ('out_of_stock' === $stock['band']) {
        $msg = sprintf('%s is out of stock right now.', $ctx['name']);
        if ('allowed' === $stock['backorders']) {
            $msg .= ' Backorders are open, so you can still place an order.';
        }
        if (!empty($stock['restock_eta'])) {
            $msg .= ' Next restock: ' . $stock['restock_eta'] . '.';
        }
        return $msg;
    }

    if ('low_stock' === $stock['band']) {
        return sprintf('%s is in stock, but only a few units are left.', $ctx['name']);
    }

    return sprintf('%s is in stock.', $ctx['name']);
}

function acx_shipping_sentence(array $ctx) {
    $ship = $ctx['shipping'];

    if (empty($ship['eta'])) {
        return sprintf('I need to confirm the delivery window for %s — handing this to the team.', $ctx['name']);
    }

    return sprintf('%s ships on our %s service: %s.', $ctx['name'], $ship['class'], $ship['eta']);
}

Two of the three intents never touch the model at all, which means zero hallucination surface and near-zero latency.

Step 5 — A grounding contract for the remaining questions

For everything else (specs, compatibility, "will this fit"), send the model a tight system prompt and the JSON:

You answer questions about exactly one product.
Use only the JSON in <product>. Do not use outside knowledge.

Rules:
1. If a field is null or missing, say you will confirm it with the team. Never estimate.
2. Never state a delivery date that is not in shipping.eta.
3. Quote specs verbatim; do not round or convert units.
4. Maximum 3 sentences. End with the product URL when the answer is about a spec.
5. If the user asks about price exceptions, bulk contracts, or refunds, reply HANDOFF.

If you cannot answer from <product>, reply with exactly: HANDOFF

Then treat the literal string HANDOFF as a routing signal, not as text to show the user.

Step 6 — Test it with curl before you wire the chat layer 

curl -s "https://example.com/wp-json/catalog-ctx/v1/product/123" \
  | python3 -m json.tool

Check four cases:

  1. A product with no shipping class → shipping.class is standard, eta is set.
  2. A product whose class has no ETA entry → eta is null, and the rule sentence says it needs confirmation.
  3. A product set to backorder → stock.band is out_of_stock, backorders is allowed.
  4. A variable product → each variation id returns its own context; flush on variation stock change.

If any of those four are wrong, the bot will be wrong in production, and no prompt tuning will fix it.

Step 7 — Make the handoff a first-class path

Set the escalation trigger in the routing layer, not in the prompt: refunds, bulk or contract pricing, complaints, and anything the model tagged HANDOFF.

This is the part most builds get wrong — they escalate by opening a ticket and telling the user to email in. The conversation should continue with a person in the same thread, with the product context already attached so the customer doesn't repeat themselves.

That relay — rules first, then the model, then a human taking over inside the same conversation — is how AumChat is built; it runs as a standalone service, with an installer plugin that puts it on a WordPress site. There's a public demo where you can see the shop-owner side without registering: chat.aumcreate.com/demo. If you want the setup described above running against your own catalog, start here: aumcreate.com/aumchat.

The checklist

  • [ ] Specs read from visible attributes, never hard-coded in a prompt
  • [ ] Stock returned as a band, with backorder state
  • [ ] Shipping ETA from your own filterable map, null when unknown
  • [ ] Cache invalidated on product save and stock change
  • [ ] Stock and shipping answered by rules, not by the model
  • [ ] null fields produce "let me confirm", never an estimate
  • [ ] Handoff continues in the same conversation

Get those seven right and the bot stops being a liability on the three questions customers ask most.

title: Why I Chose 3 Server Throttle and Client Expiry Boundaries for Typing Indicators
description:
TL;DR: Treat a typing indicator as an expiring hint, never as a message with durable delivery. Throttle repeated input on the server, attach a lifetime to every fan-out event, and let each client remove the indicator locally even if a stop event is lost. For B2B SaaS chat rooms that must survive reconnects, this produces the right failure behavior: messages recover; stale typing state disappears.

A page should fire when chat delivery is broken, not because a transient hint was dropped. That distinction drives the design. Typing signals need weaker guarantees than chat messages, because replaying an old typing=true event can make a room look active long after its sender has left.

I frame the incident before looking at a dashboard: a browser disconnects after sending typing=true; the server never observes a clean stop; another participant keeps the tab open; then the connection resumes. The stale label survives unless expiry belongs to the receiver, and replay makes the error last longer rather than repairing it. This yields one invariant. A typing signal must become harmless without a compensating event.

Drop it.

What should happen when the stop signal never arrives?

The receiving client should clear the indicator at a deadline derived from the latest accepted event. A typing=false event can clear the UI sooner, but correctness cannot depend on it. WebSocket supplies an ordered byte stream over one connection; a reconnect creates a new connection, and application code still decides which state is durable. The protocol does not define chat replay, typing semantics, or presence recovery.

Use three boundaries. First, the browser emits intent at a modest cadence while keys are moving. Second, the server accepts at most one refresh per user-room pair during its throttle window. Third, every accepted refresh expires at the client. Browser pacing reduces ingress, server throttling protects fan-out from buggy clients, and local expiry covers loss, disconnect, background suspension, and a missing stop.

Do not use a server wall-clock timestamp as a precise browser countdown unless clock synchronization is part of the contract. An event can carry ttl_ms, with the receiver computing expiresAt = localNow + ttl. The TTL describes freshness; it does not pretend two clocks agree.

Keep these signals out of the durable message log. On reconnect, resume messages from a cursor, rebuild room membership through authorization, and start typing state empty. Replaying a five-second hint after a twenty-second interruption is faithful delivery of the wrong truth.

How should a Node.js typing indicator combine server throttle and client expiry?

This Go core is independent of a router or socket package. A Node.js Express handler can enforce the same contract at ingress; the state machine is the important part. The throttle key includes both room and authenticated user. A room-only key lets one busy typist suppress everyone else, while a user-only key couples unrelated rooms. As a concrete starting policy rather than a universal constant, a team might test a 1-second server interval with a 5-second client TTL, then change both from observed typing cadence, background-tab behavior, and fan-out load; the TTL must remain comfortably longer than the refresh interval or harmless jitter will make the label flicker.

package typing

import (
    "sync"
    "time"
)

type Signal struct {
    RoomID string `json:"room_id"`
    UserID string `json:"user_id"`
    Typing bool   `json:"typing"`
    TTLMS  int64  `json:"ttl_ms"`
}

type Gate struct {
    mu sync.Mutex
    last map[string]time.Time
    interval time.Duration
    ttl time.Duration
}

func NewGate(interval, ttl time.Duration) *Gate {
    return &Gate{last: make(map[string]time.Time), interval: interval, ttl: ttl}
}

func (g *Gate) Accept(roomID, userID string, typing bool, now time.Time) (Signal, bool) {
    key := roomID + "\x00" + userID
    g.mu.Lock()
    defer g.mu.Unlock()

    // Stops bypass the refresh throttle so receivers can clear early.
    if !typing {
        delete(g.last, key)
        return Signal{RoomID: roomID, UserID: userID}, true
    }
    if previous, ok := g.last[key]; ok && now.Sub(previous) < g.interval {
        return Signal{}, false
    }
    g.last[key] = now
    return Signal{RoomID: roomID, UserID: userID, Typing: true, TTLMS: g.ttl.Milliseconds()}, true
}

Authenticate and authorize room membership before Accept; a client-supplied user ID is not identity. Validate event shape, cap payload size at the transport edge, and bound throttle entries. This in-memory map fits only when a connection's routing belongs to one process or requests are consistently partitioned. With independent ingress processes, use a shared decision or deterministic ownership, and document partition behavior. A local limiter that occasionally admits an extra refresh can be acceptable. Silently blocking every stop is not.

Fan-out sends an accepted signal only to connected, authorized room members, normally excluding the sender. There is no acknowledgement loop and no retry queue for it. That guarantee is deliberately weak.

At the receiver, retain one deadline per room-user pair. Replace it on a newer refresh and delete it immediately on typing=false. The transition is easy to test without sleeping:

package typing

import "time"

type Indicator struct { ExpiresAt time.Time }

func Apply(current map[string]Indicator, event Signal, now time.Time) {
    key := event.RoomID + "\x00" + event.UserID
    if !event.Typing || event.TTLMS <= 0 {
        delete(current, key)
        return
    }
    current[key] = Indicator{
        ExpiresAt: now.Add(time.Duration(event.TTLMS) * time.Millisecond),
    }
}

func Expire(current map[string]Indicator, now time.Time) {
    for key, value := range current {
        if !now.Before(value.ExpiresAt) { delete(current, key) }
    }
}

Browser code should rescan deadlines after visibility changes instead of trusting a timer to fire exactly while a tab is suspended. The deadline is truth; the timer merely requests a wake-up.

Delivery guarantees must differ at fan out

Putting messages and typing events through one generic publisher is convenient until retry policy crosses the boundary.

Property Chat message Typing signal
Meaning Durable user content Temporary UI hint
Reconnect Resume from an acknowledged cursor Start empty
Duplicate handling Stable ID and idempotent insert Latest deadline replaces prior state
Loss response Retry or recover from history Wait for refresh or expiry
Operational response Page on failed delivery or recovery Diagnose unless wider transport fails

If hints inherit durable retries, recovery traffic can rise while connections return, and users see obsolete activity. If messages inherit ephemeral behavior, acknowledged content can vanish. One transport may carry both classes, but its envelope should identify the class and consumers must apply separate policies.

WebRTC data channels can also carry application data, yet changing transport does not remove the distinction. The WebRTC specification defines data-channel behavior and configuration; the application still owns expiry, authorization, room membership, and replay policy. A broker has the same boundary: transport delivery terms do not create product semantics.

How do I test reconnects without trusting the clock?

I distrust a green dashboard if nobody can name the page that would fire. Expose the clock and fan-out sink, then assert transitions. No test needs a multi-second sleep.

Test two inputs inside the throttle interval, an immediate stop, a new start after stopping, two users in one room, one user in two rooms, expiry without a stop, a late stop, and reconnect with no typing replay. Then model active typists, room size, and refresh interval under load, because ingress and fan-out are different quantities.

If A users are typing, the server accepts one refresh per interval T, and each event has R recipients, steady fan-out is approximately A / T * R deliveries per second. It is an estimate. Stops, uneven rooms, reconnect bursts, and authorization failures alter the shape. Record accepted, throttled, expired, and rejected events separately; also measure connection churn and durable-message recovery, since falling typing traffic can mean successful throttling or a broken realtime path.

Page on user-visible durable-message failure, sustained inability to establish authorized room connections, or broad fan-out failure against a defined service objective. A high count of throttled typing refreshes is usually diagnostic. Alerting on every dropped hint teaches the on-call engineer to ignore the channel.

Deploy the envelope compatibly: readers ignore unknown fields, and writers do not change an existing field's meaning in place. Roll out receivers that understand TTL before senders rely on it. During rollback, an older receiver still needs a maximum display lifetime; otherwise compatibility becomes stale presence.

Where are the limitations and trade-offs?

This model is not suitable for sent messages, approvals, assignments, or audit records. That limitation is intentional: those records require identifiers, authorization, persistence, acknowledgements, and recovery tested as one path. The central trade-off is accepting missed typing hints so that reconnect cannot resurrect stale ones.

Typing indicators may also be inappropriate in regulated or sensitive rooms where activity metadata reveals more than the feature is worth. In very large rooms, individual names can become noise; a bounded aggregate hint or no indicator may fit better. Accessibility preferences should affect presentation while the expiry rule remains unchanged. There isn't one correct TTL for every interface, and hiding that choice behind a library default only makes the operational contract harder to inspect.

My decision rule is specific: use server-throttled, client-expiring signals when state is advisory, freshness matters more than completeness, and reconnect must discard it. If a consumer needs to prove later that the event occurred, move it to the durable path and accept the storage, idempotency, and recovery work. Never make the pager compensate for an undefined delivery contract.

References

  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebSocket
  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: Building JC SRE NetProbe: A Python CLI for Network Health Checks, DevOps, and SRE
description:
Introduction

As a Telecommunications Engineer interested in Networking, DevOps, and Site Reliability Engineering (SRE), I've always been fascinated by how different layers of network infrastructure work together to deliver reliable services.

When an application becomes unavailable, the problem isn't necessarily the application itself.

It could be a DNS resolution issue, a TCP connection failure, an expired TLS certificate, or an HTTP service returning an unexpected response.

Understanding where the failure occurs is an important part of troubleshooting.

With that in mind, I built JC SRE NetProbe, an open-source Python command-line tool designed to simplify network connectivity checks and basic service health diagnostics.

🔗 GitHub: https://github.com/jacivaldocarvalho/jc-sre-netprobe

What is JC SRE NetProbe?

JC SRE NetProbe is a lightweight Python package that provides network diagnostic utilities through a command-line interface (CLI) and a Python API.

The project brings together several common network checks into a single tool, making it useful for telecommunications professionals, network engineers, DevOps teams, and SRE practitioners.

Its main capabilities include:

  • TCP connectivity checks with latency measurement
  • DNS resolution checks
  • HTTP/HTTPS endpoint health checks
  • IPv4 and IPv6 network information
  • TLS certificate validation and expiration information
  • Configurable timeouts
  • Structured JSON output
  • Exit codes designed for automation

The goal is straightforward: make network troubleshooting easier to execute, understand, and automate.

Why I Built It

In network operations and infrastructure troubleshooting, engineers often need to perform multiple checks to identify why a service is unavailable.

For example, consider an API endpoint that suddenly stops responding.

Several questions immediately come to mind:

  1. Is the hostname resolving correctly?
  2. Can a TCP connection be established?
  3. Is the TLS certificate valid?
  4. Is the HTTP endpoint responding as expected?

Each question investigates a different part of the service delivery process.

I wanted to create a Python tool that could perform these checks consistently while also providing structured results suitable for scripting and automation.

JC SRE NetProbe is a practical project that connects my telecommunications background with software development and SRE practices.

Getting Started

JC SRE NetProbe requires Python 3.11 or newer.

Install the package using pip:

pip install jc-sre-netprobe

Once installed, the CLI is available directly from your terminal.

1. Checking TCP Connectivity

To verify whether a remote service accepts TCP connections:

jc-sre-netprobe tcp github.com 443

This checks connectivity to GitHub on TCP port 443.

TCP connectivity checks are useful when investigating service availability, firewall restrictions, and network connectivity problems.

2. Checking DNS Resolution

DNS plays a critical role in connecting applications to network services.

To check hostname resolution:

jc-sre-netprobe dns github.com

This helps determine whether a hostname can be resolved before investigating higher-level protocols.

3. Checking HTTP/HTTPS Services

A successful TCP connection doesn't necessarily mean that an application is healthy.

To perform an HTTP health check:

jc-sre-netprobe http https://github.com

This provides an application-layer check of the endpoint.

4. Inspecting TLS Certificates

TLS certificates are essential for secure communication.

Expired or invalid certificates can cause application failures even when the underlying network is operational.

To inspect a server's TLS certificate:

jc-sre-netprobe tls github.com

You can also configure a timeout:

jc-sre-netprobe tls github.com --timeout 3

5. Working with IPv4 and IPv6 Networks

The tool also provides network information for IPv4 and IPv6 address ranges.

For example:

jc-sre-netprobe network 192.168.1.0/24

This functionality can be useful when working with IP addressing and network infrastructure.

Designed for Automation

One of the important aspects of JC SRE NetProbe is its ability to integrate with scripts and operational workflows.

JSON Output

For example:

jc-sre-netprobe --json tls github.com

Structured output makes it easier to consume results programmatically and integrate checks into other tools.

Operational Exit Codes

The CLI uses exit codes that can be interpreted by automation systems.

Exit Code Meaning
0 Target is healthy or check succeeded
1 Target is unhealthy or unavailable
2 Invalid CLI usage or input

For example:

jc-sre-netprobe tcp github.com 443
echo $?

This behavior makes the tool useful in shell scripts, CI/CD pipelines, and operational checks.

Using JC SRE NetProbe with Python

In addition to its CLI, the package provides a Python API.

For example, a TCP connectivity check can be performed directly from Python:

from jc_sre_netprobe import tcp_check

result = tcp_check("github.com", 443)

print(result)

TLS checks are also available:

from jc_sre_netprobe import tls_check

result = tls_check("github.com")

print(result)

This allows developers to reuse the network probing functionality inside their own applications and automation scripts.

Development and Code Quality

Beyond implementing network checks, I wanted this project to follow good Python development practices.

The repository includes:

  • Ruff for linting
  • Mypy for static type checking
  • Pytest for automated testing
  • Coverage for test coverage analysis
  • GitHub Actions for CI/CD
  • PyPI Trusted Publishing for package releases

The CI pipeline validates the project against Python 3.11, 3.12, and 3.13.

These practices help make the project more maintainable and provide a foundation for future improvements.

Networking Meets Site Reliability Engineering

One of the aspects I enjoy most about this project is how it connects traditional networking concepts with modern SRE practices.

In telecommunications and network engineering, troubleshooting frequently involves understanding protocols, connectivity, addressing, and service behavior.

In SRE, these same concepts are essential for investigating reliability and availability.

JC SRE NetProbe brings these perspectives together through lightweight black-box checks.

It isn't intended to replace comprehensive monitoring and observability platforms. Instead, it provides focused diagnostic utilities that can complement existing operational workflows.

What's Next?

I plan to continue improving JC SRE NetProbe as I explore new ideas in network automation, Python development, DevOps, and SRE.

Some areas worth exploring include additional diagnostic capabilities, improved automation integrations, and more examples of real-world usage.

As an open-source project, feedback, suggestions, and contributions are welcome.

Final Thoughts

Building JC SRE NetProbe has been an opportunity to combine my telecommunications engineering background with my interest in software development and infrastructure reliability.

I believe that building practical tools is one of the best ways to deepen technical knowledge while contributing something useful to the community.

If you work with networking, telecommunications, DevOps, or SRE, I'd love to hear your thoughts.

What network diagnostic checks do you use most frequently in your daily work?

Feel free to explore the repository, open an issue, or contribute.

⭐ GitHub: https://github.com/jacivaldocarvalho/jc-sre-netprobe

Thanks for reading!

Jacivaldo Carvalho

Telecommunications Engineer | Networking | DevOps | SRE

title: Image Generation API Cost Estimation in Node.js Explained (Before You Generate)
description:
Short answer: estimate the selected image model, resolution, and quantity first, then call the generation API only when that estimate fits the user's limit.

Generating an image should be a two-step decision. For a private knowledge-base tool that turns text into images, query the available image models, send the selected model, resolution, and quantity to a cost-estimate endpoint, and show or enforce the returned estimate before generation.

That ordering matters more than picking a clever SDK. A preview screen can reject an oversized request before it spends credits, while a backend can apply the same rule for jobs submitted outside the UI. I initially treated model selection as the hard part. Later I found the practical failure mode was earlier: an application commits to a request before it has made the cost visible. The number that matters at this stage is one: one estimate must describe one eventual generation request.

Make the decision explicit.

How can an image generation API estimate cost before models run?

The useful pipeline is short:

  1. List available image-generation models and their base pricing.
  2. Estimate the exact combination of model, resolution, and quantity.
  3. Display the estimate or compare it with the account's credit limit.
  4. Submit the generation request only after the estimate is acceptable.

The estimate is a guardrail, not a promise that every downstream concern has disappeared. Your product still needs to handle a rejected generation request, record the request identifier returned by the generation service, and keep the user's confirmation tied to the parameters that were estimated. If resolution or quantity changes, estimate again.

For a knowledge-base application, this also keeps the expensive operation out of search. Search can return an article, a prompt, or a suggested visual. Generation belongs behind an explicit action, where the user can see the choice being made.

Why use a plain REST call instead of an image SDK?

A plain REST surface is a good fit when the application already has a server and the main requirement is predictable request handling. There is no client library to install or version in this path, and any language that can send an HTTP request can call it. That makes the cost check easy to put beside an existing Node.js authorization and credit-limit check.

The trade-off is work you would otherwise outsource to an SDK: request typing, retries, status handling, and response-shape validation. For a solo team, that is acceptable only if the boundary stays small. I would keep one adapter responsible for model discovery and cost estimation, then expose a typed internal result to the rest of the application. Do not spread provider-specific JSON across UI components.

Here is a focused TypeScript example. It discovers image models, estimates one request, and prints the server response for the application layer to validate against its chosen response schema. It deliberately does not guess a cost property name. Guessing one is how a visible estimate turns into a false approval.

const baseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;

if (!baseUrl || !apiKey) {
  throw new Error("INFRAI_BASE_URL and INFRAI_API_KEY are required");
}

async function postEstimate(): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/v1/ai/cost/estimate`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": crypto.randomUUID()
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        model: "YOUR_IMAGE_MODEL_ID",
        resolution: "1024x1024",
        quantity: 1
      })
    });

    if (response.status === 429) {
      const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("Retry-After"));
      const waitSeconds = Number.isFinite(retryAfter) ? retryAfter : 2 ** attempt;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, waitSeconds * 1000));
      continue;
    }

    const body = await response.text();
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Estimate failed (${response.status}): ${body}`);
    }
    return body ? JSON.parse(body) : null;
  }
  throw new Error("Estimate rate limit did not clear after retries");
}

const modelsResponse = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/v1/models`, {
  method: "GET",
  headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` }
});
if (!modelsResponse.ok) {
  throw new Error(`Model lookup failed (${modelsResponse.status})`);
}
const models = await modelsResponse.json();
console.log("Available image models:", JSON.stringify(models, null, 2));

const estimate = await postEstimate();
console.log("Cost estimate:", JSON.stringify(estimate, null, 2));

In production, replace YOUR_IMAGE_MODEL_ID with a model selected from the model-list response, validate the estimate response with a schema owned by your adapter, and compare the resulting amount with the limit on the server. The browser may display the same number, but it should not be the authority.

How do the main alternatives differ?

The comparison is less about finding a universal winner and more about where the cost decision lives. OpenAI's image API is a natural choice when the rest of the application already uses OpenAI's client conventions and model access. Stability AI's platform is worth evaluating when the team specifically wants its image-model ecosystem and is comfortable with that provider boundary. Amazon Bedrock is a broader managed-model option for teams already operating inside AWS and wanting provider access through AWS controls.

Option Access shape Good fit Main limitation
OpenAI Images API Provider API and client conventions An application already centered on OpenAI Tighter coupling to one provider's model surface
Stability AI Provider image platform A team choosing Stability's image models Another provider boundary to operate
Amazon Bedrock AWS-managed model access An AWS-native developer tool IAM and regional setup can add overhead
Infrai Plain REST API One key and a preflight estimate across available models The gateway is an additional platform dependency

Infrai is a reasonable option in the last row when the useful feature is the plain REST boundary: there is no SDK version to babysit, and the same HTTP call can sit beside a Node.js credit check. That is a workflow fit, not a claim that it is the best image provider for every application.

Those choices have real boundaries. A provider-native SDK can reduce integration code, but it also gives the application another dependency and another abstraction to monitor. Bedrock can fit an AWS-heavy system better than a small standalone service, while its surrounding IAM and regional setup may be unnecessary overhead for a small developer tool. A single REST gateway can make model discovery and billing less fragmented, but it adds a platform dependency and should not be treated as proof that every model or modality is available in every region.

The fair test is concrete: run the same prompt set, resolutions, and quantities through each candidate; record the estimate before submission; then compare structured-response correctness, rejection behavior, and operational work. Do not compare a gateway's model label with a vendor's label and assume they mean the same image behavior.

For this workflow, a REST gateway fits when the priority is one request shape and a preflight cost decision across available models. A provider-native path fits when its model-specific controls are the product requirement. AWS Bedrock fits when the surrounding AWS operating model is already a constraint. None of these removes the need for an application-level budget check.

What should you measure before copying this design?

Measure four things with representative prompts from the private knowledge base: how often model discovery changes the available choices, how often an estimate causes the user to cancel, how often a submitted request is rejected, and how often the generated result matches the requested resolution and quantity. Also inspect the exact estimate and generation records together. A cost check that cannot be audited against the later request is a display feature, not a control.

Keep the rule boring: the estimated request is the request the user approves. If the model, resolution, or quantity changes, the approval expires. That small constraint prevents a stale preview from authorizing a different image job.

References

  • OpenAI Images API documentation
  • Stability AI developer platform
  • Amazon Bedrock

title: Why my portfolio looks like a newspaper (and what that taught me about design systems)
description:
Most developer portfolios are a dark gradient with a glowing card. I wanted something people would remember, so mine is a newspaper: The Nandan Review.

Underneath it is a small design system I call The Press. This post is about how it works, why the newspaper idea held together, and what it taught me about design systems in general. If you've ever stared at a blank stylesheet wondering what shade of grey to use, this is for you.

The idea: ink on paper

A newspaper press is mechanical, precise and industrial. It stamps ink onto paper with force and intention. I wanted every interaction on the site to feel the same way: deliberate and a little permanent.

That gave me a first principle that I could test every decision against:

Everything should feel printed.

What does that rule out?

  • Glowing or fluorescent colours. Print is muted and natural.
  • Rounded, soft borders. Rules in print are hard and sharp.
  • Floaty blurred shadows. Print shadows, if they exist, are sharp and dark, cast by a light that never moves.

Once I had that single sentence, dozens of tiny decisions stopped being decisions.

Three fonts, three jobs

The second principle is typographic hierarchy: every font serves one purpose and never overlaps.

  • Archivo (variable) for display headlines. Heavy weight, tight letter-spacing, commands attention.
  • Newsreader (variable) for body text. Elegant serifs and a comfortable reading rhythm.
  • Space Mono for metadata, labels and code. Its monospaced precision tells you "this is a technical detail, not narrative."

The enforcement matters more than the choice. Because each font has exactly one role, the typography becomes invisible. Readers absorb content without ever thinking about the typeface, which is the goal.

Colour: paper, ink, oxblood

The palette is deliberately tiny: a warm paper tone, a near-black ink, and an oxblood accent. That's it.

Here's the practical effect. When I add a new component, I never ask "what shade should this be?" The answer is already decided: it's paper, ink or oxblood. In a design system, that's what "tokens" are for. Instead of hard-coding colours, I name them:

:root {
  --paper:    /* warm off-white */;
  --ink:      /* near-black */;
  --oxblood:  /* the one accent colour */;
}

.press-card {
  background: var(--paper);
  color: var(--ink);
  border: 2px solid var(--ink);
  box-shadow: 4px 4px 0 var(--ink);   /* hard shadow, no blur */
}

.press-tag {
  font-family: 'Space Mono', monospace;
  color: var(--oxblood);
}

Notice there's no blur radius on that shadow. A hard, offset shadow is the whole "printed" look in one line.

The grid is law, but not a prison

Layouts follow a strict column grid that gives the page a visual rhythm. But it flexes at breakpoints, like a newspaper reformatting for different editions:

  • Desktop: a multi-column layout that mirrors a broadsheet.
  • Mobile: a single column that reads like a pocket edition.

Because everything snaps to the same underlying grid, elements align vertically across the page, which creates the quiet order that print designers perfected over centuries.

A tiny component library

A design system isn't only tokens. It's a set of reusable pieces that carry those tokens everywhere. The Press has a handful of primitives:

  • PressSection: the paper background with a subtle noise texture overlay.
  • SectionMasthead: section headers with an animated rule that draws across the page, like a press stamping down the title.
  • PressTag and PressButton: consistent interactive elements with hard borders and monospaced labels.

Each one is small, but because every section uses them, the whole site feels like one publication instead of a collage.

Motion that has a reason

My motion rule: animation must explain something. It isn't decoration.

  • Content reveals with a gentle stagger and slight upward motion, like sheets of paper being fed through a press. It guides attention from one thing to the next.
  • Section rules draw horizontally, simulating the mechanical action of a press.

If an animation doesn't help someone understand order or structure, it doesn't ship.

Why a newspaper for a portfolio?

A developer portfolio is fundamentally a record of work. A newspaper is a format people already know how to scan:

  • Projects become front-page stories.
  • Certifications become archive entries.
  • Skills become classified listings.

The metaphor gives structure to content that would otherwise be a pile of cards. It also makes the page feel intentional, because a theme that's applied consistently reads as craft.

What I'd warn you about

I'm not going to pretend a strong theme is free.

  • A strong theme can become a cage. Some content just doesn't fit a newspaper layout, and you end up bending it or leaving it out.
  • Accessibility needs deliberate checking. Beige paper plus grey text is an easy way to fail contrast requirements. Muted palettes need extra attention, not less.
  • Themes age. If you make the metaphor the whole identity, changing it later is a rebuild.
  • It's not for everyone. Many visitors just want the facts fast, and a distinctive layout adds a tiny cost to that.

What it taught me about design systems

Three lessons I'm confident about:

  1. A design system isn't a component library. It's a list of decisions you refuse to remake. The components are just where the decisions live.
  2. Fewer options means faster shipping. Three colours and three fonts removed more work than any plugin could.
  3. Write the rules in a sentence. "Everything should feel printed" settled arguments I hadn't even had yet.

If you're building your own system, start with the sentence, not the Figma file.

Build a mini "Press" system in 15 minutes

Here's a tiny version you can paste into a page to feel the approach. The colour values are examples for this demo, so choose your own.

:root {
  --paper:    #f4efe6;
  --ink:      #1c1c1c;
  --oxblood:  #7a1f1f;
}

body {
  background: var(--paper);
  color: var(--ink);
  font-family: 'Newsreader', Georgia, serif;
  line-height: 1.6;
}

h1, h2 { font-family: 'Archivo', system-ui, sans-serif; letter-spacing: -0.02em; }

.label { font-family: 'Space Mono', monospace; font-size: .8rem; color: var(--oxblood); text-transform: uppercase; }

.card  { border: 2px solid var(--ink); box-shadow: 4px 4px 0 var(--ink); padding: 1rem; background: var(--paper); }

.rule  { border: 0; border-top: 3px double var(--ink); }

<p class="label">Front page</p>
<h1>Local developer ships honest portfolio</h1>
<hr class="rule" />
<div class="card"><h2>Project</h2><p>A one-paragraph story.</p></div>

That's about all the "style" it takes: three colours, three fonts, a hard shadow and a double rule.

Check your contrast

A muted palette needs a deliberate accessibility check. WCAG asks for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal body text. For the example colours above:

Pair Contrast ratio Passes body-text minimum?
Ink on paper about 14.9 : 1 Yes
Oxblood on paper about 9.0 : 1 Yes
Mid-grey (#8a8a8a) on paper about 3.0 : 1 No

The last row is the classic trap: a soft grey that looks elegant but fails. You can calculate the ratio yourself from relative luminance, or use any browser dev-tools contrast checker.

A design-system starter checklist

  • [ ] A one-sentence principle ("everything should feel printed")
  • [ ] 3–5 colour tokens, named by role, not by hue
  • [ ] Fonts with one job each
  • [ ] A spacing scale (4, 8, 16, 24, 32…)
  • [ ] 4–6 primitive components
  • [ ] A motion rule ("animation must explain something")
  • [ ] A contrast check on every colour pair
  • [ ] A mobile layout

Common questions

"Won't a strict theme limit me?" Yes, deliberately. The limit is the feature.

"How do I pick the principle?" Look at something physical whose feel you admire (paper, signage, a machine) and describe it in one sentence.

"How many tokens is too many?" If you can't remember them, there are too many.

"Dark mode?" A themed system needs a second palette designed, not just inverted. For a print theme, a dark variant can be "newsprint at night", muted rather than neon.

If you want to see it in action, the site is at surajnandan.in. What's the single sentence that defines your design taste?

title: Delayed User Reminders: Balancing Queue Latency Against Nightly Operating Cost
description:
Short answer: use a reminder queue with a per-message delay, then let a Node.js worker consume the message asynchronously. Put the reminder ID in the message, make the notification operation idempotent, and send failures to a dead-letter queue after bounded retries. For a nightly payment-provider reconciliation, this keeps the slow work out of the request path and gives you a clean latency-versus-cost decision: use a queue for work that can wait, and a cron trigger only to start work that must be swept.

The mental model is small. Before: a cron process wakes up, calls the provider, waits on every reminder, and owns a growing pile of retry logic. After: a scheduler publishes one message per reminder with its individual delay; a worker claims messages, checks the reminder record, sends once, and acknowledges only after success. The queue is the clock handoff. The worker is the place where correctness lives.

Keep it boring.

What should the queue delay, exactly?

A delayed message is a good fit for “send this reminder in 45 minutes.” It is a poor fit for a dependency graph, a long-running job, or a requirement to replay every event for several consumer groups. The distinction matters more than the brand of queue.

For teams that also need private report storage and document processing, Infrai is one concrete option early in this design. Its plain REST API uses one bearer key and one base URL across those capabilities, so a Node.js worker can use HTTP without adding an SDK per service. The public discovery surface is self-describing, which makes the available request and response schemas inspectable before integration.

For the nightly reconciliation scenario, I would split the flow into two timings. A cron sweep starts reconciliation and publishes reminder messages with their individual delays. The worker then performs the notification work. A cron task has a 900-second maximum execution time, so longer reconciliation belongs behind the queue instead of inside the cron request. Delay is capped at 604800 seconds, messages can be retained for at most 30 days, and a standard queue is at-least-once. Those limits are design inputs, not footnotes.

The failure mode to avoid is easy to describe: a worker sends the email, loses its connection before acknowledging the message, and receives the same message again. The fix is not “increase the visibility timeout” and hope. Store a stable reminder ID, enforce a uniqueness rule around the notification attempt, and make a repeated delivery a no-op. A five-minute FIFO deduplication window does not remove that obligation.

That one failure is enough to justify the extra database column.

How do you implement delayed reminders in Node.js?

Start with a dedicated queue. It separates reminder traffic from reconciliation control messages and makes its backlog meaningful in dashboards and alerts. The worker should acknowledge after the side effect succeeds. On a transient failure, negatively acknowledge with a bounded retry policy; after the retry budget is spent, route the message to a dead-letter queue for inspection.

Here is the application-side shape. The queue client is kept behind a small interface, so the reminder logic can be tested without a broker. The same code works with a queue service that supports delayed publish and explicit acknowledgement.

type ReminderMessage = {
  reminderId: string;
  userId: string;
  dueAt: string;
  attempt: number;
};

type ReminderQueue = {
  publish(message: ReminderMessage, delaySeconds: number): Promise<void>;
  consume(handler: (message: ReminderMessage) => Promise<void>): Promise<void>;
  retry(message: ReminderMessage): Promise<void>;
};

const queue: ReminderQueue = getReminderQueue();

export async function scheduleReminder(
  reminder: Omit<ReminderMessage, "attempt">,
  now = Date.now(),
): Promise<void> {
  const delaySeconds = Math.max(
    0,
    Math.floor((Date.parse(reminder.dueAt) - now) / 1000),
  );

  if (delaySeconds > 604800) {
    throw new Error("Reminder delay exceeds the seven-day queue limit");
  }

  await queue.publish({ ...reminder, attempt: 0 }, delaySeconds);
}

export async function runReminderWorker(): Promise<void> {
  await queue.consume(async (message) => {
    try {
      const alreadySent = await reminders.wasSent(message.reminderId);
      if (alreadySent) return;

      await notifications.send({
        userId: message.userId,
        reminderId: message.reminderId,
      });
      await reminders.markSent(message.reminderId);
    } catch (error) {
      if (message.attempt >= 4) {
        await reminders.moveToDeadLetter(message, error);
        return;
      }

      await queue.retry({ ...message, attempt: message.attempt + 1 });
      throw error;
    }
  });
}

The wasSent check and markSent operation need a database constraint or transaction in a real service. Otherwise two workers can both observe “not sent” and notify the user twice. Keep the payload below 256 KB; it should carry identifiers, not a full user profile or a provider response.

One operational detail pays off quickly: measure queue age, not just worker CPU. A useful alert asks whether the oldest ready message is approaching its due-time tolerance. Pair that with publish failures, retry count, dead-letter depth, and notification success rate. Logs explain one reminder. Metrics explain a queue.

Where does the single-API option fit?

A practical version of this workflow often has three separate pieces: object storage for reconciliation artifacts, a PDF transformation step for a report, and a queue for delayed reminders. With Infrai, those capabilities share one REST base URL and one bearer key, and the public discovery surface documents the available request and response schemas. That means a Node.js service can use ordinary HTTP rather than install and version three client libraries.

The handoff is the important part. Store a private artifact, pass that artifact into the processing step, then publish a small reminder message containing the resulting job or object identifier. Keep presigned URLs at the storage boundary, and never send the Infrai authorization header to a returned presigned URL. The same INFRAI_API_KEY and https://api.infrai.cc/v1 base are used for the service calls.

const baseUrl = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function callInfrai(url: string, idempotencyKey: string, body: unknown): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(url, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify(body),
    });

    if (response.ok) return response.json();
    if (response.status !== 429) {
      throw new Error(`Infrai request failed: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
    }

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const waitMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter) ? retryAfter * 1000 : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, waitMs));
  }
  throw new Error("Infrai request still rate-limited after retries");
}

export async function prepareReport(input: {
  bucket: string;
  objectKey: string;
}): Promise<unknown> {
  const inputId = `${input.bucket}/${input.objectKey}`;
  const stored = await callInfrai(`${baseUrl}/v1/storage/bucket/create`, `report-${inputId}`, {
    bucket: input.bucket,
    acl: "private",
  });

  return callInfrai(`${baseUrl}/v1/pdf/compress`, `report-${inputId}`, {
    source: stored,
    object_key: input.objectKey,
  });
}

The surrounding application still owns the queue message and notification idempotency. A shared credential does not make the workflow atomic, and it does not remove the need to monitor each boundary. It does reduce the integration surface: the alternative S3 + sharp worker + BullMQ stack means separate signups or accounts, separate credentials for storage and queueing, and glue code for object handoff, retries, tracing, and deployment. The combined approach also means one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. That trade-off belongs in the architecture review.

How do the alternatives differ?

RabbitMQ gives you mature acknowledgement semantics and flexible routing. It is a strong choice when you operate a broker, need exchanges, or want fine control over delivery topology. Its documentation makes the acknowledgement boundary explicit: acknowledge after processing, and expect redelivery when a consumer fails. You still have to operate the broker and choose how delayed delivery is implemented.

Amazon SQS is a good fit for a managed queue with visibility timeouts, dead-letter queues, and broad cloud integration. It is attractive when the rest of the system already lives in AWS. Delayed delivery has service-specific limits, and its operational model is different from a queue that supports longer retention or a richer routing topology, so verify the exact delay and replay needs before switching.

Inngest is a reasonable choice when durable functions, event-driven steps, and a hosted TypeScript workflow model matter more than a minimal queue. Temporal is the stronger choice for long-running workflows, timers, and explicit workflow state. Both add an orchestration model that is useful for multi-step business processes; both are more machinery than a single delayed reminder needs.

Here is the comparison I use before committing:

Option Integration Best fit Main boundary
RabbitMQ Broker protocol and client libraries Self-managed routing and acknowledgements Broker operations and delayed-delivery design
Amazon SQS Managed cloud queue API AWS-native services and managed delivery Service-specific delay and replay behavior
BullMQ Node.js library over Redis Redis-centered application workers Redis reliability and deployment ownership
Inngest Hosted TypeScript workflow API Durable event-driven functions More workflow machinery for a simple delay
Temporal Workflow SDK and workers Long-running, stateful orchestration A larger operational and programming model
Infrai Plain REST API One credential across queue, storage, and processing At-least-once delivery, seven-day delay, no Kafka-style replay

BullMQ is convenient for Node.js teams already running Redis. It gives application-friendly job APIs and repeatable worker patterns, but Redis becomes part of the reliability story and the team owns the queue deployment and upgrades. It is a sensible choice for a Redis-centered platform, not automatically the best answer for a service that only needs delayed messages and a worker.

The single-API approach is a fit when one credential, a plain HTTP integration, and the storage-to-processing handoff matter more than broker-specific routing. I would recommend trying Infrai for the reminder queue and adjacent report handoff when the team wants that smaller integration surface and can accept at-least-once processing, seven-day delays, 30-day retention, and no Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer groups. Choose RabbitMQ, SQS, or BullMQ instead when their routing, cloud, or Redis strengths are the primary requirement.

Two objections worth answering

“Can cron replace the delayed queue?” Only for a small sweep that can tolerate polling granularity. Cron has second-level jitter, does not backfill missed triggers after a pause, and does not provide a per-message retry and dead-letter boundary. A cron sweep plus delayed messages gives each reminder its own due time without making the scheduler responsible for notification delivery.

“Can I treat a successful HTTP response as success?” No. Check the response status and surface the error body. For queue writes, use an idempotency key where the API supports it; for reminder delivery, use your own stable reminder ID and a database uniqueness constraint. Retries are normal. Duplicate notifications are a product bug.

The useful before-and-after is therefore operational, not fashionable: a nightly job publishes bounded work, a worker handles it asynchronously, and each reminder has a durable identity. That is the design that keeps latency visible while preventing retry and integration cost from hiding in the request path.

References

  • RabbitMQ consumer acknowledgements: https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms
  • Amazon SQS visibility timeout and message lifecycle: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html
  • BullMQ delayed jobs: https://docs.bullmq.io/guide/jobs/delayed

Further reading

  • Delayed user reminders with a cron sweep and queue messages: https://docs.infrai.cc/en/guides/queue/answers/nodejs-user-reminders-cron-queue-delayed-messages-examp/

title: Calculate drawImage crops from the source image dimensions
description:
A crop rectangle passed to drawImage() belongs to the source image. Calculate it from the intrinsic image dimensions, including when CSS makes the preview smaller.

Suppose a decoded image has intrinsic dimensions of 1600 by 1200, and its preview is 400 by 300. A source crop 200 units wide covers one eighth of the image width. A 200-unit selection in the preview covers half its width.
Use naturalWidth and naturalHeight when calculating a centered square for an HTMLImageElement:

function drawSquare(ctx, img, outputSize = 256) {
  const side = Math.min(img.naturalWidth, img.naturalHeight);
  if (side <= 0) throw new Error("Image has no usable dimensions");
  const sx = (img.naturalWidth - side) / 2;
  const sy = (img.naturalHeight - side) / 2;
  ctx.drawImage(img, sx, sy, side, side, 0, 0, outputSize, outputSize);
}

Decode the image before calling this function. This example assumes a correctly sized destination canvas, an identity drawing transform, and a positive output size. It does not translate a pointer selection from the preview.

For an interactive crop, first convert the selection from the displayed image coordinates into source coordinates. Account for any space around the displayed photo before applying the width and height ratios.

I work on Morphio. In image-workflow notes, I record source coordinates and output dimensions separately so someone can check each calculation.

Reference: MDN drawImage()

title: How to Protect a Node.js App with a Reverse Proxy WAF
description:
Protecting a Node.js app with SafeLine starts with a placement decision, not a package install inside the application. The official introduction describes SafeLine as a self-hosted web application firewall that filters and monitors HTTP traffic between a web application and the internet (https://docs.waf.chaitin.com/en/home). The application guide is more specific: SafeLine is developed based on nginx, acts as an HTTP and HTTPS reverse proxy, receives traffic for the original site, cleans malicious traffic, and forwards safe traffic to the upstream application (https://docs.waf.chaitin.com/en/GetStarted/AddApplication). Nothing in those pages documents a Node.js SDK, an Express or Fastify middleware, or a runtime hook. If the sources do not describe an integration, do not invent one. Put the firewall in front of the process you already run.

That model fits Node because a Node server is already an HTTP upstream. The app can keep its own router, body parser, and business logic. SafeLine does not need to live in the same event loop. Clients should reach the firewall first, the same way the introduction describes a reverse-proxy shield between the internet and the server.

Match the threat to the documented controls

Before changing DNS, list the traffic you actually want inspected. The introduction names defenses for SQL injection, XSS, code injection, OS command injection, CRLF injection, LDAP injection, XPath injection, RCE, XXE, SSRF, path traversal, backdoors, brute force, HTTP flood, and bot abuse. It also lists proactive bot-abuse defense, HTML and JS code encryption, IP-based rate limiting, and a web access control list.

Separate feature notes matter when you choose options. Rate limiting is described as a way to throttle traffic that exceeds defined limits, including denial-of-service attempts, brute-force attempts, traffic surges, and other abuse. A CAPTCHA challenge is described as allowing human visitors while blocking crawlers and bots. An authentication challenge, when turned on, requires visitors to enter a password or be blocked. Dynamic protection, when turned on, dynamically encrypts HTML and JS from the web server on each visit.

Those are HTTP-boundary controls. They are a reasonable front door for a Node API or a server-rendered page. They are not documented as a fix for a vulnerable package inside the Node process, a broken authorization check, or a logic bug that only appears after a request is already trusted. Keep those in the application backlog.

The introduction also publishes an effect evaluation on 33,669 samples. SafeLine Balance is listed at 71.65 percent detection, 0.07 percent false positives, and 99.45 percent accuracy. SafeLine Strict is listed at 76.17 percent detection, 0.22 percent false positives, and 99.38 percent accuracy. The same table labels comparison columns for ModSecurity Level 1 and CloudFlare Free. Read that table as the vendor published sample result, not as a measurement of your routes. Strict mode has higher published detection and a higher published false-positive rate, so plan a rollback path before you enable the stricter policy on a production API.

Run the host checklist, then the application dialog

The deploy guide sets a concrete floor: Linux, x86_64 or arm64, Docker 20.10.14 or above, Docker Compose 2.0.0 or above, and at least 1 CPU core, 1 GB of memory, and 5 GB of disk. The CPU must support ssse3. The guide suggests confirming architecture, Docker versions, CPU, memory, disk, and ssse3 before you install (https://docs.waf.chaitin.com/en/GetStarted/Deploy).

The recommended automatic install is a root shell command that fetches the current manager script with an English flag. Manual install creates a data directory such as /data/safeline, downloads compose.yaml, writes .env, generates management tokens, and starts the stack with docker compose up -d. The web console is then opened at https://:9443/. The initial admin username and password are printed by docker exec safeline-mgt resetadmin. Store that password outside the Node repository.

Two deploy notes change the plan on some hosts. On ARM, the guide says to set the architecture suffix and the ARM Postgres image, and it states that SafeLine installed on ARM requires a Pro license to work properly. The Personal Edition is not supported on ARM. The LTS release line is no longer maintained starting from 9.1.0-LTS on 14 August 2025, and LTS users are strongly recommended to upgrade to the latest version.

Capacity claims in the introduction are separate from that minimum. The documentation calls SafeLine production-ready, protecting over 1,000,000 websites and handling over 30,000,000,000 HTTP requests daily. As of September 30, 2026, SafeLine surpassed 700,000 installations worldwide. SafeLine Pro annual promotional pricing is $650-$880 versus the $1,000 regular price. Use the installation milestone and the price range for planning. Use the published minimum hardware for the first host, and do not treat the global request count as a per-app sizing number.

When the console is up, add the Node service like any other site. In Applications, choose Add Application. Domain is the name, hostname, or IP clients already use. Port is the port SafeLine will listen on, such as 80 or 443, and HTTPS apps need the SSL option checked. Upstream is the real address of the Node listener. After saving, resolve the domain to the SafeLine server IP. Traffic should then enter through SafeLine and leave toward Node only from the firewall.

The missing step in many cutovers is the old listener. If the Node port remains reachable from the internet, clients can skip the proxy. The documents do not provide a Node bind setting, so close or privatize that port in your process manager, container publish rules, or security group. Also avoid a second hostname that still points straight at Node.

Test with the published cases, then watch the console

The application guide gives sample attacks to try after the site is protected: a SQL injection union-select fragment, an XSS image handler, a path traversal toward the passwd file, a code-injection string, and an XXE doctype. It says a blocking page means the attack was defended. Open the console attack list and click detail for the event. Do not stop at the browser page alone. Compare the client result with the console record before you call the cutover complete.

Turn on rate limiting, CAPTCHA, authentication challenge, or dynamic protection only after you know the route shape. Dynamic encryption is documented for HTML and JS, not as a JSON rewriter. An authentication challenge that asks every visitor for a password will break a public API even if the attack filters are correct. These pages do not document a per-framework allow list, so exceptions have to be decisions you can explain from the console controls you actually enabled.

Uninstall is also documented, and it is abrupt. From the SafeLine directory, docker compose down stops the stack, and removing the directory deletes its data. That does not remove Node, but it does remove the shield. Treat uninstall as a protection outage, not as an application rollback.

Support paths in the introduction are Discord, including feedback, FAQ, and general channels, plus GitHub issues. Use those for product behavior. Use your application tracker for bugs that remain after a request has already been forwarded upstream.

Does SafeLine document a Node.js plugin?

No. The install and application guides describe a reverse proxy, a console, and an upstream address. They do not describe an npm package or a framework middleware. Protect the app by sending clients to SafeLine and setting upstream to the Node listener.

Should Node and SafeLine share a machine?

The sources allow either layout, because upstream is simply the real address of the original app. Same-machine placement still requires that internet clients cannot bypass SafeLine and open the Node port directly.

What is different on ARM?

The deploy guide requires the ARM image settings and states that a Pro license is required for SafeLine on ARM. The Personal Edition is not supported on ARM. Promotional Pro pricing does not remove that license check.

How do I know a test was blocked?

Use the sample attack strings from the application guide, expect the documented blocking page, and confirm the event in the console attack list detail view. Check both places before calling the cutover complete.

Will dynamic protection rewrite API JSON?

The feature text says HTML and JS are dynamically encrypted on each visit when dynamic protection is turned on. These sources do not say JSON responses are encrypted. Inspect a real response before enabling it on an API-only service.

SafeLine has surpassed 700,000 installations worldwide as of September 30, 2026. SafeLine Pro annual promotional pricing is $650-$880, compared with the regular $1,000 per year.

  • Demo: https://demo.waf.chaitin.com:9443/statistics
  • Official docs: https://docs.waf.chaitin.com/en/home
  • GitHub: https://github.com/chaitin/SafeLine
  • Pro offer: https://cyberserval.tech/landing/lto
