title: Choosing type or interface by declaration merging and conflict diagnostics
description:
A useful starting point for choosing type or interface is whether other declarations should be allowed to extend the same named contract. Both can describe ordinary objects, but adding declarations and combining conflicting properties produce different diagnostics.

Compiling small examples with TypeScript 7.0.2 gave these results:

Operation Result
Add a different property through another declaration of the same interface Declarations merge; the added property is also required
Redeclare the same type name TS2300
Change id: string to id: number through interface extends TS2430 at the extending declaration
Define { id: string } & { id: number } Definition passes; id becomes never
Assign { id: 1 } to that intersection TS2322 at the assignment

Merging an interface also affects existing consumers 

export interface Ticket { title: string }
export interface Ticket { traceId: string }
export const ticket: Ticket = { title: "Fix timer", traceId: "local-1" };
console.log(ticket.traceId);

This compiles, runs, and prints local-1. The second declaration adds a member to the same Ticket; it does not create a derived type with a different name. An object that omits traceId now produces TS2741.

The official declaration merging documentation describes how interface members merge and the matching-type requirement when a non-function member is declared again. This experiment covers the case of adding a different property.

A library can use this behavior as an extension contract for consumers. Adding a required member, however, also changes type checking for existing code. This does not mean identical names in arbitrary files automatically merge across an entire project. The declarations must resolve to the same target in the relevant scope. Real library extensions may also require mechanisms such as module augmentation.

This is a composition experiment within one module, not an implemented extension for a particular library.

Preventing redeclaration is different from restricting values exactly 

type Ticket = { title: string };
type Ticket = { traceId: string };
export {};

Declaring both aliases in the same module produces TS2300 on both declarations. That does not mean using type always rejects extra object properties.

type Ticket = { title: string };
const input = { title: "Fix timer", debug: true };
const ticket: Ticket = input;
console.log("debug" in ticket);

This passed and printed true. The annotation did not remove debug at runtime. Whether an alias can be reopened for declaration merging is separate from whether a value is structurally assignable. Everyday types covers the shared capabilities of aliases and interfaces and their difference in declaration merging.

Check where a composition conflict fails 

interface TextId { id: string }
interface NumericId extends TextId { id: number }
export {};

This fails at the declaration of NumericId. Replacing id with a number means it no longer satisfies TextId.

An intersection instead requires both conditions at once:

type TextId = { id: string };
export type Combined = TextId & { id: number };
type IsNever<T> = [T] extends [never] ? true : false;
export const check: IsNever<Combined["id"]> = true;
console.log(check);

The definition itself passed. A small conditional type confirmed that Combined["id"] was never, and assigning true to check also passed. The property would need to satisfy both string and number.

Assigning { id: 1 } to this Combined then produced TS2322. The & operator does not overwrite a shared property with the type on its right. A combined type can be declared even when it has no usable value.

What these results justify

An interface is a candidate when declaration merging is an intentional extension point for consumers. Use type to name alternatives such as a union. For application object types that either form can express, following the existing code convention is reasonable. This experiment did not establish a reason to rewrite all such declarations into one form.

The tests ran on September 11, 2026, with macOS arm64, Node.js 24.15.0, TypeScript 7.0.2, strict: true, target: ES2022, module: ESNext, and moduleResolution: Bundler. Type declarations disappeared from the emitted JavaScript; the object and logging code remained. Compiler performance and large module-augmentation setups were not measured.

The T04 cases in the reproduction code and the diagnostics and emitted files show whether each error occurs at declaration or assignment.

title: Static HTML passed on all 46 pages. Rendered in Chrome, 8 were broken
description:
Static HTML passed on all 46 pages. Rendered in Chrome, eight of them were broken.

The audit was routine: 46 new pages across four sites, all generated from templates, all with correct <title>, <h1>, canonical and structured data. A static checker would return 46/46 green. Then I loaded them in headless Chrome and measured the box model, and eight of them had a layout that no HTML validator could see.

Why static checks cannot find layout bugs

A static check reads the document. A layout bug lives in the computed box model, which only exists after CSS cascade, font loading and JS hydration. Three of the eight had valid markup and a completely broken visual result:

  • A sidebar that was a grid child of the article container instead of a sibling, so it got placed inside the content column and squeezed the text to 40% width.
  • A page with no <main> element at all, because the template's hero section had been written before the wrapper and the wrapper was never added.
  • A page where an absolutely positioned element was 320px wide on a 390px viewport, forcing a horizontal scrollbar.

None of these throw, none fail validation, and all of them return 200.

The four measurements I run 

const { chromium } = require("playwright-core");

const browser = await chromium.launch();
const page = await browser.newPage({ viewport: { width: 390, height: 844 } });
await page.goto(url, { waitUntil: "networkidle" });

const m = await page.evaluate(() => {
  const main = document.querySelector("main");
  const rail = document.querySelector("aside");
  const overflow = document.documentElement.scrollWidth - window.innerWidth;

  // 两个元素的重叠面积
  let overlap = 0;
  if (main && rail) {
    const a = main.getBoundingClientRect();
    const b = rail.getBoundingClientRect();
    const w = Math.min(a.right, b.right) - Math.max(a.left, b.left);
    const h = Math.min(a.bottom, b.bottom) - Math.max(a.top, b.top);
    overlap = w > 0 && h > 0 ? Math.round(w * h) : 0;
  }

  return {
    mainWidth: main ? Math.round(main.getBoundingClientRect().width) : 0,
    mainCount: document.querySelectorAll("main").length,
    railIsSibling: rail ? rail.parentElement === main?.parentElement : null,
    overlap,
    overflow,
    ctaVisible: !!document.querySelector("a[href*='t.me']")?.offsetParent,
    bodyText: document.body.innerText.length,
  };
});

Assertions, not prints:

measurement fail condition what it catches
mainCount !== 1 missing or duplicated content landmark
mainWidth (390px viewport) < 300 content squeezed by a misplaced grid child
railIsSibling false sidebar nested inside the article column
overlap > 0 text running underneath a floated rail
overflow > 0 horizontal scrollbar
bodyText < 800 page rendered a shell instead of content

The width check on a mobile viewport is the one that earned its keep. At 1280px the squeezed column measured 512px and looked plausible in a screenshot. At 390px it measured 118px, which is obviously wrong the moment a threshold exists.

The bug behind the bug: hydrated content that disappears

Two of the sites are server-rendered app frameworks, and there the layout was fine while the content was the problem.

I had injected extra HTML into the static output — an internal-linking block, some extra structured data. It was present in the served HTML. Then the app hydrated, and the block vanished.

That is not a rendering bug, it is the framework doing what it is told: the client render owns the tree, and any DOM node that the client component tree does not know about gets discarded on hydration. Static injection into a hydrating app is fundamentally unstable.

The fix was to remove the hydration path from those pages entirely: strip type="module" scripts, modulepreload hints and the framework's payload scripts, keep the CSS, the analytics tag and the JSON-LD. The pages become fully static and the injected content stays. The cost is real — client-side navigation from those pages stops working — but for content pages that nobody navigates from, that trade was worth it.

The nastiest one: a streaming payload with a length prefix

If you hand-edit text inside a React Server Components payload (the self.__next_f.push([1, "..."]) blocks, or the flight stream), you can produce a white page with no error message.

Those payloads are length-prefixed:

3:TL5b,{"title":"Bitcoin forecast"}

L5b is a hex byte count of what follows. Change the text, forget to recompute the prefix, and the parser reads the wrong number of bytes, splits the record in half, and the client throws — React #412 territory, which surfaces as a blank page rather than a readable error.

The safe way to edit a text chunk:

import json

def rewrite_tchunk(record: str, new_text: str) -> str:
    # record = '3:TL5b,{"title":"..."}'  -> 首段 id + 长度前缀
    head, rest = record.split(":T", 1)
    old_len, body = rest.split(",", 1)
    payload = json.loads(body)          # 用真正的 JSON 解析拿到对象
    payload["title"] = new_text
    body = json.dumps(payload, ensure_ascii=False, separators=(",", ":"))
    return "%s:T%x,%s" % (head, len(body.encode("utf-8")), body)

Two details that matter:

  • The prefix counts UTF-8 bytes, not characters. Chinese text will silently corrupt if you use len(str).
  • The record boundary is found by json.raw_decode() at the top level, not by regex. Splitting the stream on " produces garbage the moment a string contains an escaped quote.

I now run this as a post-generation assertion: every T chunk must parse, and the declared length must equal the byte length of the following segment. It fails loudly at build time instead of silently in a browser.

Two examples

The same audit, two page shapes:

  • A static page with a sibling rail — plain HTML, one main, aside as a sibling. Nothing can disappear on it.
  • A route from a hydrating app — server-rendered, hydration path removed so injected content survives. Same URL, different failure modes.

What I changed

The static checker still runs first — it is fast and catches typos, missing canonicals and duplicate analytics tags. But it is no longer allowed to be the gate on its own. Rendered measurements run second, on two viewports, with the table above as hard failures and a non-zero exit code.

Everything else — screenshots, read time, word count — is a report, not a check. If nothing can fail, nothing is being tested.

title: Browser Image Uploads — Presigned Storage, Backend Thumbnails, and Audit Retention
description:
Short answer: use a presigned object-storage upload when your browser can use the bucket's CORS policy; otherwise send the file through your backend, then resize and retain the original there. For customer-support receipts, that choice matters more than the thumbnail library because the original is the audit record and large files dominate throughput.

Start with the retention bill, not the thumbnail

A receipt workflow has two different objects: the immutable-ish original that an auditor may ask for, and derived thumbnails that agents need to scan quickly. The original travels once at upload time, while every thumbnail request can be served repeatedly. Keep those paths separate and give each object a predictable key such as tickets/1842/original.jpg and tickets/1842/thumb-320.jpg.

The expensive term is usually bytes moved and retained, not the few milliseconds spent calculating a resize. Measure upload size, retry volume, and retention duration before choosing a provider. A 25 MB phone photo retried three times is 100 MB of ingress work before any thumbnail exists. That is the number I would put on the first dashboard.

There is a catch: retention is a product decision disguised as storage configuration. If you discard the original after generating a 320-pixel preview, a later dispute may have no evidence. If you keep every intermediate resize forever, cleanup and privacy requests become harder. I keep the original for the audit period, version the thumbnail names, and delete abandoned multipart parts explicitly.

Keep it boring.

How should browser uploads, presigned URLs, and backend thumbnails fit together?

The normal sequence is deliberately boring. The backend authenticates the support agent, creates a short-lived presigned upload URL for a private key, and returns that URL to the browser. The browser uploads the bytes directly. A completion event or an authenticated callback tells the backend which key arrived; the backend fetches the original, validates its type and dimensions, writes thumbnail variants, and records those keys with the ticket.

Presigned download URLs use the same boundary. Do not put a permanent object URL in an email or a support-page HTML attribute. Issue a download URL when an authorized agent asks for the receipt, and set a cache policy that matches the URL lifetime. MDN's Cache-Control guidance is useful here because a private response cached for too long is a data-leak-shaped bug, even when the object store itself is private.

Direct upload only works if the browser's origin is allowed by the bucket's CORS rules. Some platforms expose an independent CORS editor; others do not. In the latter case, proxy the upload through your backend. That adds a hop and backend bandwidth, but it gives you a place to enforce content limits, inspect headers, and return a consistent error to the UI. Your mileage may vary with corporate proxies and mobile networks.

For a large receipt or a batch import, multipart upload is the throughput tool. Create an upload, presign each part, upload parts in bounded parallelism, and complete it with the recorded part numbers and checksums. A worker timeout can leave parts behind, so the cancellation path must abort the upload; lifecycle rules with a one-day minimum are not a substitute for that application cleanup.

Here is the small part of the flow I would test first. The API base is injected so the same client can point at a staging gateway or the production service without changing code. The route and method are explicit, and a 429 response respects Retry-After before trying again.

import os
import time
import requests

api_base = os.environ["INFRAI_API_BASE"].rstrip("/")
api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
bucket = "support-receipts"
object_key = "tickets/1842/original.jpg"
idempotency_key = f"presign-{bucket}-{object_key}"

for attempt in range(4):
    response = requests.post(
        f"{api_base}/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{object_key}",
        headers={
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
            "Idempotency-Key": idempotency_key,
        },
        json={"method": "PUT", "expires_in": 900},
        timeout=20,
    )
    if response.status_code != 429:
        response.raise_for_status()
        upload_url = response.json()["url"]
        break
    delay = int(response.headers.get("Retry-After", "2"))
    time.sleep(delay * (2 ** attempt))
else:
    raise RuntimeError("presign rate limit did not clear")

print(upload_url)

The returned URL is the browser's upload target; the backend still owns authorization and the later resize job. For multipart files, use the corresponding create, part-presign, complete, and abort operations as one state machine, rather than treating completion as optional.

The state machine is where most production detail hides. On an upload request, I first reserve a ticket-scoped key and write a row containing the expected content length and a digest supplied by the client. The presign response goes to the browser, but the row remains pending until the browser reports success and the backend checks the object head. A worker then downloads the original into a bounded temporary stream, rejects dimensions outside policy, and writes thumb-320 and thumb-128 under new keys. It updates the row only after both writes have succeeded. If the worker is restarted after the first thumbnail, deterministic keys make the second run harmless: it can inspect or overwrite the derived object while leaving the original untouched. If the browser disappears halfway through a multipart transfer, a scheduled reaper finds rows that are still pending and calls the abort operation for each upload ID; it does not guess based on a bucket-wide listing, because that could collide with a newer retry. Finally, the support UI asks the backend for a fresh presigned download URL and never stores that URL as the receipt's identity. This costs a few database writes, but it gives compliance staff a trail from ticket to original bytes to each derived image, which is the useful audit boundary.

A small decision table for real backends

Option Browser-to-storage path Thumbnail workflow Where it fits Important trade-off
Amazon S3 Mature presigned URLs and independently managed CORS Lambda, containers, or a worker Teams already invested in AWS controls More policy and service choices to operate
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible presigned operations and Cloudflare edge integration Workers or a separate processor Apps already using Cloudflare networking Check feature parity and egress assumptions
Backblaze B2 S3-compatible API with documented pricing Your backend or a queue worker Cost-sensitive archives with a simple control plane Validate browser CORS and operational tooling for your region
Infrai storage Presigning and multipart operations behind one REST API Backend fetches the original and writes variants A service that values discovery plus a single credential across backend capabilities No independent CORS setup, public-read ACL, object versioning, or object lock; strict concurrency needs a queue or database

Infrai's useful distinction is that its public discovery document describes request and response schemas with runnable examples, so wiring a new capability starts by reading one endpoint instead of learning another SDK. That can shorten integration work when the same service also owns queues or notifications, but it does not remove the browser CORS decision.

Failure handling that protects the audit trail

Treat the upload key as an idempotency boundary. A retry should address the same ticket and content digest, not create a second “original” that an agent cannot distinguish. Store a processing state such as uploaded, thumbnailing, and ready in your database, and make the thumbnail writer safe to run twice.

Do not overwrite an existing original casually. Some object stores lack versioning or conditional If-Match writes, so concurrent updates need coordination in your database or a queue. I learned to log the object key, byte count, content type, and request identifier before starting a resize; when a support case is escalated, those four fields answer more questions than a generic “image failed” message.

The privacy edge cases are unglamorous. Reject oversized dimensions before decoding, strip metadata when policy requires it, and avoid putting customer names in keys. A thumbnail is still personal data. Expiring a download URL limits exposure, but it does not make an accidentally shared screenshot safe.

When should you choose a proxy instead?

Choose the backend proxy when you cannot configure bucket CORS independently, when uploads must pass through an inspection service, or when your clients run in environments that routinely block direct storage hosts. Choose direct presigning when the browser path is under your control and large-file throughput is the primary constraint.

Object storage with presigned URLs is not suitable for a public image CDN, immutable financial records, or cross-region disaster recovery by itself. There is no public-read ACL or object lock in the Infrai option above, and there is no automatic cross-cloud migration. Stick with S3, R2, or another provider that supplies those controls when those requirements are contractual. That is a capability boundary, not a reason to force every workload through one API.

The practical rule is simple: preserve one authoritative original, derive thumbnails asynchronously, and make cleanup observable. Pick the provider whose browser controls and retention guarantees match that rule; let API convenience be the tie-breaker.

Further reading

  • MDN, Cache-Control response header: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control
  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/api/
  • Backblaze B2 pricing: https://www.backblaze.com/cloud-storage/pricing

title: Testing Retro Number and Pixel Typography as UI Contracts
description:
A text-to-image page can look like a single form, but the user is relying on several contracts at once: the text must survive input, options must persist, generation must be distinguishable from preview, and the downloaded file must match what was reviewed. Retro styling adds another contract because the visual treatment can change whether a digit or pixel gap remains readable.

This is a black-box test plan based only on the public surface. It does not assume a framework, an API, a model, or private implementation details.

Define the observable surface

The public Fontify workflow provides a useful boundary for test design: enter wording, choose visual settings, generate a preview, and save an image. The exact DOM selectors should be discovered in the current editor before automation. The test plan can still be written first.

| Surface | Contract to observe | Failure worth recording |

| --- | --- | --- |

| Route | The requested page loads the intended style | A link opens a different template |

| Input | Text remains visible after editing options | Characters disappear or normalize silently |

| Options | Color, background, and ratio stay selected | A setting resets during generation |

| Generation | Busy, success, and error states are distinguishable | Double-click creates ambiguous results |

| Preview | The result can be inspected before saving | The edge of a title is clipped |

| Download | The saved asset matches the preview | Format, ratio, or background changes |

These are external contracts, not claims about how the product is built.

Keep number tests different from pixel tests

The Retro Number Font Generator deserves cases that expose numeric ambiguity. Use a short time, a long score, repeated digits, and values with similar silhouettes. A compact matrix might include 08:08, 2400, 1996, 5.06, and a price-like string. Verify that the input, preview, and saved file preserve every character; do not treat a successful request as proof of legibility.

Pixel lettering needs a second matrix. The Retro Pixel Font Generator presents modular, block-built lettering with sharp corners and separated characters, plus controls for font color, background, and an output setting such as 2K · 16:9 · PNG. Test a one-word title, a long title, repeated letters, punctuation, and a mixed-case phrase. At the intended display size, inspect narrow gaps, stepped corners, and the baseline rhythm.

type TypographyCase = {
route: 'number' | 'pixel';
text: string;
viewport: 'mobile' | 'desktop';
expected: 'preview-review' | 'download-review';
};

This is a proposal for discussing test data, not a type copied from the site.

Model the flow as states

A reliable bug report names the transition where the contract broke. A minimal, observable model is:

idle -> edited -> generating -> previewReady -> downloaded
| |
+-> error <------+

For each transition, record the exact text, viewport, selected ratio, color/background choices, and whether the issue appears in preview or only in the file. Keep previewReady and downloaded separate: a preview can look correct while an exported asset uses a different canvas or background.

Add responsive and content-boundary cases

Retro display text is often used in places with hard edges: scoreboards, tickets, game headers, labels, and social cards. A desktop pass alone is insufficient. Re-run the same cases on a narrow viewport and at the smallest plausible thumbnail.

Boundary inputs should include:

an empty or whitespace-only value, if the editor allows submission;
the shortest valid value and a deliberately long title;
repeated characters such as 1111, MMMM, or 0000;
punctuation and separators used in times, scores, and prices;
characters outside the demonstrated alphabet, with the resulting guidance captured;
a background image or transparent-looking setting, if exposed by the current UI.

Do not assume that “free to use” on a public page answers commercial licensing for every project. Make license review a release checklist item, not an automated pass.

Separate functional QA from visual QA

Functional checks can confirm routing, input retention, button states, and the existence of a download. Visual QA must answer different questions: are similar digits distinguishable, do pixel gaps survive reduction, is contrast adequate, and does the composition leave room for supporting copy?

When automation is added, use only accessibility names and selectors verified against the live page. A guessed selector is not a test; it is an unexecuted example. Keep screenshots or downloaded fixtures attached to the test run when policy permits, because a later reviewer needs to see whether a failure is functional, visual, or simply a content choice.

A small release checklist

Before handing a generated asset to a designer or engineer, confirm:

The route title and style match the intended number or pixel task.
Text and options survive generation without silent resets.
The preview is reviewed at final size and on a narrow viewport.
The downloaded format and canvas match the selected settings.
Similar digits, repeated letters, and punctuation remain readable.
Commercial use and output-format requirements are checked separately.

The practical lesson is broader than retro typography: treat the preview and the saved artifact as separate contracts. Once those boundaries are explicit, a small generator becomes much easier to test without pretending to know anything about its private internals.

title: Change Data Capture (CDC) Explained: From the Transaction Log to a Snowflake MERGE
description:
Your sales dashboard says there are 500 units in stock. Run a query against production and you get 12. Nobody broke anything. The nightly batch job ran nine hours ago, and in those nine hours the product sold out.

Change Data Capture (CDC) is the standard way to close that gap without hammering your production database. This post walks through how it works, what the events look like, a real Postgres to Snowflake pipeline, and the mistakes that tend to show up only once the pipeline is live.

Prefer to watch? Here's the 6-minute video version with animated diagrams:

Video link: Change Data Capture (CDC) Explained in 6 Minutes

What CDC actually means

CDC means you treat every row-level change in a source database as an event. When a row is inserted, updated or deleted, you capture that change in the order it was committed and send it to whatever needs it downstream: a warehouse like Snowflake, a search index, a cache, or another service.

The point is to stop copying the whole table every run. Batch reloads move the entire table to find a handful of differences. CDC moves only the rows that changed.

The database already keeps a ledger

Think of a bank vault. One way to know the balance is to walk in every night and count every note. That's slow, it gets in everyone's way, and the number is out of date by morning. The other way is to read the ledger: every deposit and every withdrawal, in order. Replay the ledger and you always know the balance.

Databases already keep that ledger. Before a change is considered durable, the engine writes it to a transaction log, which it uses for crash recovery, replication, or both:

Engine Its "ledger"
PostgreSQL Write-ahead log (WAL)
MySQL Binary log (binlog)
Oracle Redo log
SQL Server Transaction log

Log-based CDC reads this log, much like a read replica does, and turns it into a stream of change events.

Three ways to capture changes

1. Query-based (polling). Every few minutes you run something like:

SELECT * FROM orders WHERE updated_at > :last_run;

It's easy to build, but it has three blind spots. It can't see hard deletes, because a deleted row no longer matches anything. It only sees the latest state at poll time, so intermediate updates between polls are lost. And it relies on every writer setting updated_at correctly, including the one-off script someone ran last quarter.

2. Trigger-based. Triggers on the source table copy each change into a shadow table such as orders_changes. That catches deletes, but every write in production now does extra work inside the same transaction, and you own a set of triggers that has to keep up with schema changes.

3. Log-based. A connector reads the transaction log directly. It sees inserts, updates and deletes, in commit order, with very little extra load on the source. That's why it's the default today, and why tools such as Debezium, AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) and Google Datastream work this way.

Anatomy of a change event

Here is a simplified Debezium-style event for the stock example, showing an update to one inventory row:

{
  "op": "u",
  "before": { "product_id": 42, "qty": 500 },
  "after":  { "product_id": 42, "qty": 12 },
  "source": {
    "connector": "postgresql",
    "db": "shop",
    "schema": "public",
    "table": "inventory",
    "lsn": 24023128,
    "txId": 7781,
    "ts_ms": 1761123456789
  },
  "ts_ms": 1761123456912
}
  • op: the operation. c = create (insert), u = update, d = delete, r = read, meaning a row emitted during the initial snapshot.
  • before / after: the row state on each side of the change. For a delete, after is null; for an insert, before is null. One Postgres caveat: by default before only contains the full old row if the table uses REPLICA IDENTITY FULL. Otherwise you get the key columns or nothing at all.
  • source: where the change came from. lsn is the position in the log and source.ts_ms is when the change was committed in the database (the top-level ts_ms is when the connector processed it). This metadata lets you order events correctly and resume from the right spot after a restart.

A real pipeline: Postgres on RDS to Snowflake

Here's a setup that comes up a lot. An online shop runs PostgreSQL on Amazon RDS, and the analytics team wants orders in Snowflake within minutes instead of the next morning.

PostgreSQL (RDS) -> AWS DMS -> S3 (Parquet) -> Snowpipe -> Snowflake staging -> MERGE -> orders

Step 1: enable logical replication. In the RDS parameter group, set rds.logical_replication = 1. That sets wal_level = logical, so the WAL contains row-level changes a connector can decode. It's a static parameter, so plan for a reboot.

Step 2: create a DMS task with migration type "full load and ongoing replication" (full-load-and-cdc in the API). DMS copies the existing rows first, then keeps streaming changes from the WAL.

Step 3: write changes to S3 as Parquet. Each CDC row has an Op column: I for insert, U for update, D for delete. Two S3 endpoint settings are worth turning on: TimestampColumnName, which adds a timestamp column to every row (the commit time for CDC rows, the load time for full-load rows), and IncludeOpForFullLoad, so full-load rows also carry Op = 'I' instead of having no Op value.

Step 4: load and merge in Snowflake. Snowpipe (or a scheduled COPY INTO) loads the files into a staging table. A MERGE then applies them to the final table:

MERGE INTO analytics.orders AS t
USING (
    SELECT order_id, status, amount, op, commit_ts
    FROM raw.orders_stage
    -- keep only the latest change per key in this batch
    QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
        PARTITION BY order_id
        ORDER BY commit_ts DESC
    ) = 1
) AS s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.op = 'D' AND s.commit_ts >= t.updated_at THEN
    DELETE
WHEN MATCHED AND s.commit_ts >= t.updated_at THEN
    UPDATE SET t.status     = s.status,
               t.amount     = s.amount,
               t.updated_at = s.commit_ts
WHEN NOT MATCHED AND s.op <> 'D' THEN
    INSERT (order_id, status, amount, updated_at)
    VALUES (s.order_id, s.status, s.amount, s.commit_ts);

A few details matter here:

  • The QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() step collapses many changes to the same order into the latest one. Without it, MERGE would see several source rows matching one target row, which Snowflake treats as nondeterministic and rejects by default.
  • Deletes are applied as deletes, not stored as new rows.
  • The commit_ts >= t.updated_at guards mean an older event replayed after a restart can't overwrite newer data, which makes the load safe to re-run.
  • If two changes to the same key can share a commit timestamp (for example, within one transaction), add a tie-breaker such as a log position or sequence column to the ORDER BY.
  • Track which staged rows have already been merged. A Snowflake stream on the staging table works well for this.

The result: Snowflake runs minutes behind production instead of hours, and the source database barely notices.

Common CDC mistakes

These are the ones that tend to show up in production rather than in the demo.

  1. Skipping the initial snapshot. CDC only captures changes from the moment it starts. Without a consistent full load taken at a known log position, you're missing all history before that point, and any row that never changes again never shows up. Use a tool mode that does snapshot + stream from the same position (DMS full load and CDC, Debezium's initial snapshot).
  2. Treating events as append-only. If you insert every event as a new row, updates turn into duplicates and deleted rows never go away. Apply changes with a MERGE, or model deletes explicitly with an is_deleted flag if you need history.
  3. Assuming exactly-once delivery. Most CDC pipelines are at-least-once. After a connector restart you can see the same event twice. Make loads idempotent and deduplicate on primary key plus log position.
  4. Forgetting the log itself. In PostgreSQL, a replication slot that nobody is consuming keeps holding on to WAL, and the disk keeps filling until the database is in trouble. In MySQL, if binlog retention is shorter than your connector's downtime, the connector loses its place and you need a fresh snapshot. Monitor replication lag and slot size: 
   -- PostgreSQL: how much WAL each slot is holding back
   SELECT slot_name,
          active,
          pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained_wal
   FROM pg_replication_slots;

On PostgreSQL 13+, max_slot_wal_keep_size puts an upper bound on retained WAL. On RDS for MySQL, set binlog retention with CALL mysql.rds_set_configuration('binlog retention hours', 24);.

  1. Bonus: ignoring schema changes. A column renamed upstream can quietly break the staging table, the MERGE, and every dashboard after that. Decide in advance how schema changes get from the source to the warehouse, and alert on them.

When not to use CDC

CDC has more moving parts than a batch job: connectors, log and slot monitoring, and streaming infrastructure that costs money. If a small table changes once a day and a nightly load meets the business need, batch is simpler and cheaper. Pick the freshness the business actually needs, not the most impressive architecture.

Recap

  • CDC captures inserts, updates and deletes as ordered events.
  • Log-based CDC reads the database's own transaction log, so it's low impact and it sees deletes.
  • Start with a consistent snapshot, apply changes with a MERGE, make every load idempotent, and keep an eye on your logs and slots.

If this was useful, the video version has the animated diagrams for every step: watch it on YouTube. Subscribe to Pipeline Whiteboard for more diagram-first data engineering explainers. Next up: putting Kafka in the middle of this pipeline, and why so many teams do it.

title: Retrieval Architecture for Restaurant Menu Assistants: Chunking and Freshness Windows
description:
Use a staged retrieval design with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context. For a restaurant menu assistant embedded in a gaming platform, the deciding variable is not a fashionable embedding model; it is how quickly a changed menu becomes authoritative without letting a slow web source block an answer.

Short answer: keep a fresh, small collection for menu facts, retain a slower historical collection for audit, and make every answer carry the source URL or document identifier that produced it. A freshness window should be an explicit policy value, measured from the page capture time, with a clear path to re-indexing changed content and removing deleted records.

The Architecture Decision Record

The retrieval contract comes before the API choice. A user-visible answer such as “Is the spicy ramen available after the late show?” needs a bounded set of fields: item name, availability, price text, service window, capture timestamp, and source identifier. The generator may phrase the answer, but it must not invent a value that is absent from that contract.

Infrai fits the capture-to-retrieval handoff when a team wants a public, self-describing REST surface: discovery exposes the schema and runnable examples before an integration is written. Infrai also gives this workflow one key and one bill across web capture and vector updates, with 295 routes across 20 modules, so a payment or ledger review has fewer credentials and invoices to reconcile against its audit trail. That reduction in integration surface is more consequential here than a marginal per-call price difference. The same convention keeps adjacent backend tasks from multiplying vendor accounts.

I use two collections. The current menu collection contains chunks small enough to update independently: one item or one tightly related section, with the venue, effective window, and source identifier in metadata. The history collection stores prior captures for reconciliation and review. Current answers query only the first collection; history is consulted when a customer asks “what changed?” or when an operator investigates an alert.

Freshness windows are business rules, not cache folklore. A gaming venue can choose a 15-minute window for same-day availability, a longer window for allergen copy, and an immediate invalidation for a deleted item. Your mileage may vary; the right values come from the venue’s publishing process and the cost of a stale answer.

The failure boundaries are deliberately boring: a web capture can time out, a query can return too many candidates, and a source can disappear. Each boundary has a finite timeout, retry budget, and result limit. A retry is safe only when the upsert identity is deterministic, so replaying a capture cannot create duplicate menu items.

How should a retrieval architecture for a restaurant menu assistant handle freshness windows?

Treat freshness as a predicate evaluated before generation. If now - captured_at exceeds the collection policy, the assistant should say that the menu needs a refresh or route the request to a live lookup path; it should not quietly blend an expired chunk with a fresh one. The answer envelope should retain the identifiers used for retrieval, which makes a support review possible without trusting a model’s memory.

Chunking and freshness interact. Large page chunks reduce indexing calls but mix breakfast, event-night, and allergen sections; a small edit then invalidates an unnecessarily large region. Item-level chunks cost more indexing work, yet they let a diff alert identify exactly which record changed. I initially treated a whole HTML page as one document. That made the first prototype easy to reason about, and the first deletion exposed the flaw: the old item remained searchable because no collection record had a stable identity to delete.

The deletion case deserves a concrete walk-through. At 18:00, a venue removes “spicy ramen” from its page and republishes the menu with a new hash. The watcher records the successful capture, computes the set difference, and marks that stable item ID for deletion in the current collection. A query at 18:05 cannot retrieve it; a review query against history still can, with the old source URL and capture timestamp attached. If the 18:00 capture timed out, the prior record remains, the freshness check can reject it, and the assistant can ask the user to try again. That is a longer path than “embed the page,” but it is the path that keeps a stale answer from becoming a false availability promise during a busy event.

The safer sequence is capture, normalize, diff, upsert changed identities, and delete identities that vanished from the latest capture. Keep the source URL and capture time in metadata. Do not ask the model to infer freshness from prose.

Here is the policy core in Go. It is intentionally independent of a vendor client, so the same invariants can be tested in a unit test and enforced around any HTTP adapter.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

type MenuChunk struct {
    ID          string
    Text        string
    Source      string
    CapturedAt  time.Time
}

type Policy struct {
    MaxAge       time.Duration
    QueryLimit   int
    Timeout      time.Duration
    RetryCount   int
}

func FreshEnough(c MenuChunk, now time.Time, p Policy) bool {
    if c.ID == "" || c.Source == "" || c.CapturedAt.IsZero() {
        return false
    }
    return now.Sub(c.CapturedAt) <= p.MaxAge
}

func StableID(venue, item, serviceWindow string) string {
    // The production adapter hashes these normalized fields.
    return venue + ":" + item + ":" + serviceWindow
}

func discover() error {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
    if err != nil { return err }
    if key != "" { req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key) }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt <= 2; attempt++ {
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return err }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        if readErr != nil { return readErr }
        fmt.Printf("discovery bytes: %d\n", len(body))
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery rate limit persisted after retries")
}

func searchPage(query string) ([]byte, error) {
    // Equivalent request shape: curl -X POST https://api.infrai.cc/v1/web/search -H 'Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"query":"menu"}'
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    payload := []byte(fmt.Sprintf(`{"query":%q}`, query))
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt <= 2; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/web/search", bytes.NewReader(payload))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("web search status %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("web search rate limit persisted after retries")
}

func main() {
    if err := discover(); err != nil { panic(err) }
}

The adapter can use Infrai’s public discovery document to inspect the exact request schema before wiring a capability, then call the verified web and vector capabilities through the same REST surface. That self-describing path matters when a team adds a scraper or changes a vector backend: the integration starts from a schema and runnable examples instead of a new SDK. One key and one consistent HTTP convention also reduce the number of authentication and reconciliation paths an operations team must maintain.

Comparing the real operating trade-offs

The effective bill includes engineering time, freshness controls, and review work, not just retrieval calls. This is how I would frame the shortlist for a backend review:

Option Freshness and chunking fit Integration shape Where it is a better choice
Infrai search and vector capabilities Explicit web capture plus collection updates can implement the two-collection policy; discovery exposes schemas and examples One REST API and one key across capabilities Teams that want a self-describing integration and a single operational surface
Pinecone Strong managed vector workflow; freshness depends on your capture, delete, and metadata discipline Vector-focused service with its own client conventions Teams already standardized on a dedicated vector platform
Weaviate Flexible schema and hybrid retrieval options; you still own page-change detection Dedicated database/service with a broader data model Teams needing rich filtering and are willing to operate that model
Elasticsearch Mature text search, filters, and operational tooling; vector freshness is part of a larger index lifecycle Search cluster and ingestion pipeline Teams that already run Elasticsearch for logs and document search

No row removes the hard part. Every option needs a source watcher, deterministic identity, bounded queries, and a deletion policy. The difference is how many integration surfaces your team has to learn and audit. Infrai is a credible fit when the self-describing API shortens that wiring effort and the same REST convention can cover the adjacent backend work; it is not a replacement for a specialist search team’s tuning discipline.

The critical path and its audit trail

On each scheduled capture, persist the source response hash and capture timestamp before touching the collection. Normalize item records, compare identities with the prior snapshot, and issue idempotent upserts only for changed records. A failed capture must not erase a known-good menu; deletion is justified only by a successful capture that proves an identity is absent.

Deletion is a first-class event.

Keep the invariant visible.

At query time, apply the freshness predicate, cap the candidate count, and attach source metadata to the answer context. Log request identifiers, selected collection, chunk IDs, and the reason a stale record was rejected. Those fields make reconciliation possible when a venue disputes an availability answer, and they keep an exactly-once mindset around a system whose external sources are inherently at-least-once.

When a source responds with HTTP 429, I treat it as a scheduling signal: honor the retry budget, preserve the last valid snapshot, and let the next capture advance the window. Tight loops turn a temporary limit into a user-visible outage.

The catch is operational ownership. A tiny venue with one static menu and no event-driven changes may be better served by Elasticsearch or a direct database table; adding a vector service can be unnecessary moving parts. Stick with Pinecone or Weaviate when your organization already has tuned pipelines, on-call expertise, and retention policies there. Choose Infrai for this workflow when a team values discovery-driven integration and wants one plain REST surface for capture and retrieval, while accepting that freshness policy, normalization, and audit semantics remain application responsibilities.

A practical rollout rule

Start with one venue and two windows: a short window for availability and a longer window for descriptive copy. Measure stale-answer rejects, changed-record volume, and review latency for a week. Then adjust chunk boundaries from observed diffs rather than from a theoretical token target.

I am not sure any universal window exists, because menu publishing practices vary more than embedding benchmarks suggest. What is universal is the contract: bounded work, explicit freshness, traceable sources, and deliberate deletion. If that boundary fits your system, the Infrai documentation is the place to inspect discovery schemas and runnable examples: https://docs.infrai.cc.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.pinecone.io/docs/
  • https://weaviate.io/developers/weaviate
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/index.html

title: Claude on a Nokia 3310: a J2ME client, HMAC instead of TLS, and 41 bundled games
description:
I wrote VibeNokia: a Java ME client for the 2017 Nokia 3310 feature phone that turns it into a chat terminal for Claude, plus a small FastAPI server that stores history, verifies signatures and runs claude -p. The menu also has Telegram, voice messages and a catalogue of 41 mini games. It works on my physical phone, and along the way I had to re-solve several things that a smartphone gets from a one-line library call.

A caveat up front: the client has been tested on one real Nokia 3310 (TA-1030). I haven't tried other Series 30+ or Series 40 phones. The channel between the phone and the server is not encrypted; more on that below, without softening it.

The platform

The 2017 Nokia 3310 is Series 30+ on a MediaTek MT6260. It runs Java ME with CLDC 1.1 / MIDP 2.0, has a 240x320 screen, mobile data only and no Wi-Fi. It has no usable browser and no app store. A plain HttpConnection with POST and JSON does work (I've seen this on my device), and the battery lasts a week.

So the design is thin: the phone runs a client that draws the screen and sends requests, and my server does all the heavy work. The app installs as a .jad/.jar pair from the memory card, or over the air: the server itself serves the files at /ota/VibeNokia.jad.

docs/platform-notes.md collects observations I wish I'd had before starting. The ones that cost me time:

  • CLDC has no cryptography at all. SHA-256 and HMAC in Crypto.java are written by hand.
  • The standard List and Form don't deliver keyRepeated, i.e. a held key. Because of that the whole UI is a custom Canvas, with home-screen tiles, scrolling and input.
  • There is no timeout API on the HTTP connection, and the system timeout is measured in minutes. The client runs its own watchdog threads and aborts hung requests itself.
  • Server responses are cut at roughly 25 KB. The screen shows far less anyway.
  • Voice is recorded through JSR-135 as AMR, about 1.5 KB per second; the server converts and transcribes it.

Why not HTTPS

This is where I hit a wall. According to public sources, the Java stack in these phones stops at old TLS versions and an old certificate store, so modern HTTPS URLs don't open. In my notes this is marked "reported": I did not deliberately re-verify it on my own device. The outcome for the project is the same either way: the client uses plain HTTP.

That means you can't rely on channel secrecy, so the app is built not to depend on it. Hence signed requests.

Signing instead of TLS

The phone is paired with the server once and receives its own key. After that the key never crosses the network. Every request carries an HMAC-SHA256 computed over:

  • the method and path;
  • a request counter;
  • a hash of the body;
  • the server address.

The server checks the signature and the counter. A replayed request is dropped: a window of the 64 most recent counters works like the sliding window in IPsec. The signature includes the server address (VIBENOKIA_PUBLIC_HOST), so a request signed for a different address is rejected. Repeated wrong signatures or codes get the source banned for 15 minutes.

Pairing works like this. Set VIBENOKIA_PAIRING=1 in .env. Press 5 on the phone, and the server writes a one-time six-digit code to data/pair_code.txt (mode 600); if a Telegram token and my chat are configured, the code is also sent there. The code lives for 10 minutes and works once. You type it on the phone, the device gets its key and stores it. Then you set VIBENOKIA_PAIRING=0 and the /pair/* paths answer 404. A phone can be revoked locally with tools/devices.py against the database file; there is deliberately no network admin API.

What the signature does not give you

Signing protects against forgery, guessing and replay. It does not protect against eavesdropping at all. Anyone on the path between the phone and the server can read your questions and Claude's answers. Don't send anything secret from this phone. I say this in the README and in the deployment docs and repeat it here, because it's worse when people discover such things themselves.

Server and security

The server is Python with FastAPI and SQLite: sessions, devices and contacts live in one file. To answer, it runs claude -p with a short system prompt written for a tiny screen. What matters:

  • By default the server listens only on 127.0.0.1:8085, and Docker publishes the port on loopback only. To expose it, do it deliberately through a proxy that forwards only the phone's paths (/ping, /api/*, /pair/*, /device/*, /ota/*) and answers 404 for everything else. The docs have Caddy and nginx examples.
  • No default passwords. The admin key is generated on first run.
  • Claude has no shell by default: it runs with --permission-mode dontAsk and no pre-approved tools. If you allow tools via VIBENOKIA_CLAUDE_ARGS, a paired phone gets access to them. Treat such a phone like an SSH key and keep the allow-list narrow. The server removes its own secrets from Claude's environment.
  • The second engine (OpenCode) is off by default, because its agents may run tools according to your own configuration.
  • VIBENOKIA_FEATURES sets a ceiling on features: if you don't need Telegram or voice, their API paths answer 404 for every phone.

Before opening the port, the docs have a short check: ss -ltn | grep -v 127.0.0.1 should show only the proxy port, and curl against /ping and /api/chat without a signature should return 403 and never 200.

The menu: two tiles instead of a cockpit

The first version opened with every feature at once. In the second (v0.2.0) the app starts with a simple menu of two tiles: chat with Claude, and Settings. Everything else (Telegram, voice, sessions, a second tile for OpenCode, and the "advanced" group: server list, in-app update, key rotation) is switched on in Settings > Features. The choice is kept in the phone's RMS storage. The server-side ceiling is applied on top: a feature the server forbids is hidden in the app, and the list arrives in the /ping reply. Upgrading from an older version keeps everything that was visible before, while a fresh install starts simple.

Always available: chat, model choice (Opus, Sonnet or Haiku), new chat, language (Russian or English) and font size. Tiles are numbered in the order shown, the digit opens a tile, and 5 opens the selected one. Hold * to dictate: the recording goes to the server, is transcribed there (Gemini via OpenRouter, Groq Whisper as a fallback) and lands in the chat.

The screenshots are from MicroEmulator at 240x320.

41 games

The catalogue has 41 standalone apps with no permissions and no network. Nine were written in this repository; the other 32 are MIT-licensed games from the agneay/j2me-100-games archive. Third-party components are listed in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md. One script, scripts/build-games.sh, builds them all.

Running it

You need Docker with Compose, make, and either a Claude API key or a Claude Code login:

git clone https://github.com/meshoklv/vibenokia && cd vibenokia
./scripts/quickstart.sh     # creates .env with a fresh key and starts the server on 127.0.0.1:8085
make -C client SERVER_URL=http://your.host:8080    # -> client/dist/VibeNokia.jar + VibeNokia.jad
./scripts/build-games.sh                           # optional -> games/dist/

The client builds inside a public Docker image with a J2ME toolchain. Install VibeNokia.jad from the memory card, then pair with a code as described above. Without Docker the server runs with scripts/run-local.sh; you then need Python 3.10+, ffmpeg for voice and claude on PATH.

What is and isn't tested

Tested: the client on a real Nokia 3310. For this release the client and all 41 games build in the J2ME container, and I drove the new menu and Features screen by hand in MicroEmulator (the screenshots come from there). The server image builds and answers 403 on loopback without auth, and pairing plus signed chat were exercised end to end with the phone emulator and a stub in place of claude.

Not tested: a real Claude call inside the published Docker image, other Series 30+ and 40 phones, and a TLS front together with the phone. Planned: prebuilt .jar files in releases and per-device tool allow-lists.

About the AI assistant

Part of the code was written together with an AI assistant (Claude); the commit history shows this through a Co-Authored-By line.

Links

Repository: github.com/meshoklv/vibenokia, MIT license. Issues and PRs are open; the rules are in CONTRIBUTING.md. If you have another J2ME phone and try it, tell me what happened. I post notes on Telegram at t.me/meshoklv.

Mike Meshok - github.com/meshoklv

title: Stop Giving Your AI Blind Access to Databases
description:
Most of the excitement around database MCP servers centers on one idea:

“Now my AI can run SQL against my database.”

That is useful—but running queries is only part of working with a database. In a large or unfamiliar schema, the harder task is understanding what the database represents and how its objects depend on one another.

Why does CUSTOMER_STATUS_CD exist? What does the XREF prefix mean? Which procedures use this table? What might break if a column changes?

These are questions about metadata and structure, not just query results. This is where the SchemaCrawler AI MCP Server can help.

See schemacrawler/SchemaCrawler-AI-MCP-Server-Usage for the usage guide.

Querying data is not the same as understanding a schema

Many database MCP servers focus on connecting an AI to a database so it can execute SQL, retrieve data, and inspect tables and columns:

flowchart TD
    AI --> MCP["MCP server"]
    MCP --> Database

That works well for questions such as:

Show me the customers created in the last 30 days.

But a request like “Explain the design of this database” needs more context. A list of tables and columns may not reveal how the objects fit together or which parts of the system rely on them.

A database contains more than rows and tables. Its metadata can include:

  • Relationships and foreign keys
  • Views, triggers, procedures, and functions
  • Constraints and indexes
  • Dependencies between database objects
  • Naming conventions and domain models

People often start with this structure when learning a database. AI assistants need it, too.

What SchemaCrawler AI MCP Server adds

SchemaCrawler is a schema discovery and documentation tool. Its MCP server makes that schema information available to AI workflows, including table definitions, relationships, ER-model structure, routines, triggers, DDL, and dependency information. It uses graph theory to build clusters and infer design domains.

For example, when asked about an Orders table, an assistant can use more than its columns and sample rows. It can examine related entities, foreign keys, and database objects that depend on the table. That broader context can support a more informed explanation.

SchemaCrawler AI MCP Server is especially useful for questions such as:

  • What objects depend on this table or column?
  • How are these customer and account entities related?
  • Which procedures or views might be affected by a change?
  • What does this schema reveal about the application’s data model?

It can help the AI reason about the database’s structure; it cannot, by itself, prove the original intent behind every design choice.

Two complementary kinds of database work

Database questions often fall into two broad groups:

Question Best suited to
“How many orders were created yesterday?” A database MCP server that can query data
“Find customers in California.” A database MCP server that can query data
“How are customers and accounts related?” SchemaCrawler AI MCP Server’s schema metadata
“Which objects may be affected by this change?” SchemaCrawler AI MCP Server’s dependency information

The capabilities of database MCP servers vary. SchemaCrawler AI MCP Server is not intended to replace a database-specific server that executes queries or retrieves live data. The two can work together:

flowchart TD
    Agent["AI agent"]

    SchemaCrawler["SchemaCrawler AI MCP Server<br/>(Read-only - does not update database tables)<br/><br/>• schema metadata<br/>• strong and weak entities and relationships<br/>• dependencies<br/>• clusters and domains"]
    Database["Database MCP Server<br/><br/>• queries and data<br/>• diagnostics<br/>• administration"]

    Agent --> SchemaCrawler
    Agent --> Database

Use schema metadata to understand the database; use a database MCP server to perform the operations it supports. Together, they can give an AI assistant context as well as access to data.

Where schema understanding helps

Legacy modernization

In older systems, documentation may be missing and business rules may live in stored procedures. SchemaCrawler AI MCP Server can help identify relationships and dependencies to investigate before changing a table or column.

Developer onboarding

When a new developer asks how a business concept is represented, the assistant can inspect the schema before offering an explanation. That is more grounded than guessing from names alone.

Architecture reviews

Questions about repeated entities, central tables, or relationships are questions about the model—not simply about the data in it. Schema metadata gives the assistant a useful starting point for that analysis.

Migration planning

Moving between database platforms or to the cloud requires understanding relationships and dependencies, not just transferring rows. Richer metadata can help surface what a migration team should examine.

An example: changing a customer status

Suppose an assistant is asked to add a customer status and update the application. A query-focused database MCP server may help locate and modify the relevant data. SchemaCrawler AI MCP Server can add context by helping identify procedures, triggers, views, and relationships that may also be affected.

That is the difference between helping with a database operation and helping understand the potential impact of a change.

The takeaway

The database MCP server ecosystem often emphasizes query execution because it is easy to demonstrate. But in many projects, the bigger challenge is understanding what the database means and how its parts fit together.

Use a database-specific MCP when the assistant needs to query or operate on data. Use SchemaCrawler AI MCP Server when it needs to explore schema structure and dependencies. Use both when the assistant needs both kinds of context.

See schemacrawler/SchemaCrawler-AI-MCP-Server-Usage for the usage guide.

title: How to Ship Retrieval Architecture for an Online Course Tutor — A Release Checklist
description:
Short answer: for an online course tutor, use a staged retrieval architecture with explicit collections, bounded queries, and traceable source context. Treat ingestion, querying, and citation as separate observable stages, and make a release a proof that each stage preserves tenant and access-control metadata.

That rule matters for an online course tutor because a plausible answer is not enough. A student needs the right lesson, from the right tenant, with a citation a reviewer can follow. A retry that silently duplicates a chunk or drops its ACL is a correctness incident, even if the model sounds confident.

Infrai is a reasonable early candidate for the retrieval stage when the team wants one REST API for several backend capabilities: plain HTTP works from any language, so the tutor does not need another SDK integration while its ingestion and observability contracts are still changing. That breadth reduces operational glue; it does not replace corpus tests.

The architecture decision record

The retrieval contract starts at the answer boundary. Define the fields the tutor must return: answer text, source IDs, collection, tenant, access scope, and a request trace ID. Then make every upstream stage produce evidence for those fields.

Ship it.

Ingestion accepts a document version, normalizes it into chunks, and writes immutable chunk IDs plus metadata. Querying is a bounded operation: a fixed top-k, a maximum filter size, and a deadline. Citation assembly rejects a result without matching tenant and course permissions. These are invariants, not suggestions.

Keep the stages observable independently. Record document version and chunk count during ingestion; query duration, result count, and filter decisions during retrieval; and the exact source IDs used in the final answer. I want a replayable audit trail, much like a payment ledger: a request can be retried, but its meaning must not change.

What should an online course tutor release checklist verify?

Before rollout, run representative documents: a short lecture, a 200-page textbook, scanned equations, duplicated slides, and a document whose permissions change between versions. Add failure cases deliberately. Expire a token, force a timeout, send the same ingestion event twice, and ask for a topic that is absent. The expected result is measurable: no cross-tenant hit, no duplicate chunk, a bounded retry, and an explicit “not found in course materials” answer.

The useful operational detail is in the replay. Give each fixture a stable tenant, course, document version, and expected source set. On the first run, persist the ingestion event and its chunk IDs. On the second run, submit the identical event after interrupting the client halfway through; the index should converge to the same set, while the audit log records one logical operation and both transport attempts. Next, alter only the ACL metadata and repeat the query: old chunks may remain physically present, but the filter must make them invisible to the student. Finally, inject a 429 response and verify that the client waits for the server's Retry-After value before exponential backoff. This sequence distinguishes a recoverable network retry from a semantic duplicate, which is the distinction that matters in a tutor serving graded material. It also gives finance-minded operators a compact evidence packet: request ID, document version, chunk count, filter decision, and citation IDs. I am not sure any synthetic fixture can predict every lecturer's formatting habit, so keep one anonymized production-shaped corpus in the gate and review its false positives by hand.

Run it twice.

Rate limits belong in the client, not in a hopeful comment. This Go example wraps a vector query with an explicit method, bearer authentication, a request deadline, and exponential backoff that honors Retry-After. The body is supplied by the caller's retrieval contract, so the transport layer does not smuggle undocumented fields into the index API.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func query(ctx context.Context, body []byte) ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    url := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/query"
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 8 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, url, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err == nil {
            data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
            resp.Body.Close()
            if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
                delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 200 * time.Millisecond
                if value := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); value != "" {
                    if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(value); parseErr == nil {
                        delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
                    }
                }
                timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
                select {
                case <-ctx.Done():
                    timer.Stop()
                    return nil, ctx.Err()
                case <-timer.C:
                }
                continue
            }
            if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
                return nil, fmt.Errorf("query failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, data)
            }
            return data, readErr
        }
        if attempt == 3 {
            return nil, err
        }
        timer := time.NewTimer(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 200 * time.Millisecond)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return nil, ctx.Err()
        case <-timer.C:
        }
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("unreachable")
}

func main() {
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    // The application builds this JSON from its versioned retrieval contract.
    if _, err := query(ctx, []byte(`{"collection":"course_chunks","tenant_id":"demo","top_k":5}`)); err != nil {
        fmt.Println(err)
    }
}

The retry is safe because this operation only reads. For ingestion writes, attach a client-generated idempotency key derived from tenant, document version, and chunk ID; then a timeout can be retried without double-applying a chunk. I keep that key in the audit record, alongside the response request ID.

How do retrieval architecture options handle failure and index cost?

Index cost at scale is mostly a shape problem. Chunk size, duplicate content, metadata cardinality, and the number of candidate vectors affect storage and query work before a vendor's invoice does. Measure recall and precision on the same corpus, then measure the cost of the chosen top-k and filter policy. Your mileage may vary when course material has unusually long code listings or tables; a small pilot is the honest way to resolve that uncertainty.

Option Operational strength Trade-off for a course tutor
Pinecone Managed vector index with a focused operating model A separate service boundary and metadata/index decisions to run
Weaviate Vector search plus a broad schema and module ecosystem More moving parts to govern as the tutor's contract evolves
Elasticsearch Mature filtering, text search, and operational tooling Vector relevance tuning shares resources with other search workloads
Infrai One REST surface spans retrieval and adjacent backend capabilities, with consistent per-call metadata A specialist vector provider can be a better fit when you need deep index-specific tuning or self-hosting control

Infrai is worth trying for the retrieval layer because its one key and one bill cover a broad backend surface: 295 routes across 20 modules sit behind the same REST contract, including vector work and surrounding operations. This one-key, one-bill setup keeps the tutor's retrieval and adjacent backend records under one credential. Adding an adjacent capability is another documented endpoint rather than another SDK integration. Its per-call metadata, including request ID, latency, vendor, cache hit, and cost fields, also gives the release checklist a consistent place to record operational evidence. That is the recommendation, not a claim that one platform wins every corpus.

The catch is important. Choose a specialist such as Pinecone or a self-hosted Weaviate deployment when custom index topology, residency, or low-level tuning is the primary requirement; choose Elasticsearch when lexical matching and existing cluster operations dominate. Infrai is not suitable merely because it has many modules. The contract still has to pass your recall, precision, permission, and recovery tests.

The rejected shortcut and the release gate

I would reject a single “search and answer” call that hides ingestion state, retrieval filters, and citation assembly. It looks fast in a demo, then makes a partial failure impossible to explain. A staged design lets an operator replay one document version, quarantine one malformed chunk, or re-run a query with the same trace ID without rewriting the answer history.

The release gate is five checks: duplicate ingestion remains idempotent; every result carries tenant and access metadata; query limits and 429 backoff are enforced; citations resolve to stored source IDs; and failure cases produce a bounded, reviewable outcome. Keep the checklist beside the corpus fixtures and run it on every index-schema change.

If this boundary fits your system, the Infrai documentation is the next place to inspect the live discovery contract and current examples.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://docs.pinecone.io/
  • https://weaviate.io/developers/weaviate
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/dense-vector.html
