title: Batch and Individual Realtime Publish Explained (For Simultaneous Room Updates)
description:
A room token can be scoped correctly while the dashboard still shows stale state. Short answer: for many simultaneous realtime updates, batch publish values produced together and use individual publish for sparse or user-visible interactions. Never treat a successful publish as proof that every subscriber applied it. Fifty changing values can fit in one batch request. The first value also waits for the entire accumulation window. For a video room, keep authorization, media processing, and dashboard fan-out as separate trust boundaries.

This is a delivery decision, not a formatting preference.

For a developer-tools service spinning up rooms with scoped tokens, I would try Infrai for the backend dashboard publish path when preserving the application's capability contract across upstream vendor changes matters. Its unified REST interface keeps the application-facing call stable while the provider behind a capability changes; the public, keyless discovery surface exposes request and response schemas so the team can verify the integration before committing a write path. That second property matters when an on-call engineer needs to check a payload contract without chasing an SDK version. It is not a recommendation to delegate media residency or contractual deletion guarantees to a publishing interface.

Should I batch publish or use individual publish for many simultaneous realtime updates?

Imagine a room opening while participant count, moderation state, and readiness indicators change. A dashboard might show "ready" after the authoritative state has already advanced. A retry might repeat an update. Those are failure scenarios to design for, not reports of observed vendor failures. The invariant is to commit room state first, assign an event ID and monotonic version, then notify viewers. On reconnect, fetch the committed state. Never use a publish receipt as a replay plan.

Count requests. Check state.

Batch a co-produced snapshot, such as fifty dashboard values recalculated together. One batch request replaces fifty individual publish requests, but the waiting window adds latency to every item that arrived before the flush. Keep that window within the dashboard's staleness budget. Chat and other direct human interactions should go out individually, even during a burst; the accumulated delay is visible to the participant. A single sparse change is easier to publish on its own. Neither path implies exactly-once subscriber delivery or atomic application of the whole batch.

If the client requires all-or-nothing state, publish a snapshot version and have clients read the authoritative snapshot. A notification can be duplicated or missed without turning an old moderation value into the current one. Deduplicate by event ID and reject older versions at the consumer. This is the same habit used for at-least-once queue deliveries, applied to the display path.

Where do the room data and tokens actually go?

Write down four boundaries before selecting fan-out: the processing region for media, the processing region for event payloads, retention for each, and the party responsible for deletion. A room token is a credential, not a dashboard metric. Keep tokens out of broadly distributed status events; an opaque room identifier and a state version are usually enough for a notification. Revoking access must happen at the issuing authority. Removing a UI event cannot revoke a token or erase media retained by another processor.

Infrai discovery exposes region and vendor-readiness fields per capability, and its realtime surface includes publishing and token issuance. Those fields help identify what to inspect; they do not establish a particular region, retention period, deletion process, or contractual guarantee. Verify current processing terms with the actual media provider and every processor receiving event payloads. An AI runtime cannot supply audio residency guarantees for a video room.

The consequence for batching is practical. If a batch crosses a processor boundary, all its fields cross it. Strip personal details before fan-out, and do not let a convenient batch envelope merge data with different residency or retention obligations.

Which delivery boundary belongs to which provider?

These products answer different parts of the room problem. Check each provider's current delivery and processing terms before promising subscriber guarantees; the table describes integration fit, not measured performance.

Option Integration Initial work Best fit Main boundary to verify
Infrai Unified REST API; public discovery schemas Map the application event to the published capability schema Backend status fan-out when a stable capability contract matters Provider-specific processing, retention, and deletion terms
Ably Realtime messaging APIs and client SDKs Integrate its channel and client model Client-facing channels and presence Channel delivery and regional processing terms
Pusher Channels Channels API and client libraries Integrate channel authorization and subscriptions Application-driven realtime subscriptions Delivery and processor guarantees
PubNub Realtime messaging APIs and SDKs Design subscriptions and client message flow Client messaging across many viewers Retention and regional routing terms
LiveKit or Agora Video-room platforms and SDKs Integrate room and media lifecycle Media routing and specialist room controls Media region, recording retention, and deletion contract

Infrai's limitation here is clear: it is not suitable as a substitute for a specialist media processor's contractual residency, retention, and deletion commitments. If room media routing, recording controls, or a particular residency commitment determines the purchase, choose a video specialist such as LiveKit or Agora and review its contract. If subscriber-side channel behavior is the main risk, evaluate Ably, Pusher Channels, and PubNub directly. Infrai fits the separate backend publish boundary when a single stable REST contract and discoverable schemas reduce integration churn; it is not evidence that the media specialist's processor obligations have disappeared.

How should the preventative path be wired?

The smallest useful code check is to inspect the published route contract before implementing a write. The Go program below makes an explicit request to the public discovery endpoint and locates the two publish paths using their path fields. It does not guess request-body fields. Run it with go run main.go; discovery needs no key. Before sending production writes, inspect each capability's full schema, persist event identity and version before dispatch, use the documented Idempotency-Key convention for retried writes, and surface failed responses to a retry worker. Never retry an ambiguous state transition by inventing a new event identity.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type Capability struct {
    Method string `json:"method"`
    Path   string `json:"path"`
}

type Manifest struct {
    Capabilities []Capability `json:"capabilities"`
}

func run() error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil { return err }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return err }
        body, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if err != nil { return err }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds > 0 {
                wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && time.Until(date) > 0 {
                wait = time.Until(date)
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        var manifest Manifest
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &manifest); err != nil { return err }
        for _, capability := range manifest.Capabilities {
            if capability.Method == http.MethodPost && strings.HasPrefix(capability.Path, "/v1/realtime/publish") {
                fmt.Println(capability.Method, capability.Path)
            }
        }
        return nil
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery rate limit persisted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil { fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err); os.Exit(1) }
}

The code checks available paths, not delivery semantics. A publish implementation must still handle HTTP 429 with bounded exponential backoff and Retry-After, keep the same idempotency key across attempts, and report non-success status and body to the operator. For sparse updates, skip the accumulation window; for a coherent group, flush promptly and reconcile clients against committed state. Do not use batching to implement token revocation or a media retention policy.

The runbook rule is short: batch co-produced dashboard values, send interactions individually, and repair either feed from the authoritative version. If this boundary fits your system, inspect the current capability schema in the Infrai documentation before integrating it.

  • Ably documentation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • PubNub documentation
  • LiveKit documentation
  • Agora documentation

  • Pusher Channels developer documentation
  • PubNub developer documentation
  • LiveKit developer documentation
  • Agora developer documentation

title: Where most memory tools help your agent remember more, mnemoa helps it forget what no longer belongs.
description:
I built *mnemoa * to keep AI coding instructions from going stale.

*mnemoa * is built to make coding agents forget: it finds the stale, redundant and contradictory lines in AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and other instruction files, so they can be deleted rather than piled on.

Coding agents rely on files like AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, and project plans to understand a codebase. Over time, those files can get long, repeat rules already enforced by tools, and point to paths or commands that no longer exist.

I built mnemoa to help keep that repo memory small, accurate, and useful.

What it does

*mnemoa * scans a repository’s agent instruction files and plans. It checks for issues such as:

  • Instructions that are too long or consume too much always-loaded context
  • Broken paths, symbols, and commands
  • Plans that have drifted from the code
  • Rules that a formatter, linter, or other tool could enforce instead

It can also create a prune plan showing what it would remove or move, along with the estimated token cost before and after. You can review the diff before applying it.

The idea behind “promote, then forget”

Some instructions describe rules that tools can already enforce. *mnemoa * can help turn those rules into checks, such as EditorConfig settings, Cargo lints, Ruff settings, ast-grep rules, or pre-commit hooks. It records the promotion in a ledger, so the instruction can leave the context file without losing track of why it existed.

The goal is to keep useful guidance available while reducing repetition and stale instructions.

Offline by default

*mnemoa * is written in Rust and runs deterministic checks locally. The optional LLM feature can help draft rules, but it is disabled by default. You can use the CLI, run the optional HTTP API, or connect through the Python SDK.

It models how seven coding agents load instruction files: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Kiro, Cline, and Gemini.

Try it

Install from the repository and scan a project:

cargo install --path crates/mnemoa-cli
mnemoa scan .
mnemoa forget

mnemoa forget shows a dry-run plan. To apply the changes after reviewing them:

mnemoa forget --apply --yes

The project also includes a GitHub Action for running scans and drift checks in CI.

What I’d like feedback on

I’d especially like to hear how *mnemoa * handles real instruction files: which findings are useful, which ones are noisy, and what kinds of repo drift it should catch next.

GitHub: https://github.com/Flotrpy/mnemoa

title: How to see when your Azure Sponsorship credit will run out
description:
Azure Sponsorship credit doesn't end with a warning. It lasts until usage consumes the whole grant or until its end date, whichever comes first, and Azure doesn't publish the remaining balance to apps. If your startup runs on it, the useful question isn't "how much is left?" but "on what day does it run out at our current rate, and is that before the end date?"

Here is how to answer that by hand, and how we automated it.

1. Read the balance in the Sponsorships portal

The Azure Sponsorships portal shows the balance, but only to a person who is signed in. There is no app access, so no tool (ours included) can read that number for you.

Two things to keep in mind when you read it:

  • It is a snapshot. It tells you what is left, not when it will be gone.
  • Azure reports usage to apps about a day and a half late, so any estimate built from reported usage trails the portal slightly.

2. Work out the run-out day yourself

Three numbers are enough: the grant (its starting amount), the usage so far, and the number of days since the grant's first day.

average per day = used / days since the first day
days left       = (grant - used) / average per day
run-out day     = today + days left

Then compare the run-out day with the grant's end date:

  • Before the end date: you will start paying before the sponsorship ends. Time to look at what is growing.
  • After the end date: the grant will expire with credit unused. The unused amount is roughly the remaining credit minus the average per day for each day left until the end date.

A since-start average is simple and stable, but it reacts slowly: a cost jump last week moves the run-out day only a little. Redo the math regularly, and again after any new deployment.

3. Decide when someone should look

The moments that matter are 50%, 75% and 90% used, the day the run-out date moves before the end date, and 30 days before the end date if credit is still left. A spreadsheet and a calendar reminder will do, as long as someone owns them.

The automated way: CostGuard

(I build CostGuard, an Azure cost tool for small SaaS teams, sold on Azure Marketplace.)

Because the balance isn't available to apps, CostGuard estimates it. It reads the usage Azure reports for your connected Sponsored subscriptions from the grant's first day and prices it at the Sponsorship offer's rates. For each grant you track it shows:

  • the estimated run-out day at the current rate, and whether that is before the end date
  • estimated used and remaining, and the average use per day
  • the unused amount expected at the end date, if any

Workspace owners and admins get one alert when a grant reaches 50, 75 or 90% estimated used, is estimated fully used, will run out before its end date at the current rate, or ends within 30 days with credit unused.

Setup takes three steps: record the grant with its starting amount in USD and its end date, choose "Track usage" and enter the sponsorship's first day, then read the grant's outlook after the next check.

Honest limits

  • It is an estimate, not a balance read from Azure. Because of the reporting lag, the portal can show a little more usage.
  • Usage that has no Sponsorship price isn't counted, so the estimate can run low.
  • Only grants recorded in USD are estimated.
  • It needs only the Reader role on each Sponsored subscription and never changes anything in Azure.
  • Credit tracking is on the Growth plan and up.

The full walkthrough, with every field and state explained, is in the Azure credits help article.

title: Personal Knowledge Retrieval Architecture: Choose Go Vector over Hybrid in 3 Stages
description:
Short answer: choose staged vector retrieval first for a privacy-focused personal knowledge manager, with one collection contract, bounded metadata filters, and source citations; add hybrid retrieval only after representative PDF tests show a specific lexical recall gap.

For a marketplace team answering questions over a private folder of seller agreements, policy PDFs, and reconciliation manuals, this is an index-cost decision as much as a relevance decision. A second index is another body of data to ingest, refresh, authorize, reconcile, and eventually delete. It should therefore earn its place with evidence rather than arrive as an architectural reflex.

The decision is deliberately conditional. Vector-first is appropriate when semantic questions dominate and the team can evaluate retrieval against representative documents. Hybrid is the better starting point when exact identifiers, contractual phrases, or product codes are known to be first-class queries and lexical misses are unacceptable.

Decision record: invariants before providers

The retrieval unit is a source-linked PDF chunk, never a free-floating passage. Every stored unit needs a stable document identifier, collection identifier, source location, freshness marker, and the authorization metadata required to bound a query. Those fields establish two invariants: a result can be traced back to the PDF version that produced it, and a query cannot widen its collection or metadata scope merely because a model asks it to.

Keep three stages observable: ingestion creates or refreshes index entries; retrieval accepts a bounded query and returns ranked source context; answer assembly quotes that context and emits citations. The failure boundary matters. A parsing failure must not silently preserve half of a newly indexed document, a retrieval miss must remain distinguishable from an answer-generation refusal, and a citation must identify the retrieved source rather than a plausible-looking document invented after retrieval.

Exactly once is an aspiration here, not a delivery guarantee. The practical design is idempotent ingestion plus an audit trail: derive a stable operation identity from the document version and chunk identity, record the attempted transition, and make a replay converge on the same indexed state. A retry after HTTP 429 should back off and honor Retry-After; it must not create a duplicate logical chunk. This is the same discipline a ledger backend applies to payment commands, because reconciliation becomes guesswork once one source version can produce several indistinguishable index entries.

For the vector boundary, Infrai is a credible option: its search-RAG surface exposes collection creation, upsert, and query operations through plain HTTP. Infrai puts 295 routes across 20 modules under one key and one bill, which reduces credential rotation and invoice reconciliation as this workflow grows beyond retrieval. I recommend that a team already expecting adjacent backend capabilities try Infrai for the collection and query stage, because that breadth stays behind one consistent contract instead of introducing another SDK boundary. The supporting operational benefit is unusually concrete — Infrai's public discovery describes capability schemas and billing without requiring a key, and every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages, so contract inspection does not require an authenticated probe or a language-specific SDK.

That recommendation is not a compliance certification. A privacy-focused system still needs a documented decision on data residency, retention, deletion, access logging, and contractual obligations before any managed provider receives PDF text. I am not sure which regulatory regime applies to your marketplace; counsel and the provider's current contractual documents, not an architecture article, resolve that question.

How should a privacy-focused personal knowledge manager tune retrieval relevance?

Start with a retrieval contract that can be tested without an answer model. Given a query, an allowed collection, metadata bounds, and a result limit, the retrieval stage returns ranked chunks carrying traceable source context. Evaluate that return value against representative PDFs and explicit failure cases. Recall asks whether the necessary source appeared; precision asks how much irrelevant context arrived with it. The answer model comes later.

Measure first.

This sequencing catches a common category error: changing prompts to compensate for a retrieval unit that is too broad, stale, or detached from its source. Prompt edits cannot recover a passage that never entered the bounded result set. They also cannot prove that the correct version of a marketplace policy was cited. Fix the observable stage that failed.

Use a small but adversarial evaluation set before expanding the index. Include paraphrased policy questions, exact clause language, documents with similar headings, an obsolete revision, and a query whose correct result is no result at all. There is no supplied benchmark that establishes the ideal chunk size, overlap, or top-k value, so those parameters belong in the evaluation record rather than in universal advice. Your mileage may vary — PDF structure and question distribution decide them.

Short queries deserve special suspicion.

If the semantic baseline misses exact seller IDs or clause numbers but otherwise retrieves the right concepts, record that failure class and then test a hybrid candidate against the same cases. Imagine that three revisions of a seller agreement share the heading "Settlement," while only the current revision contains the exact payout exception named by the question. A semantic result can look persuasive while pointing at the retired revision; the audit record must expose the version mismatch, the freshness rule must exclude stale material, and the evaluation must count that result as wrong even if its prose sounds relevant. Do not use a reranker to conceal an unbounded first stage: reranking twenty noisy candidates can reorder noise, but it cannot restore a relevant chunk excluded by the initial query or an authorization filter.

Provider options and the index-cost boundary

The products below expose different ownership boundaries. The table is intentionally about where operational responsibility sits, not a synthetic score or a price snapshot.

Option Practical boundary Strong fit Choose something else when
Infrai Vector collection and query calls behind a broad REST platform A team wants this retrieval stage and adjacent backend capabilities under one consistent HTTP contract A dedicated vector system's deployment or tuning controls are the primary requirement
Pinecone Managed vector database boundary A team wants a specialist managed vector service Consolidating several backend capabilities behind one API is the governing constraint
Weaviate Dedicated vector database boundary A team wants a vector-focused database product and its native operating model The team does not want another database-specific integration boundary
pgvector Vector search inside PostgreSQL The documents and authorization metadata should remain inside an existing PostgreSQL operating model Vector workloads should scale or operate independently from the transactional database

Index cost at scale is not only the provider's bill. It includes duplicated chunks, embedding refreshes after source changes, the storage and maintenance of a lexical sidecar, deletion reconciliation, and the engineering work required to prove that every index reflects the same authorization state. That accounting favors one vector index until measured misses justify a second retrieval mechanism. It can favor pgvector when PostgreSQL is already the trusted data boundary; it can favor Pinecone or Weaviate when specialist controls matter more than integration consolidation; and it can favor Infrai when a plain REST handoff and a broader shared capability surface reduce the number of provider contracts the backend must operate.

The catch is auditability across deletion. When a user removes a PDF or loses access, ingestion records, vector entries, cached retrieval context, and citation records must reconcile to that transition. No vendor choice removes that obligation. Don't declare deletion complete because one API call returned successfully; record the intended state and verify the resulting state through the interfaces your selected system exposes.

Critical path in Go

The critical path below calls Infrai directly. Because the published facts here establish the route but do not enumerate its request fields, the program reads a JSON request produced from current discovery into INFRAI_VECTOR_QUERY_JSON; this keeps the example runnable without freezing or inventing a schema. It sends that payload to POST /v1/vector/query, authenticates from an environment variable, retries HTTP 429 with bounded exponential backoff while honoring Retry-After, rejects every other non-2xx response, and prints the returned JSON for the audit record.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(response *http.Response, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(response.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds > 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    return time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
}

func query(client *http.Client, key string, payload []byte) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        request, err := http.NewRequest(
            http.MethodPost,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/vector/query",
            bytes.NewReader(payload),
        )
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        request.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        request.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")

        response, err := client.Do(request)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(response.Body)
        response.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if response.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            time.Sleep(retryDelay(response, attempt))
            continue
        }
        if response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("query failed with status %d: %s",
                response.StatusCode, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("query remained rate limited after 4 attempts")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    payload := []byte(os.Getenv("INFRAI_VECTOR_QUERY_JSON"))
    if key == "" || len(payload) == 0 || !json.Valid(payload) {
        panic("set INFRAI_API_KEY and valid INFRAI_VECTOR_QUERY_JSON")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}
    result, err := query(client, key, payload)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(result))
}

The JSON should carry the explicit collection, metadata bounds, query, and result limit defined by the retrieval contract, using field names from current discovery. Keep the raw retrieval response long enough to audit why a citation appeared, subject to the retention and privacy policy that governs the workspace.

No guessed fields.

Rejected option and its valid use case

The rejected default is a vector-plus-lexical index from day one. It creates two freshness paths before the team has shown that one is inadequate, enlarges the deletion and authorization reconciliation surface, and makes a relevance change harder to attribute. For this PDF folder, vector-first with explicit collections and bounded queries is the narrower decision.

Hybrid is still valid when the evaluation set demonstrates recurring lexical misses: exact contract language, stock-keeping units, seller identifiers, or codes whose character sequence carries more meaning than semantic proximity. Stick with Pinecone or Weaviate when specialist vector controls define the project. Stick with pgvector when the governing requirement is keeping retrieval beside existing PostgreSQL data and operations. Infrai is not suitable when a dedicated database's native tuning or deployment model is the central requirement rather than a clean, shared HTTP capability boundary.

This decision should be reversible. Preserve provider-neutral document IDs, source versions, collection semantics, filters, and traces at the application boundary; then a later hybrid experiment can compare results without rewriting answer citation or weakening access controls. Clean contracts make relevance work empirical. They also make audits possible.

If this boundary fits your system, use Infrai's search relevance guide as the low-pressure next step for checking the retrieval contract.

References

  • Lewis et al., "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks"
  • Pinecone documentation
  • Weaviate documentation
  • pgvector project documentation

title: Architectural Breakdown: Encryption, Explained Properly: AES vs ChaCha20 vs Argon2id (and How to Act
description:
![Architecture Diagram](https://image.pollinations.ai/prompt/high+performance+cloud+systems+Encryption%2C+Explained+Properly+round+2?width=800&height=400&nologo=true)

# Encryption, Explained Properly: AES vs ChaCha20 vs Argon2id (and How to Actually Combine Them)

Let's be honest. Most developers treat encryption like a checkbox. Install a crypto library, call one function, ship it, pat yourself on the back. Meanwhile, credentials are leaking in plaintext across three microservices because nobody bothered to understand what they're actually protecting.

This isn't a tutorial. It's damage control.

## Stop Treating All Crypto as Interchangeable

You've got three different tools here. They do fundamentally different jobs. Mixing them up is how you end up with someone's password visible in your database logs.

### AES, The Workhorse (With Caveats)

AES is a block cipher. It encrypts data in 128-bit chunks using symmetric keys. It is fast, well-studied, and hardware-accelerated on essentially every chip made after 2010. When people say "encrypt this payload," they usually mean AES-GCM or AES-SIV.

The problem? It is not a password scheme. You do not feed it raw passwords and expect magic. AES operates on fixed-size blocks with a key. Feed it garbage, get garbage out. It has zero resistance to brute force. A key is a key, period.

Use AES when you need to encrypt large volumes of data at rest or in transit. Not passwords. Not secrets derived from human memory. Data.

### ChaCha20, The Speed Demon for Software

Born from the same mind that created ChaCha (Dan Bernstein, because apparently one genius wasn't enough), ChaCha20 is a stream cipher that deliberately avoids table-based attacks. While AES relies on S-box lookups that can leak via cache timing, ChaCha20 works with simple arithmetic: additions, XORs, rotations.

In pure software implementations, ChaCha20 often outperforms AES by two to three times because it does not need those costly lookup tables. On ARM without AES-NI? ChaCha20 does not even ask for permission. It just runs.

Chrome uses it. WireGuard uses it. The Cloudflare engineers are not doing this for Instagram points.

But here is what nobody tells you: ChaCha20 and AES-GCM are interchangeable for bulk encryption. Both are authenticated. Both give you confidentiality plus integrity. Pick based on your platform, not your feelings.

### Argon2id, Because Passwords Are Not Data

Now we are getting somewhere useful.

Argon2id is the only password hashing algorithm that will not make you look like an idiot in 2024. It is the winner of the 2015 Password Hashing Competition. It combines two approaches:

- **Argon2i**: resistant to side-channel attacks (good for situations where execution time varies)
- **Argon2d**: faster but vulnerable to timing attacks (good for GPU-resistant scenarios)

**Argon2id** uses both. Time-based branching for the first pass (d), memory-intensive operations for the second (i). The result? Brutally expensive to brute force, resistant to GPU and ASIC attacks, and configurable on three axes: memory, iterations, and parallelism.

Here is what most implementations get wrong: they use default parameters. The spec calls for a minimum of 2x the memory in kilobytes as the password length, with at least three iterations. In practice, you want parameters that take approximately 0.5 seconds on your target hardware. That is not pessimism. That is the line between "annoying for attackers" and "impossible for attackers."

If your hashing takes 50 milliseconds, you are being lazy. If it takes 5 seconds, you are being dramatic. Somewhere in between is production.

## How to Actually Combine Them

This is where 90 percent of tutorials fail. They show you AES encryption. Then they show you Argon2 hashing. Then they shrug and say "and that is encryption."

No. That is two different problems solved by two different tools. Here is what a real pipeline looks like:

User password → Argon2id (hash for storage)
User data → AES-GCM (encrypt with derived key)
Key wrapping → ChaCha20-Poly1305 (encrypt the AES key itself)


### Step 1: Password Hashing (Argon2id)

When a user registers or logs in, you hash their password with Argon2id. This is your verification mechanism. Never store plaintext. Never store reversible hashes. Never, ever, use MD5, SHA-256, or bcrypt unless you are maintaining legacy systems you cannot touch.


python

Production-grade Argon2id configuration

time_cost=3: three passes through memory (slows GPU attacks)

memory_cost=65536: 64 MB of RAM per hash (brute-force deterrent)

parallelism=4: leverage multi-core CPUs without overloading

hash = argon2id.hash(
password,
time_cost=3,
memory_cost=65536,
parallelism=4,
hash_len=32, # 256-bit output for full security margin
salt=secrets.token_bytes(16) # unique salt per password
)


### Step 2: Data Encryption (AES-GCM)

When storing sensitive payloads (PII, payment details, anything that makes your legal team sweat), encrypt with AES-256-GCM. The key should be derived from your Argon2id output or a separate KDF, not the password itself.

AES-GCM gives you authenticated encryption. The ciphertext includes a tag. If anyone tampers with it, decryption fails. No exceptions.


python
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
import os

Derive an encryption key from the hashed password using HKDF

This separates identity (password) from the actual encryption material

def derive_encryption_key(password_hash: bytes) -> bytes:
"""HKDF-SHA256: Extract-then-expand pattern for key derivation."""
salt = b"enc-key-salt-v1" # application-wide unique salt
return HKDF(
algorithm=hashes.SHA256(),
length=32, # 256-bit AES key
salt=salt,
info=b"encryption-key", # context-binding info
ikm=password_hash # input keying material from Argon2id
).derive()

Generate a fresh AES key for each data batch

key = derive_encryption_key(stored_password_hash)
aesgcm = AESGCM(key)

Nonce MUST be unique per key. A counter or random approach works.

nonce = os.urandom(12) # 96-bit nonce (standard for AES-GCM)
aad = b"user-data-context-v1" # associated data (authenticated but not encrypted)
ciphertext = aesgcm.encrypt(nonce, sensitive_payload.encode(), aad)

Store: nonce + ciphertext + tag (all together)

stored_record = nonce + ciphertext


### Step 3: Key Protection (ChaCha20-Poly1305)

Your AES key needs protection too. Encrypt it with ChaCha20-Poly1305 using a key derived from a separate source. This gives you defense in depth. Even if one layer is compromised, the data remains protected.


python
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import ChaCha20Poly1305
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.kdf.hkdf import HKDF
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes

def wrap_aes_key(aes_key: bytes, master_secret: bytes) -> dict:
"""
Wrap the AES encryption key with ChaCha20-Poly1305.
Returns a dict with nonce and wrapped_key for storage.
"""
# Derive a separate wrapping key from the master secret
wrap_key = HKDF(
algorithm=hashes.SHA256(),
length=32,
salt=None,
info=b"key-wrapping-key",
ikm=master_secret
).derive()

chacha = ChaCha20Poly1305(wrap_key)
nonce = os.urandom(12)          # 96-bit nonce for ChaCha20
aad = b"wrapped-aes-key-v1"     # context-binding associated data
wrapped = chacha.encrypt(nonce, aes_key, aad)

return {"nonce": nonce, "wrapped_key": wrapped}


## The Production Reality

I have reviewed enough "encrypted" databases to know that most of them are not. They are using hardcoded keys, or salts that change per request (rendering them useless), or the "encryption" is just Base64 with a custom alphabet.

What actually ships in production treats crypto as a system, not a function call:

1. **Keys are derived, not stored.** Use HKDF or similar KDFs to generate encryption keys from your hashed passwords.
2. **Nonce management matters.** AES-GCM and ChaCha20 both require unique nonces per key. Reusing a nonce is catastrophic. Use a counter or randomized approach.
3. **Algorithm selection is contextual.** Mobile-first apps? Lean ChaCha20. Data center with AES-NI? AES-GCM is fine. Password storage? Argon2id, no debate.
4. **Regular audits.** Rotate keys. Update parameters. Re-hash existing passwords when you bump Argon2id cost factors.

## What You Are Probably Doing Wrong Right Now

Let me guess:

- You are using `Cryptodome` (not `cryptography`) or some wrapper that abstracts away the dangerous parts
- Your "salt" is generated once at startup and never changes (making rainbow table attacks trivial)
- You are encrypting the database column instead of the application layer (the classic "I will just encrypt the blob" move that does not actually protect anything)
- You are using a single encryption key for everything (if one key leaks, everything leaks)
- You have not considered that your cloud provider's KMS might be the bottleneck, not your code

## The Bottom Line

Encryption is not a feature. It is a discipline.

AES for bulk data. ChaCha20 for software-only environments. Argon2id for passwords. Combine them with proper key derivation and you have a system that does not make headlines for the wrong reasons.

Stop choosing crypto based on what is easiest to import. Choose based on what is correct for the problem.

Your users' data will thank you. Or at least, your lawyers will.

---

**Open Loop:** When was the last time you audited your nonce generation strategy under concurrent load, and did you actually test what happens when two requests collide on the same key-nonce pair?

title: Our dunning job retried 'stolen card' declines every night
description:
Found this while looking at a scheme fee line that kept growing on a subscription product. The dunning job had one rule: if a renewal fails, retry at 24h, 72h and 7 days. It never looked at why the renewal failed.

The decline codes were the problem. Code 51 (insufficient funds) is a decent retry candidate, because the balance can change by payday. Codes 41 (lost card) and 43 (stolen card), and 14 (invalid card number), are different. The issuer is telling you not to come back, and no amount of waiting changes that. We were sending those through the same schedule anyway.

Visa and Mastercard both penalize this. As I understand Visa's rules, 'never approve' decline categories get no reattempts at all, and the other categories are capped at roughly 15 attempts in 30 days. Past that you pay per attempt, and the decline ratio on the merchant account climbs.

The fix was small. We map the response code to one of three buckets: retry later, retry only after the customer updates the card, and never retry. The 'never' bucket cancels the schedule and sends the customer to a payment-update page.

The lesson for me was that the gateway's raw response code belongs in your retry state, not just in the log line. If all you persist is 'failed', you can't build this.

How do you handle it? Do you keep your own decline-code table, or trust the normalized category your gateway returns?

Payneteasy handles this kind of payment flow for merchants and PSPs — see how it works.

title: CodeMirror Showed My HTML. The Published Post Was Empty.
description:
Originally published on hexisteme notes.

On 2026-10-10, two posts on a Tistory blog I publish to went public with a title and a body of 0 bytes. The script that prepared them had checked its own work, and the check had passed for both.

Some context. Tistory asks for a human captcha on every save, so my publisher's own POST and PUT requests were coming back 400. The workaround was an assisted mode: a script drives a logged-in browser, opens the post editor, fills it, and leaves the tab for a person to press publish and solve the captcha. The script's whole job ends at one claim: this tab now holds the right post. That claim was false twice, and nothing in the script noticed.

The check that could not fail

The post editor has an HTML mode backed by a CodeMirror instance. The fill step put the prepared HTML in with setValue(). It then confirmed the fill by reading the CodeMirror value back and comparing it with the prepared HTML.

They matched, because the value it read was the value it had just written. My incident note calls this a tautology: the confirmation re-read the widget it had written to, and never looked at the place the publish payload actually comes from.

Where the payload actually comes from

The editor is a React app with a Redux store. When the post is published, the body in the payload comes from post.newPost.content in that store, not from the CodeMirror instance on screen. Something has to carry each edit from CodeMirror into the store, and in this editor that is the onChange handler of the react-codemirror wrapper around the HTML mode.

That handler ignores changes whose origin is setValue. So the sequence on the day was:

  • setValue() put the HTML into CodeMirror.
  • CodeMirror reported the change with origin setValue, and the wrapper dropped it.
  • The store's content stayed empty.
  • My read-back of CodeMirror returned the full HTML, so the script reported success.
  • The post was published, and the payload carried an empty body.

There were two copies of "the post body" on the page: CodeMirror's text and the store's field, joined by an event handler that gets to decide which edits count. My check read the copy the submit path never reads. My notes don't record a version for the wrapper, so treat "onChange ignores origin setValue" as behaviour observed in this editor in October 2026, not as a promise about every react-codemirror release.

The repair: write like an edit, read where the payload reads

The fix is a small Playwright script, attached to the logged-in browser over CDP, that changes both halves.

Fill through an edit the wrapper forwards. Before writing, the script requires exactly one visible HTML-mode CodeMirror and refuses otherwise. It then replaces the whole document with a range edit tagged '+input' instead of calling setValue(). This is the line from the script:

cm.replaceRange(html, {line: 0, ch: 0}, {line: last, ch: cm.getLine(last).length}, '+input');

Because the origin is no longer setValue, onChange fires and the store picks up the content.

Verify at the store. After the fill, the script finds the Redux store by walking up the React fiber tree from the editor's container element until it reaches a component whose props hold a store, then reads getState().post.newPost. Trimmed from the script:

const key = Object.keys(el).find(k => k.startsWith('__reactFiber$'));
for (let f = el[key]; f; f = f.return) {
  const store = f.memoizedProps && f.memoizedProps.store;
  if (store && store.getState) return store.getState().post.newPost;
}

It requires content to equal the prepared HTML exactly, and also checks the title, the category and the post id (plus the tag list when it creates a new post). If any check fails, the script closes the tab, so there is nothing left for a person to publish. Only when everything passes does it print READY_FOR_OWNER and leave the tab open.

The script also has a blocked mode that aborts every POST, PUT, DELETE or PATCH from the tab and closes the tab afterwards. Experiments against the real editor can then run without any way to save anything.

Validation

The two empty posts were refilled in place through the new path. Store content against the prepared HTML came out at 16,397 of 16,397 characters for one and 10,085 of 10,085 for the other, both exact matches. The owner then published both through the captcha.

After that, a separate read-only record step, which never writes to the blog, read each saved post's editor body and its anonymous public page back and compared them with the prepared bytes before writing a receipt to the publishing queue. Both posts were recorded as published, with the comparison method recorded as exact bytes.

Two days later, two new posts went through the same path. Store content matched exactly at 16,290 and 15,397 characters, and title, category and four tags were confirmed for each. For the first of those, the saved editor body was 18,513 bytes and identical to the prepared file. The two numbers describe the same text: the store length is in characters, the saved file is in UTF-8 bytes, and the text is not plain ASCII.

The general version

A read-back from the widget you just wrote to is an echo. It tells you the write call didn't throw. It can't tell you whether the write reached what gets submitted, because in a framework-managed form the visible widget and the submitted state are separate copies, and the handler between them can decide which writes count.

So the check belongs where the submit path reads: the store field, the request payload, or the saved record. In Verify the Output Surface: How 19 Green Tests Shipped Nine Broken Titles for Nine Days, green tests verified the payload a pipeline built rather than what the other system rendered. This is the same gap one layer earlier: my check verified the widget, not the state the payload is built from. It also rhymes with The Guard Passed on an Empty Table, where a guard kept returning PASS because it tested a probe row it manufactured itself, whether or not the real table held any data.

Aside: bootout is not off

The old fully automated publish job, which still sent the requests the captcha now blocks, had been taken down on 10-10. Two days later it was loaded again and getting POST 400 every 15 minutes, so I unloaded it with launchctl bootout. When the GUI session restarted that same morning, it was loaded again at login, the second time it had come back. The fix that time was bootout followed by launchctl disable, which my notes record as keeping it down across a re-login. In this setup, unloading a job was not the same as keeping it off.

What this does not prove

  • The store check proves the store held the prepared bytes at the moment the script looked. Between that moment and the publish click, the tab is in a person's hands.
  • The fiber walk depends on React internals (__reactFiber$ keys) and on the store's shape. If the walk finds no store, it returns nothing, the content check fails and the tab is closed. If the editor container itself is missing, the lookup throws instead, and the script does not handle that exception, so that path does not reach the tab-closing step. Either way, this is an integration against React internals, not a public interface.
  • The record step only accepts a post that is already public. It can refuse to write a receipt; it cannot take an empty post back down.
  • A correct fill doesn't make the bookkeeping correct. One of the later posts went out with exact bytes, but the queue refused to record it because the worklist had moved to a newer revision in the meantime. The guard behaved as designed and I didn't bypass it, so the queue has no receipt for that post.

More notes at hexisteme.github.io/notes.

title: Understanding the PHP Interpreter: Trends and Technical Insights
description:
The Core Engineering Challenge

PHP serves as a general-purpose scripting language designed specifically for web development, addressing the need for a fast, flexible, and pragmatic solution for powering websites from simple blogs to major platforms. Its architecture is built to handle dynamic content generation, making it an indispensable tool in modern web applications.

Architectural Blueprint & System Internals

The PHP interpreter is written in C and incorporates several key features, including an extensive test suite, a robust set of built-in functions, and support for various extensions. The architecture allows for efficient memory management and execution speed, crucial for high-performance web applications. The recent version, PHP 8.5.12, includes critical updates that fix two vulnerabilities, underscoring the importance of ongoing security in PHP's development.

Developer Experience (DX) & Implementation

Setting up PHP from source requires a few dependencies, including autoconf, bison, and re2c, along with optional libraries like libxml2 and libsqlite3 for a full-featured installation. The following commands outline the installation process:

On Ubuntu: 

sudo apt install -y pkg-config build-essential autoconf bison re2c libxml2-dev libsqlite3-dev

On Fedora: 

sudo dnf install re2c bison autoconf make ccache libxml2-devel sqlite-devel

On macOS: 

brew install autoconf bison re2c libiconv libxml2 sqlite

Once dependencies are installed, developers can build PHP using:

./buildconf
./configure --enable-debug
make -j4
make install

Technical Trade-offs & Performance Bounds

While PHP is powerful, it is not without its limitations. The community has discussed issues like segmentation faults in JIT compilation in PHP 8.1, highlighting potential risks when adopting newer versions without thorough testing. Additionally, the extensive test suite, while beneficial, can add complexity to the development cycle.

Community Pulse: What Developers Are Saying

Real-world discussions reveal ongoing concerns, such as Issue #7817 regarding random segmentation faults in specific PHP versions. This emphasizes the importance of community feedback in identifying and addressing critical bugs.

The Verdict

PHP remains a cornerstone of web development, with its latest release reinforcing its commitment to security and performance. However, developers should weigh the challenges of version upgrades and community concerns against the benefits of adopting PHP for their projects.

title: From Ansible to AI: Automating Network Diagnostics with sping
description:
Imagine this: a deployment just finished, something is slow, and you have 60 machines in an Ansible inventory.

You could SSH into each one. You could run ping 60 times. You could copy terminal output into a spreadsheet and spend the next half hour figuring out which hosts actually have a problem.

Or you could turn that inventory into a machine-readable network report, filter it in a few seconds, and hand the evidence to a script—or even an AI assistant.

That's one of the reasons I built sping, a small, open-source network diagnostics CLI written in Rust.

The live terminal view is nice. But the surprising part is what happens when you stop treating ping output as text.

The trick: JSON instead of lines of ping output

A regular monitoring session can stream newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON):

sping example.com --view json

Each line is a new measurement, with fields such as rttavg, losspct, jitter, quality, trend, and—when available—network context and diagnostic findings.

For a list of machines, there's a different mode:

sping --batch hosts.txt -c 10 --view json -o fleet.ndjson

One final JSON object per target. The targets are probed in parallel, with 10 probes each. The result isn't a screenshot or an unstructured log; it's data you can filter, compare, archive, and analyze.

Here are five things you can do with it.

1. Turn an Ansible inventory into a network health report

Ansible already knows which machines exist. Let's reuse that information.

If you have an INI or YAML inventory, use ansible-inventory to resolve it into a plain host list. This example prefers ansible_host when an alias points to a different address:

ansible-inventory -i inventory.ini --list \
  | jq -r '._meta.hostvars | to_entries[] | (.value.ansible_host // .key)' \
  | sort -u > hosts.txt

sping --batch hosts.txt -c 10 --view json -o fleet.ndjson

That's your inventory transformed into a network snapshot. No agent to install on every machine, no dashboard to deploy.

If you already maintain a text file containing one IP or hostname per line, skip the Ansible step and pass it straight to --batch.

2. Show only the machines that need attention

Now for the useful part. Rather than reading everything, ask jq for machines with no replies or at least 20% packet loss:

jq -r '
  select(.sent == 0 or .received == 0 or .loss_pct >= 20) |
  "\(.target_host): \(.received)/\(.sent) replies, \(.loss_pct)% loss"
' fleet.ndjson

Suddenly, a long inventory becomes a short list to investigate.

Want to make this part of a deployment preflight? Check TCP instead of ICMP, especially on networks where ping is filtered:

status=0
sping --batch hosts.txt --tcp 22 -c 3 --view json -o ssh.ndjson || status=$?
[ "$status" -le 1 ] || exit "$status"

jq -s -e --argjson expected "$(wc -l < hosts.txt)" '
  length == $expected and
  all(.[]; .sent == 3 and .received == 3 and (.refused // 0) == 0)
' ssh.ndjson

That last command exits unsuccessfully unless every expected host answered all three TCP attempts on port 22 without a refusal.

A TCP refusal is still a network response, but it doesn't mean SSH is accepting connections. And an open TCP port doesn't guarantee a successful login. This is a connectivity gate, not an application health check.

Operational detail: sping may skip hostnames that fail DNS resolution (and warn on stderr), so compare the number of JSON records to the expected host count. The preflight above does exactly that. In batch mode, sping can also return exit code 1 when a host receives no replies; that isn't the same as a CLI/runtime error (2).

3. Compare the network before and after a change

Ever changed a firewall rule, VPN, switch, or routing policy and then wondered which machines became worse?

Keep two snapshots:

# Before the change
sping --batch hosts.txt -c 10 --view json -o before.ndjson

# After the change
sping --batch hosts.txt -c 10 --view json -o after.ndjson

Then show the hosts whose packet-loss percentage increased:

jq -n -r \
  --slurpfile before before.ndjson \
  --slurpfile after after.ndjson '
  ($before | map({key: .target_host, value: .loss_pct}) | from_entries) as $old |
  $after[] |
  select($old[.target_host] != null and .loss_pct > $old[.target_host]) |
  "\(.target_host): \($old[.target_host])% -> \(.loss_pct)% loss"
'

You can do the same with average latency or jitter. A before/after report turns a vague "the network feels worse" into something you can investigate. It's an observation from the machine running sping, not proof of what caused the change.

4. Give an AI evidence instead of a screenshot

This is the part I find especially interesting.

Don't ask an AI to guess whether your infrastructure is healthy. Give it a small, structured report with actual measurements:

jq -s '[.[] | {
  host: .target_host,
  ip: .target_ip,
  sent, received, loss_pct, rtt_avg, jitter,
  quality, trend,
  diagnosis: (.diagnosis // [])
}]' fleet.ndjson > ai-report.json

Now paste ai-report.json into an AI assistant, or pass it to a local model, with a prompt like:

Group these hosts by symptoms. Prioritize which ones I should investigate first. Highlight total loss, intermittent loss, high latency, and consistent patterns. State what the data doesn't prove. Don't assume an ICMP timeout means the server is down. Suggest the next checks, based only on the supplied measurements.

That's the workflow I find exciting:

Ansible inventory → sping → NDJSON → deterministic filters → AI-assisted triage.

The AI isn't doing the network measurements. sping is. The model helps you organize and interpret the evidence.

If hostnames or internal IP addresses are sensitive, redact them or use a trusted local model before sharing the report.

5. Drill into one suspicious host with --diagnose

Batch mode answers which machines deserve a closer look. For a single problematic endpoint, sping 1.7.1 has an experimental follow-up mode:

sping example.com --diagnose -c 10 --view json > incident.ndjson

When the target stops answering, sping can try additional checks: alternative IPv4/IPv6 connectivity, TCP ports 443 and 80, and a bounded traceroute. Then you can inspect the additional findings:

jq -s '.[-1] | {
  target: .target_host,
  diagnosis: (.diagnosis // []),
  active_diagnosis: .active_diagnosis,
  gateway: .gateway,
  wan: .wan
}' incident.ndjson

The distinction matters: silence isn't proof of a firewall, and a successful TCP response isn't proof that the application is healthy. --diagnose reports observations, including checks it couldn't complete. It's experimental, single-target only, and intentionally separate from --batch.

The bigger idea

I didn't want sping to be just a prettier ping.

I wanted a tool that's useful when you're looking at a terminal and when nobody is looking at the terminal: in scripts, CI jobs, inventory audits, incident reports, or an AI-assisted troubleshooting workflow.

The terminal UI is for humans. The JSON is for everything you might build around it.

sping 1.7.1 runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows, is licensed under MIT, and doesn't require a cloud service.

  • GitHub repository
  • v1.7.1 release and binaries
  • JSON contract (v1)

I'd love to hear what you'd build with it. What network check do you still run manually that should really be a script?

title: VPS ou GPU para rodar IA? A conta em reais (Hostinger x RunPod, out/2026)
description:
Resposta rápida: se o seu projeto de IA chama uma API (OpenAI, ElevenLabs, Murf), você não precisa de GPU: uma VPS de ~R$ 46/mês roda o bot, o n8n e a fila. GPU só entra quando o modelo roda no seu servidor e não cabe em CPU, e aí o certo quase sempre é alugar por hora e desligar.

Transparência: este post tem links de afiliado. Se você assinar por eles, o Sinal Aberto pode receber uma comissão, sem custo extra para você.


Fluxograma do Sinal Aberto. Preços oficiais consultados em 22/10/2026.

Os números (páginas oficiais, 22/10/2026)

Dólar a R$ 5,02 + 3,5% de IOF no cartão (o spread do banco entra por cima).

Opção O que é Preço oficial Aprox. em R$ c/ IOF
Hostinger KVM 1 VPS 1 vCPU, 4 GB RAM US$ 6,49/mês* ~R$ 34/mês
Hostinger KVM 2 VPS 2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM US$ 8,79/mês* ~R$ 46/mês
Hostinger KVM 4 VPS 4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM US$ 12,99/mês* ~R$ 67/mês
RunPod RTX A5000 GPU 24 GB, por hora US$ 0,27/h ~R$ 1,40/h
RunPod RTX 3090 GPU 24 GB, por hora US$ 0,50/h ~R$ 2,60/h
RunPod RTX 4090 GPU 24 GB, por hora US$ 0,89/h ~R$ 4,62/h
RunPod A100 80 GB GPU 80 GB, por hora US$ 1,79/h ~R$ 9,30/h

*Preço promocional da Hostinger no plano de 24 meses, pago adiantado; o KVM 2 renova a US$ 14,99/mês (~R$ 78). A página da RunPod diz "atualizada em 8/10/2026"; disco de volume custa à parte (US$ 0,10/GB/mês com o pod ligado).


Com ~10 horas de RTX 4090 no mês você já pagou o equivalente a uma VPS KVM 2 inteira.

A conta que quase ninguém faz

  • GPU ligada 24/7 sai caro: uma RTX 4090 a US$ 0,89/h por 730 horas dá ~US$ 650/mês, perto de R$ 3.376 com IOF. Para servir um modelo o dia todo, compare com serverless antes.
  • GPU por algumas horas é barato: 40 horas de RTX A5000 no mês (gerar um lote de áudio, fazer fine-tune de um LoRA, transcrever um backlog com Whisper) ficam em ~US$ 10,80, uns R$ 56.
  • O que fica ligado 24/7 é a parte leve: bot de Telegram, n8n, API que chama a ElevenLabs, banco de dados. Isso é trabalho de VPS.

A arquitetura que recomendamos para quem está começando

  1. VPS pequena 24/7 para o que precisa estar sempre no ar: o app, a fila de tarefas e as chamadas de API.
  2. GPU por hora sob demanda só para o trabalho pesado, criada por script e desligada ao terminar (pod parado com volume ainda cobra o disco).
  3. API paga por uso para o que já existe pronto: voz (ElevenLabs/Murf), LLM, transcrição.

Checklist antes de assinar

  1. Seu modelo roda em CPU com quantização? Teste antes de alugar GPU.
  2. Quantas horas de GPU você usa por mês, de verdade? Anote por uma semana.
  3. Ponha o preço de renovação da VPS na conta, não só o promocional.
  4. Some 3,5% de IOF e o spread do seu cartão em tudo que é cobrado em dólar.

Alternativa de VPS barata com promoções sazonais: RackNerd (os preços mudam a cada promoção; confira na página antes de decidir).

Fontes: hostinger.com/vps-hosting e runpod.io/pricing, consultadas em 22/10/2026; IOF de 3,5% (Decreto 12.499/2025). Não rodamos benchmark próprio neste post: os números são de preço, não de desempenho. Texto produzido com assistência de IA.
