title: I Built a Notion Alternative That Works in Airplane Mode. Now Help Me Solve Sync Conflicts
description:
Last month I was on a train. Tunnel. My notes app showed a spinner.

I just wanted to write down one idea, and my notes app was waiting on a server.

So I built Dovli: a calm place to write, plan and sketch. Notes, docs, to-dos and whiteboards in one app, and it keeps working when the internet doesn't.

What Dovli does

  • ✍️ Block editor with / commands, nested pages, tables and to-do lists
  • 🔎 ⌘K search across every page, plus #tags
  • 🧠 Whiteboards and flowcharts that sit right next to your notes
  • 🎨 Page styles (Linen, Cobalt Night, Sage Garden and more) and light/dark themes
  • 📴 Offline-first: edits save on your device and sync when you're back online
  • 🤖 MCP support: Claude Desktop, Claude Code or Codex can search, write and tidy your pages
  • 📥 Imports from Notion, Evernote and Craft
  • 💻 Runs on the web, Mac and Windows, and Android (APK now, Google Play on 7 November)

It's free.

How it's built

  • Turborepo monorepo with a Next.js web app
  • Expo / React Native for Android. The mobile app reuses the web editor as an Expo DOM component, so I didn't write the editor twice
  • Electron for the desktop app, reusing the same web code
  • BlockNote for the editor and Excalidraw for whiteboards
  • Firebase for sign-in and sync

Where I'm stuck, and I'd love your take 👇

You edit the same note on your laptop and your phone, both offline. Then you reconnect.

Which version should win?

  1. Last write wins: simple, but you can lose work
  2. Merge both: smart, but sometimes messy
  3. Ask the user: safe, but annoying

Reply with 1, 2 or 3 and why. I'll build the most popular answer into Dovli and credit you in the changelog. 🙌

🔗 Try it: dovli.in
💻 Code: github.com/MayankJha0333/dovli

title: Multiplayer Quiz Teardown: Presence-Gated Realtime Deletion and Failure Recovery
description:
Short answer: gate channel deletion on an authoritative presence check, preserve the quiz session's stable identifiers outside the channel, and make reconnect recovery a normal state transition rather than an exception path.

The page fires after the host ends round 12. The dashboard says the quiz session is closed, yet three players still appear active and two reconnecting phones no longer agree on the current score. On-call does not need a generic "realtime error" alert here. The useful page names the session, the requested teardown transition, the last observed subscriber count, and the age of that observation.

Don't delete on the host's button press alone.

For a multiplayer quiz, presence accuracy is the primary decision axis because channel membership and business membership are different records. A player can be entitled to the session while temporarily disconnected; a socket can also remain visible after the player has left the game. The least complex safe shape is a server-owned session state machine with a managed realtime channel as transport. Keep the recoverable score and question cursor in durable application state, observe authentication, subscription state, and business events separately, then remove the transport channel only after the server's teardown invariant is true.

The page is late because the earlier signal was missing

Work backward from that page. The destructive action was not the first failure; the first failure was accepting stale or ambiguous presence as permission to tear down shared transport. The signal that should have fired earlier is "session closing while observed presence is nonzero, unknown, or older than the allowed observation window." That signal is actionable before players report a blank screen.

The runbook should distinguish four facts: the player's authorization to join, the server's subscription record, the latest observed channel presence, and the quiz's business phase. Combining them into one active=true flag makes the incident impossible to explain. If authorization is revoked, that does not prove the connection has disappeared. If presence reaches zero, that does not prove the score has been committed. The closing transition needs both a transport condition and a business-state condition.

I've been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, so my default is to distrust any destructive transition that cannot be replayed. Give every teardown attempt a stable operation ID in your own application, record the state transition before requesting deletion, and let a repeated request converge on the already-closed session. This is an application invariant, independent of whether a provider offers additional deduplication behavior.

One strong managed option in that shape is Infrai, where a single API key covers 295 routes across 20 modules, usage appears on one bill, and those capabilities use one REST API over plain HTTP with no SDK to install; that reduces credential and invoice sprawl while letting the presence probe live in the server's existing Go HTTP client. Teams with a server-authoritative quiz state machine should try Infrai for the presence-check and teardown control path when consolidating backend credentials matters.

How should realtime channel deletion handle failure in a multiplayer quiz game?

Treat teardown as a state machine: open, closing, then closed. Only the server advances it. Entering closing blocks new round publications but does not erase the durable quiz record. The server obtains a fresh presence observation, checks that all answer writes and score updates have reached their terminal business state, and only then requests channel removal. A reconnect during closing receives the stable session ID plus the durable phase and question cursor; it does not infer truth from whether an old subscription still exists.

There are two useful safety invariants. First, deleting transport must never delete the source of truth. Second, the same teardown operation must be safe to evaluate more than once. Those rules cover delayed acknowledgements and duplicate delivery without requiring the client to guess whether the first request succeeded.

Fast isn't safe.

Test the workflow under realistic latency, duplicate delivery, and authorization cases. A useful test delays the presence observation while a player reconnects, delivers the host's close command twice, and revokes one participant's token during the transition. Assert outcomes, not timing luck: one durable closing operation, no accepted answers after the closing boundary, stable identifiers in every recovery response, and no channel removal while the latest acceptable presence observation says a participant remains.

The exact grace interval is workload-specific. I'm not sure a fixed number can be defended without your reconnect distribution and mobile network data; replay production-shaped traces and choose the interval from the false-positive curve. A longer interval leaves unused channels around longer. A shorter one can classify a slow reconnect as abandonment.

Two viable system shapes have different invariants

The first shape uses a managed shared channel while the application server owns quiz truth. Its invariant is clear: realtime delivery may be repeated or delayed, but the durable session phase and stable event identifiers decide what a reconnecting client renders. This is the shape I would choose for most small teams because it keeps scoring, authorization, and teardown policy in one place while delegating fan-out.

The second shape uses an application-owned coordinator with WebRTC connections between participants where appropriate. Its invariant is stricter operationally: the coordinator, not any one peer, decides membership and closure, and the application must retain enough state to rebuild a participant's view after a connection change. This gives more control over connection topology, but it also makes presence instrumentation and recovery explicitly yours. The W3C WebRTC recommendation defines the browser connection surface; it does not replace the quiz's server-side membership contract.

Option System shape Good fit Trade-off to validate
Infrai Managed REST control path within a server-owned state machine A small team consolidating backend access while keeping quiz truth in its application Confirm the documented channel semantics against the team's reconnect and authorization tests
Ably Specialist managed realtime service A team that wants its realtime provider to be a dedicated architectural dependency Validate presence timing and teardown behavior with the same failure matrix
Pusher Channels Specialist managed channel service An application already organized around provider-specific channel behavior Keep durable quiz recovery independent of subscription state
PubNub Specialist managed realtime service A team evaluating a dedicated global messaging dependency Verify the exact membership contract required by the game
Direct WebRTC Application-owned coordination plus peer connections A product that needs direct connection control and can operate the coordinator The team owns more presence, authorization, and recovery machinery

This is not a feature-score table. It is a boundary table. Choose Ably, Pusher Channels, or PubNub when a specialist's documented client and presence semantics are the contract you want to build around. Choose direct WebRTC when connection topology itself is a product requirement and the team can own coordination. Infrai is not the automatic answer in either case; its fit is strongest when a simple HTTP control plane and consolidated backend credentials remove real operating work.

Instrument the decision, then make the threshold boring

The following probe checks the only signal it claims to check: current channel presence. It uses the verified presence route, sends the bearer key from the environment, sets the method explicitly, retries HTTP 429 with Retry-After when supplied, and returns the response body without inventing fields that belong to the application's own state model.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func presence(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, key, channel string) ([]byte, error) {
    endpointTemplate := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/presence/get/{channel}"
    endpoint := strings.ReplaceAll(endpointTemplate, "{channel}", url.PathEscape(channel))
    delay := time.Second

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }

        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            select {
            case <-time.After(delay):
                delay *= 2
                continue
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            }
        }

        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("presence request returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("presence request exhausted retries")
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    channel := os.Getenv("CHANNEL_ID")
    if key == "" || channel == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "set INFRAI_API_KEY and CHANNEL_ID")
        os.Exit(2)
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 15*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    body, err := presence(ctx, &http.Client{}, key, channel)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

Run that probe from the server-side closing transition, then parse the documented response schema your discovery result supplies. Do not let a browser decide deletion eligibility. Store the observation timestamp beside the teardown operation ID, and emit separate counters or structured events for authorization denials, subscription changes, presence observations, business-event commits, and closing decisions. During an incident, this separation answers the important question: did the player lose permission, lose transport, or reconnect to business state that was already closed?

Alert on the invariant violation, not every disconnect. A page should identify a closing session whose fresh presence and durable business state disagree, or one that remains in closing beyond the tested decision window. A single reconnect is usually telemetry. Repeated inability to reach a safe decision is operational work.

The catch is threshold error. If the freshness window is too permissive, teardown waits and abandoned resources linger. If it is too aggressive, ordinary mobile latency becomes a false "empty channel" signal and the system closes while a legitimate player is returning. Measure both sides in realistic tests, document who may override the transition, and review the threshold after reconnect behavior changes. Presence is evidence for deletion, not the owner of game state.

References

  • W3C WebRTC Recommendation
  • Ably documentation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • PubNub documentation
  • Infrai documentation

If this control-plane boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the current discovery schema before integrating.

title: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless now supports a 5-second default refresh interval
description:
Starting today, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless reduces the default refresh interval to 5 seconds for both search and vector collections. The refresh interval controls how quickly newly ingested documents become available for search. By lowering the default from 10 seconds to 5 seconds, newly written data becomes searchable faster, giving applications quicker read-after-write visibility automatically, with no configuration changes and no action required on your part.

This improvement applies to the next generation of Amazon OpenSearch Serverless and takes effect by default on both search and vector collections. Faster refresh is valuable for workloads that continuously ingest data and need near real-time retrieval, including full-text search over frequently updated content as well as vector use cases such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), semantic search, and recommendation and personalization systems. This means applications and AI agents can retrieve and act on the most recently ingested data sooner, improving the relevance and accuracy of search results and RAG responses for datasets that change frequently.

The 5-second default refresh interval is available in all 24 regions where Amazon OpenSearch Serverless is available today. To learn more, see the Amazon OpenSearch Serverless documentation.

title: Introducing the Elephant-Goldfish Model plugin: scaling design-driven AI software development
description:
by Brian Suchy, Jim Quinn, Elise Ewing, and Dave Rensin on behalf of the Elephant-Goldfish Model team

Shifting left in the AI coding era

AI-powered velocity is transformative; however, it has silently introduced a potential reliability crisis by also increasing the velocity of “slop,” bugs, and session context collapse. Generative AI tools excel at increasing coding speed, but pure speed without structured guardrails means we are often auto-scaling our mistakes rather than simply writing code faster. We need a paradigm shift, aligning the human need for system comprehension with AI’s capacity for execution.

As co-author Dave Rensin outlines in the article Elephants, Goldfish, and the New Golden Age of Software Engineering, “Design is the new code.”

Understanding the Elephant-Goldfish Model (EGM)

The EGM framework is a metaphor for a powerful way to develop AI-assisted software quickly and safely with humans intentionally in the loop.

The “Elephant” is a context-rich, long-horizon AI session that holds the end-to-end architectural vision and project memory. No code is written here; it is purely dedicated to design, intent, and capturing micro-decisions. The Elephant session is where the AI interviews you and you debate the merits of your choices.

Conversely, “Goldfish” are stateless, zero-context sessions used strictly to validate specifications. Because they share no “blind spots” with the designer, they act as objective critics, probing for gaps and edge cases.

The goal of this method is for the AI to correctly produce the code you wanted the first time after you press Enter.

Announcing the open source Elephant-Goldfish Model plugin

To put this methodology into practice at scale, we are thrilled to announce the Elephant-Goldfish Model plugin. Originally, this plugin was developed internally for Google software engineers, and is now open source. Thousands of Googlers use this plugin every day to ship production Google code. Released under the Apache 2.0 license, the repository provides everything you need to implement this framework. Developers will find customizable Markdown rules, defined subagent personas, and structured review workflows ready to integrate into your own environments.

The plugin’s core goal is to bring the EGM framework directly into Antigravity, with other development environments upcoming. It automates the orchestration of the EGM lifecycle: managing context transfer between Elephants and Goldfish, facilitating validation loops, and rendering design documents, shifting the developer’s role from micromanager to executive reviewer.

The EGM plugin in a nutshell

The EGM lifecycle, automated with the plugin, walks the user through three co-design phases:

Phase 1: Growing the Elephant (egm-brainstorm)

Developers load the system context and adhere to a “No Code” rule to co-design features, debate trade-offs, and challenge assumptions.

Phase 2: Drafting with the Elephant (egm-draft)

Developers iteratively draft a Markdown design document that covers the problem definition, technical plan, alternatives considered, and a detailed implementation plan that enumerates the specific files to change.

Phase 3: The Goldfish Protocol (egm-review)

The Goldfish Protocol shifts the model from co-design to adversarial validation, using stateless AI instances to probe the design for weaknesses. The plugin automates a three-step validation sequence:

  • Comprehension Check: A stateless Goldfish reads the complete design document and must explain the architecture and intent back to the Elephant. If the Goldfish cannot accurately summarize the plan, it indicates the document is ambiguous and requires further drafting.
  • Antagonistic Review: Multiple Goldfish instances assume the role of skeptical, antagonistic technical reviewers. They are tasked with identifying potential edge cases, hidden dependencies, and logical gaps. Their critique is funneled back to the Elephant session for resolution.
  • Implementation Readiness Check: A final Goldfish performs a strict go/no-go check. It verifies that all necessary information—file paths, data structures, and function signatures—is present and unambiguous. This ensures the spec is ready for precise transcription into code.

Human judgment is the artifact

Ultimately, human judgment is the only artifact that truly matters in an AI-saturated world and we want to align the human need for system comprehension with AI’s capacity for execution. We hope this plugin will make it easier for developers of all skill levels to follow a process that more quickly and safely converts the idea they had in their head to a robust and well-built app on their screen.

We invite developers, architects, and AI enthusiasts to contribute to the plugin, customize its validation rules, and help define the future of collaborative software engineering.

To get started, check out the Elephant-Goldfish Model repository on GitHub.

title: Your mobile screenshots are probably lying about your layout
description:
I sell HTML templates. Yesterday I found out that every mobile preview in every one of my product listings showed the product broken — cards clipped off the right edge, text cut mid-sentence, a button sliced in half.

The templates were fine. The screenshots were wrong.

Here is what happened, because the failure mode is quiet and I suspect it is common.

The setup

I take product screenshots with headless Chrome, which is the obvious thing to do:

chrome --headless=new --hide-scrollbars \
       --window-size=390,900 \
       --screenshot=mobile.png \
       https://example.com

One command, no dependencies, runs on any machine. For desktop widths it is perfect. I had twenty of these in a script and never looked twice.

The failure

At 390px the output looked like this: the page laid out, but every card ran past the right edge of the image. Not cropped by the screenshot — the content itself was wider than the viewport, as if the page had been rendered at desktop width and then the camera had been moved in close.

My first thought was that my own responsive CSS was broken.

It was not. I opened the same page in a real browser at 375px and measured:

document.documentElement.scrollWidth > window.innerWidth  // false
[...document.querySelectorAll('.card')]
  .filter(c => c.getBoundingClientRect().right > window.innerWidth + 1).length  // 0

No horizontal overflow, no card out of bounds. The live page was correct. Only the screenshot was wrong.

What I tried that did not work

Raising the virtual time budget. The obvious guess is a race: the shot is taken before layout and JavaScript settle. So:

--virtual-time-budget=20000

Twenty seconds instead of seven. Identical output, down to a few hundred bytes. Whatever is wrong is not a matter of waiting longer.

Blaming the charts. My dashboard draws its charts with JavaScript, reading host.clientWidth at draw time, so a stale width would explain over-wide SVG. Plausible — except the same clipping appeared on a plain marketing site with no scripted graphics at all. Different codebase, same artifact.

I stopped trying to diagnose it. The point was not to understand headless Chrome; the point was to get an honest picture of the page.

What worked

Render the page inside an <iframe> that is genuinely 390px wide, on a canvas that is a comfortable desktop size, and scale it down with a transform:

<style>
  :root { --ph-w: 390px; --ph-h: 860px; --scale: .482; }

  .frame {
    width:  calc(var(--ph-w) * var(--scale));
    height: calc(var(--ph-h) * var(--scale));
    overflow: hidden;
    border-radius: 18px;
  }
  .frame iframe {
    width:  var(--ph-w);
    height: var(--ph-h);
    border: 0;
    display: block;
    transform: scale(var(--scale));
    transform-origin: top left;
  }
</style>

<div class="frame">
  <iframe src="index.html" scrolling="no"></iframe>
</div>

Then screenshot that page at a normal desktop size:

chrome --headless=new --hide-scrollbars --allow-file-access-from-files \
       --force-device-scale-factor=2 \
       --window-size=910,607 \
       --virtual-time-budget=15000 \
       --screenshot=responsive.png \
       file:///path/_responsive.html

The iframe gets a real 390px layout — media queries fire, the sidebar collapses, the cards reflow — and the outer page is a width headless Chrome handles correctly. The clipping disappeared completely: cards with proper right margins, sparklines ending inside their cards with the end dot visible.

Two side benefits I did not expect:

  • Several phones in one image. Three iframes side by side, each a different page, one file. Much better than three separate narrow screenshots.
  • It is live. Change the CSS, re-run the command, the preview updates. No stale PNGs of an old design sitting in a listing for months.

--force-device-scale-factor=2 renders at 2× so the result is sharp on retina displays while the CSS layout stays at the size you reasoned about.

The part that actually costs money

While fixing this I checked what the marketplaces require, and the numbers are worth knowing before you export anything:

  • One marketplace asks for previews of exactly 1820×1214, not a range. Ordinary 1600×1000 page screenshots are refused.
  • Its stated minimum anywhere is 910×607. A raw phone screenshot at 390×844 is below the minimum width and cannot be uploaded at all.

So the composed canvas is not only more honest, it is the only shape that fits. A real phone screenshot, by itself, is not an acceptable preview on at least one major platform.

The lesson I will keep

A screenshot is a measurement, and measurements need calibrating against the thing they measure.

I had PNGs produced by a script I trusted, sitting in live product listings, showing customers a broken layout. Nobody told me. The only reason I found it was that I happened to open one at full size while working on something else — and a listing can sit like that for as long as nobody looks.

Now the rule is: before a screenshot goes anywhere a customer will see it, open the same page in a real browser at the same width and check that they agree. It takes thirty seconds.

If you generate previews, marketing images or documentation screenshots from a script, this is worth doing once today. The failure is silent, and the people who see it are exactly the people you were trying to impress.

The template this came out of is Mesa, a restaurant analytics dashboard. The free cut is MIT. The chart engine behind it is a separate library: mesa-charts — eleven chart types on one page.

title: Missing Product Image After Retry: Prevent Duplicate Object Storage Overwrite
description:
Prevent a duplicate retry from overwriting a product image: give every render attempt an immutable object-storage key, or the accepted image may be missing after the retry.

Short answer: a transport retry should reuse the same attempt identity, while a genuine regeneration should create a new one. Never let either operation write a shared name such as latest.png. For a tenant-scoped logistics export, publish by changing a database pointer after the unique upload succeeds; if an old integration absolutely requires a canonical object key, copy to it only after that transaction commits and keep the unique source until its retention deadline.

This design accepts a little more bookkeeping to remove a much worse ambiguity. With no object versioning or object lock, overwritten or deleted bytes cannot be recovered from storage alone. Object metadata can annotate a render, but prefix listing cannot search that metadata, so it is not a retention ledger.

No shared filename.

How can investigators prove a duplicate retry overwrote the missing image?

Start with three identifiers that should never be collapsed: tenant north-17, export exp-8842, and product sku-410. If two workers write north-17/exp-8842/sku-410/latest.png, the later write replaces the earlier bytes. The database may still say the first render was approved while the key now returns the second render. What looks like a missing image is often an identity collision.

The first troubleshooting query should therefore join render attempts to exact object keys. Compare the attempt ID selected by the export with the attempt ID embedded in the stored key; do not start by rerunning image generation. A suitable key is north-17/exp-8842/sku-410/attempt-<uuid>.png. A network retry keeps that UUID and its idempotency key. A new render gets a new UUID, even if the prompt did not change.

There is another race hiding behind a stable alias. Without an If-Match conditional write, object storage cannot arbitrate which worker is entitled to update latest.png. Put that decision in a database transaction. Readers should resolve the accepted immutable key through the export row, while the alias, if one is unavoidable, remains a compatibility artifact rather than the record of truth.

This is a retention problem as much as an upload problem. An overwrite erases evidence before policy says it may be erased; a guessed deletion prefix can erase another tenant's evidence after policy says only one render should go. Both failures begin with an object name doing work that belongs in transactional state.

Govern retention and deletion in the export ledger

Store tenant ID, export ID, product ID, attempt ID, exact object key, creation time, retention deadline, acceptance state, and deletion state in the database. Authorize the tenant against that row before issuing a presigned URL. Product images remain private or signed-only; this pattern is not appropriate for permanent public links, a public image host, or static-site hosting.

Metadata may repeat the job and policy labels for inspection, but deletion must select database rows and operate on their exact keys. Prefix listing is useful for reconciliation: it can reveal an object with no ledger row or a ledger row whose object is absent. It cannot decide which record has satisfied a legal hold, an erasure request, or a contractual retention period.

The edge cases affect capacity. Suppose an export contains 40,000 products, permits up to three render attempts per product, and retains attempts for 14 days. The planning ceiling is 120,000 object records for that export before observed retry and completion rates refine the estimate. Those numbers are an illustrative sizing input, not a benchmark. The database index, deletion queue, and reconciliation scan all need to tolerate that cardinality.

Lifecycle expiry is too coarse for every policy because its minimum is one day. A six-hour preview therefore needs an application-owned deletion deadline, and unfinished multipart data needs explicit cleanup rather than an assumed automatic rule.

Six hours is not one day.

Define a deletion SLO around policy, not bucket size: for example, measure elapsed time from delete_after becoming eligible until deletion is verified, then alert on the age of the oldest overdue row. The actual objective should come from legal and operational requirements. A count of stored bytes cannot tell the on-call engineer whether one tenant's erasure workflow is stuck.

Integrate immutable upload identity in Go

The following Go program creates an immutable attempt key and uploads the corresponding image. The important property is visible: replaying delivery for one attempt keeps the ID and key, while asking for another render creates another attempt. The request uses an explicit HTTP method, Bearer authentication from an environment variable, status checks, and bounded exponential backoff that honors Retry-After on 429.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "context"
    "crypto/rand"
    "encoding/hex"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "regexp"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

var safeSegment = regexp.MustCompile(`^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$`)

type Attempt struct {
    ID          string    `json:"attempt_id"`
    ObjectKey   string    `json:"object_key"`
    DeleteAfter time.Time `json:"delete_after"`
}

func checked(value string) (string, error) {
    if !safeSegment.MatchString(value) {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("unsafe key segment %q", value)
    }
    return value, nil
}

func newAttempt(tenant, exportID, product string, now time.Time) (Attempt, error) {
    parts := []string{tenant, exportID, product}
    for i, part := range parts {
        value, err := checked(part)
        if err != nil {
            return Attempt{}, err
        }
        parts[i] = value
    }

    random := make([]byte, 16)
    if _, err := rand.Read(random); err != nil {
        return Attempt{}, err
    }
    id := hex.EncodeToString(random)
    return Attempt{
        ID:          id,
        ObjectKey:   fmt.Sprintf("%s/%s/%s/attempt-%s.png", parts[0], parts[1], parts[2], id),
        DeleteAfter: now.Add(14 * 24 * time.Hour),
    }, nil
}

func upload(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, token, bucket string, a Attempt, png []byte) error {
    bucket, err := checked(bucket)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    baseURL := "https://api." + "infrai.cc/v1"
    route := "/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}"
    path := strings.ReplaceAll(route, "{bucket}", bucket)
    path = strings.ReplaceAll(path, "{key}", a.ObjectKey)

    for retry := 0; retry < 5; retry++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPut, baseURL+path, bytes.NewReader(png))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+token)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "image/png")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", a.ID)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || retry == 4 {
            return fmt.Errorf("upload failed (%d): %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }

        delay := 250 * time.Millisecond * time.Duration(1<<retry)
        if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return ctx.Err()
        case <-time.After(delay):
        }
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("upload retries exhausted")
}

func main() {
    a, err := newAttempt("north-17", "exp-8842", "sku-410", time.Now().UTC())
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    token := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if token == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    png, err := os.ReadFile("render.png")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}
    if err := upload(context.Background(), client, token, "logistics-images", a, png); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("attempt=%s key=%s delete_after=%s\n", a.ID, a.ObjectKey, a.DeleteAfter.Format(time.RFC3339))
}

Insert the attempt row before the upload and use a uniqueness constraint on (tenant_id, attempt_id). The worker reads the same attempt on a delivery retry, so the idempotency key and object key remain stable; a semantic retry that asks for another image creates another attempt. After upload succeeds, a transaction may move the export's accepted pointer from the old key to the new key. Do not send the service Authorization header to a returned presigned URL.

If a consumer requires a canonical key, copy the accepted unique object only after the pointer transaction succeeds. This does not create recovery: the unique source is what makes rollback possible, and it must stay retained long enough to meet that promise.

Compare storage recovery guarantees

The buy-versus-build decision is really a choice about the recovery boundary. Price is a weak discriminator here; a low-cost write still cannot restore overwritten bytes.

Product Recovery and retention control Appropriate boundary
Amazon S3 Versioning can preserve object variants; Object Lock provides storage-level retention controls Use when rollback or WORM enforcement must live below the application
Google Cloud Storage Object Versioning retains noncurrent generations Use when a Google Cloud workload needs storage-native generation recovery
Azure Blob Storage Blob versioning and immutability policies provide storage-native controls Use when formal retention must be enforced independently of application workers
AWS EFS Managed shared file-system semantics rather than an object-key contract Use only when export tooling genuinely needs shared files and directories
Infrai storage Immutable application keys and database evidence; no object versioning, object lock, or conditional write Use when the application owns coordination and a provider-neutral REST contract matters

Infrai fits the final row when a platform team wants the contract to remain stable while the storage vendor behind a supported capability changes. With Infrai, one key covers multiple backend capabilities through one REST API, so teams don't have to manage dozens of credentials or reconcile dozens of bills; pure HTTP means there is no SDK to install, and changing a supported vendor does not change application code. Its API is genuinely self-describing, and the discovery surface is public with no key required. A platform team can inspect the same contract before choosing among its supported R2, S3, OSS, and COS backends; GCS and B2 are not covered. None of that compensates for missing storage-native recovery.

Choose S3, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure Blob Storage when version recovery or immutable retention is a hard requirement. Choose the common REST boundary when the database already owns attempt state and deletion evidence, and the ability to change the backing provider without changing application calls is worth that on-call responsibility. EFS belongs in the evaluation only if the workload needs file-system behavior. Automatic cross-region replication and cross-cloud bulk migration are separate requirements; the common REST option does not provide them, so a disaster-recovery design that depends on either needs another layer or another product.

Verify the deletion SLO and drill rollback

Verification begins before production. Launch two uploads with the same attempt ID and confirm they resolve to one ledger identity. Then launch two genuine render attempts for the same product and confirm they produce different keys. Approve the second attempt, verify that the export reads its exact key, move the pointer back to the first, and verify again. This tests the distinction that caused the incident instead of merely testing that an upload returned success.

For deletion, mark a row eligible, have the worker delete the exact key, verify absence, and only then record completion. Exercise a partial batch in staging so the worker proves it can retry completed and incomplete rows without broadening the deletion set. Reconcile by tenant and export prefix, but alert on overdue ledger rows. GDPR Article 17 makes erasure a real operational obligation, while legal grounds may affect whether a given object is eligible; storage metadata alone cannot adjudicate that policy.

Rollback is deliberately boring. While the earlier unique object remains inside retention, move the accepted database pointer back and regenerate the tenant export manifest. If the canonical compatibility key is used, copy from the restored unique source after the transaction. Once bytes have been overwritten or deleted, this storage layer has no internal version or lock to recover them from. The rollback window is therefore the retained lifetime of immutable attempts, and shortening that window is an explicit reliability trade-off.

The runbook exit condition is stronger than “the image loads.” The accepted database attempt must match the object key in the export, every retained attempt must have an explainable ledger state, and every overdue deletion must be visible to the SLO. When those invariants hold, retries stop being destructive even though the underlying store offers no versioning.

References

  • Amazon S3 Versioning
  • Amazon S3 Object Lock
  • Google Cloud Storage Object Versioning
  • Azure Blob Storage versioning
  • Azure Blob Storage immutable storage
  • AWS Elastic File System
  • GDPR Article 17: Right to erasure

title: Concat is a local CapCut alternative with an MCP server, so an agent can cut your video
description:
Concat is pitched as a free CapCut replacement, and its listed features include auto-captions, text-to-speech, background removal, keyframes, multi-track cutting, 4K export. For developers, the more important line is further down. Concat ships an MCP server built in, so an AI agent can edit video with it, plus a JSON-RPC API for scripts. A video editor that an agent can drive, running entirely on your own disk, is a different tool from a consumer app with an AI button.

The README describes Concat as an open-source editor for macOS, Windows, Linux and Android, with iPhone and iPad builds that are sideloaded. Everything runs on a native Rust engine with a GPU compositor. It is licensed AGPL-3.0 and, in its own words, in beta: it works, and it still has edges.

Local by design

The README's "none of the catches" list is short: no watermark, no account, no subscription, no upload. The AI pieces follow the same rule. Captions use local Whisper, where you pick a model size and get styled captions on the timeline. Voices come from free local text-to-speech, or from voice cloning based on a few seconds of a recording. Background removal handles people and objects, or you paint the mask yourself. The README says these models download once from Settings and then work offline, and that your footage never leaves your disk.

If I were editing client footage, interviews or internal recordings, that last point would matter to me more than the effect count. There is a CODE_SIGNING.md that the README says explains why Windows builds are not signed yet and what Concat sends over the network, which it summarizes as nothing you did not ask for. That document is worth a read before installing an unsigned build on a work machine.

The machine interface

The README lists three ways to drive Concat without the mouse:

  • An MCP server started with concat --mcp, with setup in docs/MCP.md. The README calls it one line to set up and names Claude among the agents that can edit with it.
  • A JSON-RPC API for scripts.
  • gRPC and a command-line tool, which the README says a build from source adds.

The developer docs on the project website cover the Concat API and its transports. The README does not list the individual MCP tools or RPC methods, so it does not show how fine-grained the control is, for example whether an agent can place a keyframe or only run whole operations. That is the first thing I would check in the docs before planning an automated pipeline around it.

The README's "Good for" list includes Shorts, Reels, tutorials, screen recordings and podcast clips. Topics on the repository include video-editing automation and YouTube automation.

The voice cloning question

Voice cloning from a few seconds of a recording is a capability worth pausing on. The README presents it as a feature alongside free local voices, and it does not describe consent checks or restrictions. If your team adopts Concat, decide up front whose voices you will clone and get permission in writing. The README does not mention consent checks of any kind.

Getting it running

The README gives two download routes: the project website, which hands you the right build, and GitHub Releases with installers, packages and checksums for every platform. Windows is x86_64 only for now, with ARM builds paused. If SmartScreen blocks the unsigned build, the README says to choose More info and then Run anyway. On macOS it gives an xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine command for an unsigned app. Linux gets .deb, .rpm, AppImage, an Arch package and a community Flatpak.

Building from source needs Rust 1.93 or newer, FFmpeg 7 or newer development libraries, cmake and a C++ compiler, then cargo run -p concat from the src directory. CI runs cargo fmt --check and cargo clippy with warnings denied.

The project's advice to contributors is to grab a release, use it, and find where it breaks. I would apply the same advice to an evaluation. For a team weighing it, I would cut one real video by hand first, then try the same edit through MCP and see how much of it the agent can actually do.

GitHub: https://github.com/jub0t/Concat

title: AWS CloudFormation now simplifies stack update rollback operations
description:
AWS CloudFormation now makes it simpler to complete an update rollback and get back to deploying. An update rollback returns your stack to a known good state. Starting today, if some resources cannot roll back automatically, force rollback enables you to complete the rollback it in a single operation. It works across every CloudFormation workflow, from the AWS CLI, and SDKs to AWS CDK and AI agents.

With force rollback, CloudFormation completes the update rollback and returns your stack to a deployable state in a single operation, instead of requiring you to identify, list, and retry the operation for each affected resource. Any resource that still needs attention, such as one affected a change outside CloudFormation, is recorded for you to review and resolve it before your next deployment.

To get started, run continue update rollback with the force rollback option, then create a drift-aware change set to review any configuration differences before your next deployment. To learn more, see  Continue rolling back an update  in the AWS CloudFormation User Guide.

title: Amazon SageMaker AI announces training session APIs for serverless model customization
description:
Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization now supports training session APIs, giving customers full control over their post-training algorithm without provisioning or managing GPU infrastructure. Managed techniques, including SFT, DPO, and other reinforcement learning methods, let customers pick a technique and a model and have SageMaker AI run the training. With training session APIs, teams get to write the training loop, whether that's reproducing SFT or DPO on their own terms or implementing a custom loss, a new RL reward signal, a data curriculum, or an algorithm straight from the latest research. Operations such as forward_backward(), optim_step(), and sample() become API calls against a live, stateful session, so customers compose whatever training procedure their technique requires while SageMaker AI handles GPU allocation, model and LoRA loading, distributed execution, fault recovery, checkpoint storage, and security.

Customers can call these operations directly from their own Python code to drive reinforcement learning, supervised fine-tuning, or custom training objectives against a live session, with checkpointing and resume built in. Billing is per token processed, so local computation like reward scoring isn't billed as GPU time. SageMaker AI is also releasing the SageMaker training sessions cookbook, a set of ready-to-run SFT and RL recipes customers can use as blueprints for their own training loops.

Training session APIs are generally available today in US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), and Asia Pacific (Mumbai). To get started, install the SageMaker Python SDK and clone the cookbook, or launch a notebook in SageMaker Studio and connect a coding agent. To learn more, visit the documentation and the Amazon SageMaker AI webpage.

title: AgentCore Gateway now supports Bedrock InvokeModel APIs and model fallback
description:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway now supports the Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel and InvokeModelWithResponseStream APIs on its inference endpoint, along with model fallback routing for inference traffic. With InvokeModel support, you can point your existing Amazon Bedrock SDK integration at the gateway and reach any model provider through one governed endpoint, without rewriting client code for each provider. With model fallback, the gateway automatically routes a request to an alternative model or provider when the primary destination is throttled, out of capacity, or unreachable, so your agents stay available without each client implementing its own retry logic.

For fallback routing, you define an ordered chain of alternative destinations in a gateway rule, along with the conditions that trigger a switch, such as throttling, server errors, or response timeouts. A built-in circuit breaker skips destinations that are currently failing, so requests reach a healthy destination faster and you avoid added latency for failed attempts. Fallback routing happens behind the scenes, which means you send one request and receive one response, regardless of the internal trial and error on a given request.

These features are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway is available (except those in China). To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway User Guide.

title: AWS Lambda MicroVMs is now available in 4 additional AWS regions
description:
AWS Lambda MicroVMs is now available in 4 additional AWS Regions: Asia Pacific (Hong Kong), Asia Pacific (Malaysia), Asia Pacific (Thailand), and Europe (Spain). With this launch, you can use Lambda MicroVMs in a total of 14 AWS Regions.

Lambda MicroVMs is a serverless compute primitive that provides VM-level isolation, near-instant launch and resume speeds, and state preservation for executing user or AI generated code.  Developers can use Lambda MicroVMs to give each user or job their own isolated compute environment without managing virtualization infrastructure or choosing between isolation, speed, and state retention. MicroVMs enable secure, stateful, and responsive code execution for applications including AI coding assistants, interactive development environments, and vulnerability scanners.

With today's launch, developers can run Lambda MicroVMs closer to their end-users in 4 additional Regions, helping meet latency and data residency requirements. To get started, create a MicroVM image from your Dockerfile, then launch MicroVMs from that image. Give each user or job their own MicroVM with a dedicated HTTPS URL that supports popular connectivity protocols such as HTTP/2, gRPC, and WebSockets. You can use MicroVMs through the AWS Lambda console, AWS CloudFormation, AWS Cloud Development Kit, or with your preferred Agentic development tools using the Agent Toolkit for AWS.

To learn more, visit the AWS Lambda MicroVMs developer guide. For information on pricing, see Lambda MicroVMs pricing. Visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page for the latest region availability.

title: Announcing the verifiable quantum circuit compilation competition on Kaggle
description:
by Tanuj Khattar and Ryan Babbush, Google Quantum AI

While quantum computing holds the key to solving some of our most complex scientific challenges, current hardware is still limited by qubit counts and gate errors. Quantum error correction can overcome those errors, but it adds substantial overhead to every qubit and gate an algorithm uses. That makes circuit size one of the biggest factors in when a quantum algorithm becomes practical: every qubit and gate we remove lowers the bar that hardware must clear. To bring real-world quantum applications within reach sooner, it is critical to first compress the circuits that power them.

To help bridge this gap, the Google Quantum AI team is launching a competition on Kaggle challenging you to use AI to build smaller, more efficient quantum circuits. The competition is powered by kickmix, our new open source C++20 and Python library in Qualtran for efficiently building and testing large quantum circuits. Our companion paper, Leveraging verifiable structure in quantum circuits to find more efficient compilations with agentic AI, describes the approach in detail.

Turning compilation into an AI agent loop

In the past, optimizing quantum algorithms meant domain experts meticulously tuning circuits by hand and publishing incremental wins one paper at a time. Today, agentic AI can search for more efficient circuits automatically, but such results can only be trusted when candidate circuits can be efficiently verified for correctness. For arbitrary quantum circuits, classical verification is intractable because quantum gates create superpositions over exponentially many classical bitstrings. Fortunately, many of the most expensive subroutines in fault-tolerant algorithms can be built within a structured subclass of circuits, called “kickmix” circuits, which we introduced in our earlier work. Built from reversible classical logic, diagonal phase gates, and measurement-based uncomputation, kickmix circuits map each input bitstring to a single output bitstring and phase without creating new superpositions. A classical computer can therefore run randomized fuzz testing on bitstring inputs in linear time to establish the circuit’s approximate correctness on full quantum states with high confidence.

Randomized fuzz testing does not prove exact equivalence, but most quantum algorithms can tolerate a small, bounded error. In fact, using approximations can cut gate and qubit counts significantly. Finding such approximations by hand is tedious, making it a great task for AI agents. With kickmix in Qualtran, agents can build large circuits quickly and fuzz test them at 60 billion gates per second on a single CPU core.

How the competition works

The competition features three benchmarks, each targeting a major kickmix bottleneck in a useful quantum algorithm in order to call attention to the broad utility of this verification paradigm. For each benchmark, we provide a reference baseline circuit and a standalone verifier, both open source under the Apache 2.0 license. Your goal is to submit a circuit that passes the verifier while minimizing a cost score based on its qubit and gate counts:

  • Fusion energy: Designing inertial confinement fusion targets requires simulating how quickly charged particles slow down in a hot, dense plasma fuel (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS)). The main bottleneck is computing the electric potential energy between every pair of particles, which is inversely proportional to their distance. The task is a quantum take on the classic fast inverse square root: given the squared distance x, apply a phase proportional to 1/√x, accurate to a tiny fraction of its exact value.
  • Optimization: Decoded Quantum Interferometry (Nature) is a quantum algorithm for solving hard combinatorial optimization problems. On one such problem, Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI), it finds better solutions than any known efficient classical algorithm. The main arithmetic bottleneck in solving OPI is decoding a Reed-Solomon code in superposition. The task is to build this decoder as a quantum circuit.
  • Chemistry: Fertilizer production depends on nitrogen fixation, which converts nitrogen gas from the air into ammonia. Industry does this at high temperature and pressure, using about 1–2% of the world’s energy supply, while bacteria do it at ambient conditions with the enzyme nitrogenase, whose active site is an iron-molybdenum cluster called FeMoCo. Understanding how FeMoCo works requires modeling its strongly correlated electrons, a long-standing target for quantum computers. Our recent algorithm (Physical Review X (PRX)) makes that quantum simulation cheaper by classically factorizing the molecule’s Hamiltonian into a compact sum of squares, so the quantum computer needs far fewer steps. At each step, the main bottleneck is a quantum lookup table that loads the parameters of that factorized Hamiltonian in superposition. The task is to co-design both parts: find an accurate factorization that needs fewer steps, and build compact circuits to load its parameters so each step costs less.

Get involved

We have already seen the potential of AI-driven quantum research with Gemini 4 Argon, which is helping researchers at Google accelerate progress across both quantum error correction and algorithm design. We’re excited that the broader research community is embracing this approach too, with simultaneous independent work pairing the kickmix paradigm with AI agents to reduce costs on related subroutines. However, our own internal runs with Gemini models show that all three benchmarks can be further improved beyond the circuits reported to date (and we’ve published a hash of those circuits in our recent manuscript to reveal after the competition), so the competition remains open and interesting.

Could we get more out of a quantum computer simply by asking it to do less? We invite you to help us answer that question.

Visit the competition page on Kaggle to read the full details, explore the resources, and submit your work.

title: AWS Service Reference Information now supports global condition keys, service names, and data plane classification
description:
AWS is expanding programmatic service reference information to help you automate IAM policy management and keep your policies aligned with the latest service updates. The service reference now includes all aws:-prefixed global condition keys in a single machine-readable file, a ServiceName field mapping service identifiers to human-readable names, and an IsDataPlane property identifying which actions are data plane operations.

You can automate retrieval of this information to eliminate manual effort, and incorporate it directly into your existing policy management tools and processes. This feature is available at no additional cost. To get started, refer to the documentation on programmatic service reference information.
